entries.title: Abolition
entries.summary: Abolition is a political vision, a structural analysis of oppression, and a practical organizing strategy working towards a society that addresses harm without relying on prisons, police, military, or other violent systems.
entries.body:
Today, more people are discussing and contemplating prison abolition than ever before. Decades of collective organizing have brought us to this moment: Some are newly aware that prisons, policing, and the criminal punishment system in general are racist, oppressive, and ineffective.

Prison industrial complex abolition is a political vision, a structural analysis of oppression, and a practical organizing strategy. While some people might think of abolition as primarily a negative project—“Let’s tear everything down tomorrow and hope for the best”—prison industrial complex abolition is a vision of a restructured society in a world where we have everything we need: food, shelter, education, health, art, beauty, clean water, and more. These things are foundational to our personal and community safety.

Every vision is also a map. As freedom fighter Kwame Ture taught us, “When you see people call themselves revolutionary always talking about destroying, destroying, destroying but never talking about building or creating, they’re not revolutionary. They do not understand the first thing about revolution. It’s creating.” Prison industrial complex abolition is a positive project that focuses, in part, on building a society where it is possible to address harm without relying on structural forms of oppression or the violent systems that increase it.

An abolitionist journey ignites other questions capable of meaningful and transformative pathways: What work do prisons and policing actually do? Most people assume that incarceration helps to reduce violence and crime, thinking: “The criminal punishment system might be racist, sexist, classist, ableist, and unfair, but it at least keeps me safe from violence and crime.”

Facts and history tell a different story: Increasing rates of incarceration have a minimal impact on crime rates. Research and common sense suggest that economic precarity is correlated with higher crime rates. Moreover, crime and harm are not synonymous. All that is criminalized isn’t harmful, and all harm isn’t necessarily criminalized. For example, wage theft by employers isn’t generally criminalized, but it is definitely harmful.

Even if the criminal punishment system were free of racism, classism, sexism, and other isms, it would not be capable of effectively addressing harm. For example, if we want to reduce (or end) sexual and gendered violence, putting a few perpetrators in prison does little to stop the many other perpetrators. It does nothing to change a culture that makes this harm imaginable, to hold the individual perpetrator accountable, to support their transformation, or to meet the needs of the survivors.

A Black, Indigenous, and people of color survivor-led transformative justice movement has emerged in the past two decades to offer a different vision for ending violence and transforming our communities.

A world without harm isn’t possible and isn’t what an abolitionist vision purports to achieve. Rather, abolitionist politics and practice contend that disposing of people, by locking them away in jails and prisons, does nothing significant to prevent, reduce, or transform harm in the aggregate. It rarely, if ever, encourages people to take accountability for their actions, instead delegating responsibility to a third party—one that has been built to hide social and political failures. An abolitionist imagination takes us along a different path.

None of us has all of the answers, or we would have ended oppression already. But if we keep building the world we want, trying new things, and learning from our mistakes, new possibilities emerge.

Here’s how to begin.

First, when we set about trying to transform society, we must remember that we ourselves will also need to transform. Our imagination of what a different world can be is limited. We are deeply entangled in the very systems we are organizing to change. White supremacy, misogyny, ableism, classism, homophobia, and transphobia exist everywhere. We have all so thoroughly internalized these logics of oppression that if oppression were to end tomorrow, we would be likely to reproduce previous structures. Being intentionally in relation to one another, a part of a collective, helps to not only imagine new worlds but also to imagine ourselves differently. Join some of the many organizations, faith groups, and ad hoc collectives that are working to learn and unlearn—for example, what it feels like to actually be safe or those that are naming and challenging white supremacy and racial capitalism.

Second, we must imagine and experiment with new collective structures that enable us to take more principled action, such as embracing collective responsibility to resolve conflicts. We can learn lessons from revolutionary movements, like Brazil’s Landless Workers Movement, that have noted that when we create social structures that are less hierarchical and more transparent, we reduce violence and harms.

Third, we must simultaneously engage in strategies that reduce contact between people and the criminal legal system. Abolitionists regularly engage in organizing campaigns and mutual aid efforts that move us closer to our goals. We must remember that the goal is not to create a gentler prison and policing system because, as I have noted, a gentler prison and policing system cannot adequately address harm. Instead, we want to divest from these systems as we create the world in which we want to live.

Fourth, as scholar and activist Ruth Wilson Gilmore notes, building a different world requires that we not only change how we address harm, but that we change everything. The prison industrial complex is linked in its logics and operation with all other systems—from how students are pushed out of schools when they don’t perform as expected to how people with disabilities are excluded from our communities to the ways in which workers are treated as expendable in our capitalist system.

Changing everything might sound daunting, but it also means there are many places to start, infinite opportunities to collaborate, and endless imaginative interventions and experiments to create. Let’s begin our abolitionist journey not with the question, “What do we have now and how can we make it better?” Instead, let’s ask, “What can we imagine for ourselves and the world?” If we do that, then boundless possibilities of a more just world await us.
entries.authorBio: Kaba is an organizer, educator, curator, author whose work focuses on ending violence, dismantling the prison industrial complex, transformative justice, and supporting youth leadership development. This chapter was adapted from Kaba’s book We Do This ’Til We Free Us.

epigraphs.quote: People do abolition every day when they connect to their community, learn how to take accountability, and foster communal responsibility for preventing and responding to harm. Abolition is within our reach; it’s up to us to build it.

entries.pullQuote: We must remember that the goal is not to create a gentler prison and policing system.

entries.title: Adaptation
entries.summary: The living systems that support us can regenerate and evolve, and so can we.
entries.body: We can’t keep going this way. We are destroying the very things that support our wellbeing—from the land, water, air, and the living beings who inhabit them, to our connectedness, creativity, and cultures. Beautiful solutions are aligned with the cycles of life, working with the natural world as it is, rather than fighting against it or trying to control it. They move slow enough that what we take from the earth can grow back, and fast enough that we can be around to teach each other how they work. They are flexible and attentive so that we can adapt as the world changes around us. Adaptation is not about trying to live the same way in a changed world, but rather about adjusting our understanding of what thriving looks like in the world as it is, while protecting the possibility of a world to come.

entries.title: Artist and Freelancer Co-ops in Europe
entries.summary: Artists are some of the original gig workers...
entries.body:
Artists are some of the original gig workers. The word “gig” comes from “engagement,” a performance associated with a single contract—one-off and occasional. Working in the fields of arts and entertainment means dealing with multiple clients, inconsistent employment, and multiple workplaces. Because of these conditions, artists often face economic challenges. They have difficulty accessing health insurance, retirement, family and sick leave, unemployment benefits, and other benefits and protections that standard employees might receive.

Starting in the 1980s, artists in various countries across Europe who had precarious working conditions chose to cooperate to obtain professional recognition and more predictable contracts. They formed worker-owned cooperatives that allowed them to gain access to social protections and strengthen their sense of community.

One of the longest running artist cooperatives in Italy is Doc Servizi. It was founded in 1990 by musicians seeking to obtain decent work, share job opportunities, create working teams, and organize training to increase their expertise. Since its birth, Doc Servizi has formally employed its members, who are also its owners. They are thus able to maintain the independence associated with freelancing but can also receive social protection due to their status as co-op employer. Doc Servizi offers digital platforms and other services to support members’ self-management. Today, the cooperative remains focused on entertainment but is also part of Rete Doc, a bigger network of Italian cooperatives that covers all sectors of the cultural and creative industries and comprises more than 8,800 worker-members.

In the late 1990s, similar experiments began in Finland and Belgium with two cooperatives: Lilith and Smart. In order to guarantee its worker-members the status of employees and provide them with a safe and secure work environment, in 1997, Lilith was created in Helsinki by a group of musicians and producers. Today, Lilith is the biggest Finnish cooperative of workers in creative fields with more than 400 members. Smart, or the Société Mutuelle des Artistes, is a multi-stakeholder cooperative founded to support artists to develop their activities through the provision of shared services and a digital platform that makes it easier to invoice for their work. In the beginning, Smart was created in 1998 as a nonprofit association, but it became a multi-stakeholder cooperative in 2016. At first it was aimed at artistic and creative workers, but it later opened up to all freelancers and, recently, to platform workers. In the cooperative, the workers are shareholders, co-investors, and salaried employees through either fixed-term or open-ended contracts. Smart is now a network of cooperatives and companies that stretches across nine countries in Europe and has about 32,000 workers in its membership.

More recent examples of cooperation among musicians are DiGiDi and Resonate. The Danish DiGiDi was founded in 2003 as a cooperative digital music distribution service and today counts more than 6,500 members, including labels and artists. Resonate is an Irish multi-stakeholder cooperative that since 2015 has offered streaming music services with the purpose of bringing together the core stakeholders of the music economy. Both cooperatives are designed to offer more sustainable careers for their members and to value the creative work of musicians.

Contingent and unreliable working conditions are not only common in the arts and creative industries but, especially with the spread of casualization and automation, also characterize employment in other sectors. In many parts of the world, self-employed workers in industries ranging from software development to food delivery, and from education to journalism, have turned to cooperatives for fairer contracts and greater control over their time. As the cooperative sector grows, it is increasingly able to shape public policy.

In 1994, a French activist named Elisabeth Bost helped to formalize a new cooperative model, the Business and Employment Cooperative (BEC), to address the needs of isolated, self-employed workers in any field, enabling them to share common resources and services. Each BEC supports the “employee entrepreneur” in many ways: legal, administrative and accounting management, business administration, job creation, training, and peer-to-peer exchange. In France, about 155 cooperatives with 12,000 employee-entrepreneurs are organized on the BEC model. The model has been adopted in Switzerland and the Czech Republic, and similar forms exist in Morocco and Tunisia.

As ever more jobs are absorbed by the gig economy, worker-owned cooperatives represent a viable means of mitigating the isolation and unreliability faced by increasing numbers of workers. Working together instead of working alone, artists and cultural workers can gain more control over the market and the future of work as a whole.
entries.authorBio: Martinelli is the director of the Centro Studi Doc Foundation, based in Verona (Italy), where she oversees research and advocacy. Martinelli has a Masters Degree in Philosophy, as well as a Ph.D in “Human Capital Formation and Labour Relations” from the University of Bergamo and Paris VIII Vincennes-St.-Denis.

entries.title: Association of Recyclers of Bogotá
entries.summary: They have been known as scavengers, reclaimers, recicladores, and waste pickers...
entries.body:
They have been known as scavengers, reclaimers, recicladores, and waste pickers. They exist in the informal sector, often in low- to middle-income countries where formal work can be nearly impossible to find. In consumerist societies, waste pickers find opportunity where others only see garbage: they earn income by sorting through what would otherwise linger on the streets or get sent to landfill, collecting anything that can be processed and reused.

Waste is a particularly pressing issue in Bogotá, Colombia, a city of nearly 10 million people. In 2011, the city government proposed auctioning $1.7 billion in contracts to private waste companies. This threatened the informal sector of recicladores who, for decades, had been working to keep their city clean by sorting through waste, diverting reusable and recyclable materials from landfill.

This proposal also posed environmental threats. For private waste management companies, it is more profitable to send waste into the landfill than to repurpose it, since companies do not pay to use public landfills. Once there, waste pollutes the air and water, and emits methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Failing to recycle also drives up the demand for raw materials like wood and petroleum, which leads to deforestation and oil drilling.

The work of recyclers and waste pickers is vital to reducing the ecological impact of cities. In parts of the world where people have little economic power, informal work like waste picking is widespread. There are 20 million recyclers worldwide, many of them in China and Brazil.

In Bogotá, recicladores work long hours in rough conditions, sorting through many tons of waste and selling what they reclaim to processors or middlemen. Their lack of recognition in the formal economy means that employment protections don’t apply to them, and they often experience abuse by police and sexual harassment at worksites. While mature capitalist countries may look at this as an obsolete industry, many recicladores don’t necessarily want new jobs. To begin with, they want safer working conditions.

The city of Bogotá did not pay recicladores for their work until 2013, when the mayor of Bogotá acknowledged their environmental contribution. At the time, he announced a payment system for recicladores, so they could be paid for their work and not just for the resale value of collected waste. Today, these workers get paid by the city government for every ton of recyclable materials they collect. This compensation is in addition to any other payment recyclers might receive from selling materials they find.

This victory was in large part due to the efforts of the Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá (ARB), which has fought for—and won—rights for waste pickers for over several decades. Nohra Padilla Herrera, a third-generation recycler, organized the association in the 1980s in response to the poor working conditions she faced. Individuals like Herrera frequently inherit informal recycling work because there aren’t money-making alternatives for them or their families. Organizing into cooperatives, trade unions, and associations is crucial for informal workers in Brazil to be able to fight for their rights. This organization aids them in gaining formal recognition of their work and participating in decision-making processes.

The association aims to improve the economic and social conditions for the marginalized recicladores and to provide recognition through cooperative associations. It represents 24 cooperatives, made up of about 3,000 recyclers. The kind of mutual support that the recyclers practice in ARB emanates directly from their daily experiences; they have limited capital to form businesses, so they rely on community.

When Herrera and her crew of recyclers began organizing themselves, they didn’t expect their efforts to turn into a decades-long movement with many victories along the way. They just hoped to be able to earn enough to support their families. Now, recicladores have official recognition and rights, their own recycling centers, and company agreements. Waste pickers’ organizing has also gone global, with groups worldwide learning from their counterparts in other cities about organizational models for securing their rights. Herrera serves as a leader in the Latin American & Caribbean Network of Recyclers. In 2008, ARB hosted the first International Conference of Waste Picker Organizations with representatives from 40 countries, including Brazil, China, and India.

The Brazilian waste pickers’ cooperative Amanecer de los Cartoneros has grown to become the biggest in the world. Its workers go door-to-door to collect recyclables and process more than 300 tons of recyclables per day. The SWaCH cooperative in Pune, India has secured the right for women to drive the trucks that collect community waste. This cooperative has expanded to process organic waste too, contributing to the building of zero waste systems.

Around the world, recyclers like Herrera are organizing to demand dignity and recognition for the work they do. In societies where many refuse to view recyclers as workers, this organizing has led to real solutions, paving the way for more effective, ecological waste systems led by those who work on our streets.
entries.guidesBio: Padilla Herrera is a third-generation waste picker from Bogotá, Colombia, and winner of the Goldman Environmental Prize for her activism on behalf of Colombian recyclers. Fernandez is the waste picker global coordinator for Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing, a global network dedicated to improving the working conditions of the working poor—especially women—in the informal economy.

epigraphs.quote: The main challenge is that society does not see us as workers … instead of having political support, we were shunted, displaced, erased even.
epigraphs.attribution: Nohra Padilla, recycler and founder of Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá.

entries.title: Autonomous Self-Defense in Cherán
entries.summary: Armed guards stood at every entrance and exit of Cherán, an Indigenous P’urhépecha community within the Mexican state of Michoacán...
entries.body:
Armed guards stood at every entrance and exit of Cherán, an Indigenous P’urhépecha community within the Mexican state of Michoacán. These watchers were local volunteers who protected their pueblo from unwelcome cartels, politicians, and others deemed dangerous, working to ensure that the violence that shook the town in the late 2000s and early 2010s would never return.

The small urban center of the rural community was surrounded by expansive mountains, which formerly teemed with lush old-growth pine forests. By 2008, however, deforestation rates were accelerating across the region, leaving behind large swaths of dead stumps—scars representing years of people’s struggles against the activities of talamontes (illegal loggers). The loggers and their hired mafia gunmen cleared dozens of hectares per week: first, to sell timber for easy money and, second, to establish lucrative avocado plantations to capitalize on surging global demand. Endless caravans of trucks, stacked high with stolen wood, rumbled through Cherán on a daily basis.

Community members attempted to reason with the loggers. Many local farmers and activists were abused, murdered, or disappeared. Others sought help from the police or military, to no avail. The people of Cherán, finding themselves on their own, had to fight back.

By 2011, about 70 percent of Cherán’s territorial forests had been destroyed. A group of Cherán mothers and grandmothers, tired of feeling powerless, met in secret to form a plan that would protect their life-giving woodlands. Unlike the pockets of young townspeople who had been rising up against the loggers wearing masks, the women wore no face coverings. “They were braver than us,” says Cherán resident Ricardo Torres, “so we started taking our cues from them.”

On April 15, 2011, the señoras took five loggers hostage. Seeing what was happening, community members ran to furiously ring the downtown church bell while others ignited fireworks—making any commotion they could to get the people of Cherán into the streets and actively defending their land.

Townspeople erected makeshift barricades to monitor traffic and, along the roadways, positioned the torched mechanical remains of seized logging trucks. Neighbors lit fogatas (bonfires) on street corners. Traditionally the place where families would meet to share a meal and conversation, people moved their kitchens from inside the home to out in the street so that neighbors—fearful of retribution—could come together to care for one another, keep an eye out, and feel safer.

After the townspeople succeeded in driving out most of the loggers through their actions, they took their struggle to the mayor and police force—considered enablers and colluders by many—who had sprung into action only to demand the release of the hostage loggers. “We had gone to the major political parties, seeing what they could do to help,” Torres says, recalling how politicians were accustomed to visiting Cherán. “But they were only interested in us during election campaigns, for our votes.” Recognizing the futility of appealing to authorities, the townspeople declared that no national political party or politician would ever be welcome in Cherán. All electioneering would be banned, too.

The town’s focus turned to building shared community governance. With the support of scholars from Mexico and abroad, the people of Cherán waged a lengthy legal battle in federal court to have their Indigenous sovereignty recognized and to govern themselves under a customary law system based on ancestral governance models. In doing so, they sought to revive their traditional Indigenous model of governance.

“On November 2, 2011, the Federal Electoral Tribunal, Mexico’s maximum authority on elections, ruled we had the right to choose our own leaders as per our own customs,” Torres says. “They ordered the state congress to reform the law in our favor and the electoral institute to facilitate this change.” The mayor was replaced with a democratically elected, 12-person council. Under this system all prospective councilors must first be endorsed by their respective neighborhood assembly—symbolically called fogata, in honor of the street fires first lit for safety after the expulsion of the loggers. An assembly can include 20, 30, or even 50 families, and it is the forum where neighbors discuss issues, seek consensus, and make decisions.

The assemblies also act as a “first filter,” a screening process for people wanting to access political power. “We select our representatives this way,” Torres says, “because when people are nominated and vetted aloud by those who truly know them, they are evaluated for their past actions—not mere political promises.”

Among its duties, the council controls the community security force, made up of independent volunteers that run the town’s security checkpoints and conduct daily patrols of the forest. Thanks to this protection, García says, Cherán’s residents do not fear being out after dark—as is common in other areas of the state—and they not only have some of their beloved forest still intact, but also continue regenerating it by planting new saplings. “Today, at the edges of where our territory meets those of neighboring communities, there is a defined border: on our side, verdant forest,” Torres says, “and, on the other, industrial avocado plantations.”

In its role as the commercial and academic hub for the nearby villages, Cherán is losing its language. Torres laments that his own and younger generations barely know their ancestral tongue. “I understand it somewhat but cannot speak it—my kids even less so,” he says. “But that doesn’t mean we’re not P’urhépecha, that we don’t think Indigenously.” Little by little, the community’s renewed solidarity and honoring of traditions are getting townspeople of all ages in touch with their roots.

The realities of Cherán’s self-defense and organization have continued to evolve since the residents’ initial coup, and profound challenges have arisen along the way. But the town remains a testament to what can happen when people have the courage to imagine and live out what safety really means to them.

“Historically, our community has had a great ability to organize itself, to practice jaropikua,” Torres says, using a local word that roughly means “mutual aid.” “P’urhépecha is not just a language; it’s a lifestyle, a vision.”
entries.guidesBio: Torres is an instructor of social economics at Instituto Tecnológico Superior P’urhépecha in Cherán, Michoacán, Mexico, and a member- owner of an architecture co-op. García works for Jesuitas por la Paz (Jesuits for Peace), a Catholic- run social-welfare program in Mexico that collaboratively advances community participation in governance, economic solidarity, public education, and more.

epigraphs.quote: Sometimes violent events happen near Cherán, but here in the town center all is calm. We recognize that the government will never be able to provide this sense of security that we’ve built for ourselves. Today, we’re reforesting our territory, we’re doing things that serve our children and the future.
epigraphs.attribution: Ricardo Torres, community member of Cherán

entries.title: Baraza
entries.summary: Originating in East Africa, a baraza is a kind of large community gathering held to discuss import- ant matters, share information, make collective decisions, and hold leaders to account. It is one of many customary practices of direct democracy.
entries.body:
Countless elders, adults, youth, and children converge beneath tents or in the shade of an old tree. The group welcomes those who join. The first agenda item is presented for deliberation.

“Baraza” is a Swahili word for large community gatherings that have been part of the fabric of village life in East Africa long before European colonization. Similar gatherings happen under other names in a variety of forms around the world, especially in the Global South. They provide a space for villages to participate in collective problem solving and can attract hundreds or even thousands of people. Political movements and organizations can tap into these spaces to bring forward critical issues, such as mitigating climate change, curbing domestic violence, or exposing a corrupt local leader. Barazas are a reminder that democracy is about more than voting and elections— it also means creating spaces where people can hear from one another and continue to participate in the issues that matter to them.

While barazas don’t always hold official power, their social power is real. Incompetent civil servants, greedy businesspeople, and dishonest politicians usually refuse to show up at barazas, for fear of being publicly shamed for their actions. Powerful individuals who do attend may feel social pressure to make amends for any harms they have caused to their communities.

Barazas often assemble during crises affecting a whole community, enabling people to propose and discuss possible solutions. Once a solution is agreed upon, participants may form teams to develop plans for implementing it. Barazas are horizontal, directly democratic mechanisms for community organizing.

While it would be reductive to say that all precolonial East African societies practiced collective leadership, baraza-like meetings are ancient. Later in postcolonial history, shared decision-making was an integral component of the early years of ujamaa, a cooperative economics ideology and program championed by socialist Julius Nyerere where approximately 250 families would collectively govern their land and community. More recently in Abim—one of Uganda’s districts most neglected by the state—barazas have been used to evaluate the extent to which civil servants used local tax revenues responsibly. These citizen meetings offered stronger community oversight of local infrastructure, ultimately improving Abim’s roads and bridges.

Inspired by victories like this, the dispersed resistance network Solidarity Uganda organizes fireplace gatherings—the customary “meeting place” in many East African societies—to deliberate on issues like education, governance, and human rights. In 2022, a series of murders of university students in Bushenyi prompted members of one fireplace gathering to create a strategy that would force district leaders to take the matter seriously. They resolved to padlock local government offices, which prompted police to publicly address the matter they had neglected and deploy night patrols. There have been no murders in the area since.

People around the world have organized baraza-like gatherings under various names. Even while living under abhorrent fascism and violence, the people of Kurdistan gather regularly through one of the most intricate systems of direct democracy globally. The Constitutional Movement in Kuwait from 1986 to 1992 employed diwanyat, or local assemblies held at personal homesteads, to organize at a time when street protests were illegal. Due to cultural norms, police would never enter a diwanya. Diwanyat enabled mass mobilization, fueling a movement that eventually achieved the reinstatement of the suspended constitution.

Barazas and equivalent gatherings throughout the world emerge differently in different communities, but they tend to share a few basic steps. A coordinating team of volunteers determines the time, location, and agenda. That team then announces it to the public by tacking a sign to a centrally located bulletin board, posting on social media, or sending announcements home to the parents of school children. When the baraza convenes, the participation of all who show up is valued. Although driven by the discussion and input of attendees, barazas are most effective when they have an agenda to keep them on track. Lastly, if appropriate, coordinators inform participants of the next baraza’s time and location, and encourage them to invite others.

Not merely a mechanism for changing policies and making decisions, barazas practice sharing power and responsibility. They prefigure a world where vast distance between “governance” and “the people” is not inevitable. In the shade of the baraza, neighbors discover new aspects of their collective self-actualization and nudge more formal institutions toward genuine accountability.

Wilmot is a writer, organizer, and social bandit from Pennsylvania, now living in East Africa. entries.title: Be Transparent
entries.summary: If we can’t talk about it, we can’t change it.
entries.body:
People in power withold and misrepresent information as a form of control. It allows them to manipulate our collective perception of reality. That’s one of the reasons why a free press is so important to democracy. Good journalism makes the world more transparent and gives us the information we need to govern ourselves and hold others accountable.

We don’t need to depend on journalists alone. As we build this more beautiful world, we can take steps toward radical honesty in everything we do, including in our communities and workplaces. When a business openly shares its employees’ wages and benefits, the workers can use the information to organize against exploitation. When a community organization writes a report about a project that has failed, people can learn to avoid repeating past mistakes. When neighbors regularly communicate with each other in healthy ways, they are more likely to notice opportunities to improve their community with collective action.

Often, information is hidden because revealing the truth would require admitting imperfection or failure. It is true that transparency can create tensions. But as American abolitionist Frederick Douglass once said, “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.” We must overcome any aversions we hold toward tension and disagreement if we are to build an honest society. The ability to respectfully disagree with one another allows us to have critical conversations about strategy, ethics, and many other topics necessary for societal transformation.

Similarly, we must also overcome a culture of discarding people when they make mistakes. We need cultures of mutual respect and practices of transformative justice, where it is safe for people to be honest with each other. We must create environments where people know that, even when they mess up, it is possible to make amends and restore relationships.

Transparency requires us not only to be honest and share information with others, but also to be able to receive information from others. We must be able to listen and disagree while still holding one another’s inherent worthiness.

entries.title: Berea College
entries.summary: Founded more than 150 years ago with a mission to make higher education accessible to poor white and free Black students, Berea College was the first school in the US South to be sexually and racially integrated...
entries.body:
Founded more than 150 years ago with a mission to make higher education accessible to poor white and free Black students, Berea College was the first school in the US South to be sexually and racially integrated. Founder John Fee was an abolitionist who started an anti-slavery church in 1853, which also served as a one-room school. Fee and his colleagues were expelled from Madison County, Kentucky by pro-slavery factions in 1859, but they returned after the Civil War and officially incorporated the college, named Berea after an open-minded town in the Bible. Its first class, in the 1866–67 school year, consisted of 96 Black students and 91 white students.

Berea’s mission has adapted to changing times. Its 2022–23 student population of 1,450 boasted national and international learners alike, but the private, liberal arts college has remained committed to educating diverse students from the Appalachian region. In the fall of 2022, 27 percent of the student body identified as Black, 15 percent as Hispanic, and 40 percent of the student body came from Appalachia (including 33 percent of all Black and 34 percent of all Hispanic students). Additionally, 8 percent of all students are international, representing 71 countries. Berea has gender-inclusive housing, and the recently founded bell hooks center equips students with ways “to imagine and enact new relationships” beyond gender and racial hierarchy.

What unites students is their academic potential and economic need. Berea College covers all students’ tuition—valued at roughly $44,300 a year per student— with federal grant money for low-income families, ardent fundraising, and its $1.4 billion endowment. A “financial eligibility requirement” means that 97 percent of students are undergraduates who have significant financial need. The cost of housing, meals, and books are prorated based on family income, with average family income estimated at $29,296 in 2019. In the same year, 59 percent of students in the incoming class had their costs fully covered. Nationally, the average Class of 2020 graduate in the United States carries $32,731 in student-loan debt. In contrast, 49 percent of Berea students graduated debt-free. As the average amount of student debt increases across the United States, it is decreasing at Berea. Over half of Berea’s students are of the first-generation of their families to attend college.

The school fiercely and innovatively breaks the mold of today’s elite colleges in both cost to its students and its community and service-oriented approach. In the mid1960s, Berea initiated programs for students to engage in community service in the Appalachian region and beyond, a legacy that continues through the college’s Center for Excellence in Learning Through Service. In 1970, Berea created the Appalachian Center, which established a curriculum in Appalachian Studies that informs and empowers students both from and outside the region. With the motto “Tradition, Diversity, Change,” the Center’s work embraces all of Appalachia’s diverse peoples, celebrates their cultural richness, and explores tangible ways for students to work with these communities.

Berea regards students as regional and international investments, not as revenue streams. Student organizations at Berea are active in different religious, gender, environmental, and social justice movements—in the spirit of the college’s motto, drawn from the Book of Acts: “God has made of one blood all peoples of the Earth.” Community-service initiatives sponsored by the college are plentiful, such as Berea Kids Eat. In the city of Berea, over 85 percent of youth enrolled in school participate in the free National School Breakfast and Lunch Program. Through coordinating resources from local farmers, the college, and state and federal programs, the Berea Summer Food Service Program ensures kids in the region receive food year-round. Meals are free for youth with no income requirements, registrations, or limits on the number of meals.

Unlike other private institutions with robust endowments, Berea does not funnel funds to build extravagant amenities to attract prospective students. Instead, it maintains a careful budget and internally produces much of what it needs. To offset the cost of operating the college, all Berea students work at least 10 hours per week in over 120 different departments. They serve as teaching assistants, groundskeepers, information technologists, staff at the college-owned hotel, artisans in the workshop that produces and sells mountain crafts, and more. Students also tend to the 250-acre organic farm situated on campus, producing beef, goat, chicken, pork, and vegetables for the school’s cafeteria.

Students receive a Labor Transcript upon graduation that chronicles their work experiences. The Labor Program is guided by five learning goals and expectations that illustrate the program’s commitment to developing both hard and soft skills, critical thinking and problem solving. The program also supports students to gain experience in work roles that are relevant to their fields of study. Roughly half of all students do internships as well. In short, students are para-professionals who help operate all aspects of the college, an experience they recognize as preparing them to get things done. Berea is one of only nine federally recognized Work Colleges in the United States, which are subject to special regulation by the Department of Education.

Although graduates find jobs around the nation and are successful in national graduate and professional schools, Berea College’s attention to learning about and serving the region helps students see the value of long-term local commitment. Although educated youth are known to leave the region, 67 percent of all Berea’s graduates from Kentucky and elsewhere in Appalachia since 2010 have decided to stay.

Faculty and staff salaries at Berea are lower than at other colleges, but professors are no less qualified. Over 90 percent of the full-time faculty hold the highest available degree in their field. These professionals are deeply dedicated to the college’s students and ideals. To help faculty and staff better understand the lives of their students, Berea offers continuing education, including a pair of week-long tours. One brings staff and faculty into Appalachia to learn about the history, economics, politics, religions, and stereotypes of the region. Another is a civil rights tour through Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. With a ten-to-one student-to-faculty ratio at the college, knowledge and understanding of students’ backgrounds is crucial for professors.

Despite pressures to commercialize and standardize, Berea College strives to realize its roots and reason for being: the values of inclusion, equity, and impartial love.

entries.title: Build for Access
entries.summary: We need each other, and so we need to build in ways that meet each other’s needs.
entries.body:
We are, each of us, many different things to many different people. We are children and parents and neighbors and teammates and workers and friends, and so much more. The world we are building must be for all of us, and for all the roles we play.

When we build for access, we support each other to live in our communities as complex, whole people. We celebrate and uplift the necessary wisdom that comes from living in systems not designed for us, because that’s where the solutions are. Wisdom from struggles for disability justice, such as the Principles of Disability Justice from Sins Invalid, teach us that a more accessible world is better for all of us.

We need to have access to the knowledge, resources, institutions, and support that allow each of us to offer our unique contributions. We must design for this from the beginning. If access is an afterthought, we’re doing it wrong—and we’re likely doing it for the wrong reasons. We need to build for access because we need to be able to show up for each other and be powerful together. People who dream in languages other than English are leading the way out of a colonial mindset, so we need those languages centered in our planning and organizing processes, not just in our output. People with disabilities are experts at adaptation, so we can’t afford to try to address the climate crisis without their leadership.

Access needs are not always visible. About 14 percent of the global population is illiterate. Many millions of children arrive at school hungry. More than 300 million people are affected by depression. Access means understanding how unjust systems cause these problems and creating solutions that work to end those systems and heal from them, which we can only do with the help of those who have been harmed.

Access looks like community meetings held outside of work hours that offer healthy food, childcare, wheelchair accessible entrances, translation, and a ride home. It is textbooks and classrooms, healthcare, banks, and social services that are created and run by the people who actually use them. It is institutions and movements that love the people inside them, recognizing that they are magnificent, complex people who have specific and necessary medicine that will help us all get free, if they have the support they need. It is time and space for rest, care, and healing so that we can keep going for a long time.

entries.title: Carolina Textile District and COVID-19
entries.summary: Western North Carolina has long been a center for manufacturing, especially of textiles and furniture...
entries.body:
Western North Carolina has long been a center for manufacturing, especially of textiles and furniture. Despite free-trade agreements, which stripped jobs from communities on both sides of the US-Mexico border, one in four people in North Carolina’s Western Piedmont region still work in manufacturing. Many Guatemalan Mayan immigrants have settled in the area to work in textiles and furniture production. Over the years, they have shaped the region by campaigning for dignified workplaces. Organizer Molly Hemstreet witnessed their struggle to unionize a production facility in Morganton, North Carolina, and began to wonder: Could workers own and operate their own companies?

In 2008, Hemstreet and leaders from the Mayan community co-founded a sewing cooperative, Opportunity Threads. They drew on inspiration from Frank Adams, an early architect of the Highlander Folk School (now the Highlander Research and Education Center). Opportunity Threads has become one of the largest immigrant-led sewing co-ops in the United States, with more than 50 workers as of 2020.

Aiming to expand cooperativism across the textile industry and strengthen local supply chains, Hemstreet collaborated with the area’s economic development association and a textile research and development center to establish the Carolina Textile District (CTD). Fueled by its mantra, “be big by being small together,” CTD is a network that brings together over 30 small manufacturers, including Opportunity Threads, and is led by nine partners, representing 1,500 workers in total. Members cooperatively govern, train new workers, share contracts and contacts, develop strong ethical standards for the industry, and share their struggles and joys.

When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the United States in early 2020, CTD was well-positioned to produce personal protective equipment and cloth face masks. Pivoting its textile and furniture member-companies to manufacture medical supplies was a challenge with many moving parts. It required consulting with doctors and public-health professionals, navigating ever-changing federal guidelines, prototyping masks and gowns, sourcing medical-grade materials, organizing the cohorts of manufacturers, connecting with markets and sponsors, developing a cohesive warehousing and distribution center, upscaling production, and overseeing quality control. As factories in Western North Carolina were shuttering, CTD was not only safely keeping open their plants, but hiring as well. The pandemic underscored the need for CTD and accelerated the network’s growth.

Opportunity Threads was the hub for CTD’s sewn goods during the pandemic. Worker-owners responded quickly, putting their technical skills to use in developing market-ready goods. Other CTD members came on board to help. Since CTD members had several years of “coopetition” under their belts, the network rapidly developed new products and increased production. At one point, they were producing 50,000 units per week, which kept over 60 mills humming. “We have achieved so many things that we probably would not have been able to accomplish in a company owned by one person,” says Maricela Lopez, a worker-owner at Opportunity Threads.

Through this project, CTD supplied 190,000 sanitary gowns to North Carolina’s Department of Health and Human Services and over 500,000 facemasks and other personal protective equipment to frontline workers. Additionally, it generated $2 million in revenue for its textile and furniture manufacturers. According to Sara Chester, CTD co-founder and Industrial Commons co-executive director, “When weekly mask production hit 40,000 units, [we] realized something tremendous was being achieved.”

Instead of communities having to wait for companies to come in and to solve economic, health, and social problems, cooperative industry networks can solve critical problems quickly and creatively. This model is one replicable example of how rural communities can actively build an industry ecosystem where workers own a secure supply chain, collaborate in mutually beneficial ways, and solve their communities’ most pressing problems.

entries.title: Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society
entries.summary: After the end of Zimbabwe’s war of liberation in 1980, 22 ex-freedom fighters came together to start a new life by founding a cooperative farm called the Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society...
entries.body:
After the end of Zimbabwe’s war of liberation in 1980, 22 ex-freedom fighters came together to start a new life by founding a cooperative farm called the Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society. For them, this was a new battle: “a battle for economic independence.” The founding members of Chitsvachirimurutsoka were able to raise the money to buy land, equipment, and farming tools by combining their demobilization allowances—sums of money given to former fighters by the government, amounting to approximately $128 in US dollars a month per person. Using traditional skills, members began crop and livestock production. They grew maize, sugar beans, and sunflowers.

The first three years were challenging. The members did not have the business skills to efficiently manage the farm. To make matters worse, bad droughts ruined the crops, leaving little to harvest and the farm in debt. This made life very difficult, and the cooperative lost three members who abandoned the project.

Chitsvachirimurutsoka made it through these challenging early days, living up to the meaning of its name: “There is no gain without sweat.” Management of the cooperative was improved through business training given to the members. While drought is an ongoing issue, Chitsvachirimurutsoka has learned to manage it. As a result, it has had many profitable years and has invested proceeds in improving the living standards of members and developing of the wider community. For Chitsvachirimurutsoka, contributing to the community is an essential part of being a cooperative. Over the last few decades, members have dug boreholes to provide clean water, built and repaired roads, started a preschool on the farm, paid for funerals, and supported sick and orphaned people in their community, in addition to many other contributions.

A key pillar of the cooperative’s mission is to solve food insecurity. Every day at the farm, from seven in the morning to seven at night, members sell poultry, vegetables, and other products at affordable prices. Most of the customers come from nearby Epworth, a settlement of about 300,000 people, many of whom are poor. Chitsvachirimurutsoka also supplies food to several community institutions including a cafeteria, some schools, and local clinics.

Chitsvachirimurutsoka’s general meeting, which occurs three or four times a year, is the supreme authority guiding the cooperative’s actions. Here, members make major decisions such as approving by-laws, regulations, codes of conduct, and the action plan and budget for each year. The general meeting elects the Management Committee, the policy-making body of the cooperative which oversees budgets and plans to ensure the cooperative is on track to meet its goals. The committee members serve for three years (but can be removed if they are not performing well).

The chairperson of the committee appoints a coordinator to implement resolutions passed at the annual general meeting held in December. This coordinator reports to the Management Committee and must be approved by a majority of members. Once appointed, it is the coordinator’s responsibility to ensure that the cooperative brings in enough revenue and keeps costs low enough to reach the net profit goals set by the committee. The coordinator manages all other cooperative members. In this way, Chitsvachirimurutsoka has a traditional business structure with the coordinator as the boss, except during general meetings when the members are collectively in charge.

However, Chitsvachirimurutsoka is not like a private company where a small number of shareholders make major decisions and control all the profit. Every member of Chitsvachirimurutsoka Cooperative Society holds shares in the enterprise, so that each receives dividends when the co-op profits or shares in its losses. Members actively participate in decision-making and work in positions that make sense for them. Women are treated the same way as men, and there is much consideration for children, dependents, and disabled people.

The success of Chitsvachirimurutsoka and other cooperatives of the early 1980s has encouraged the formation of hundreds of cooperatives in Zimbabwe. In keeping with one of the international cooperative principles, “cooperation among cooperatives,” these cooperatives started to organize themselves at the district level, where they came together to share information, ideas, experiences, and resources, including a revolving loan fund, a machinery pool, and bulk buying and marketing arrangements. The same happened at provincial and national levels, with cooperatives pooling together transportation and group insurance, as well as standardized accounting and auditing to assist the members and their initiatives. Though later economic and political crises would hit the cooperative movement hard, these early advances should be celebrated for their democratic and grassroots development model.

entries.title: Choose Collective Courage
entries.summary: Our strength lies in what we can do together.
entries.body:
There are people and institutions whose drive for profit threatens to destroy everything we have. We can summon the courage to challenge them, to meet our own needs, create our own realities, and defend what we create. Collective courage is about choosing to stick with the hard work of fighting together, even when it may mean giving some things up.

We borrow the term “collective courage” from our friend Jessica Gordon Nembhard and her book, Collective Courage: A History of African American Economic Thought and Practice. It is a phrase that can come to life in many contexts. Whether it’s creating a mutual aid network, campaigning for a policy, protesting discrimination, registering new voters, organizing a community meeting, or running for office, our work cannot be neatly separated into issue areas. It is the work of survival and thriving, and it means innovating and evolving to meet the needs of each moment, and supporting each other when obstacles arise.

A community can hold a vision and an awareness of what could be, but they must choose to bring it into being and respond to the consequences that arise from its creation. Any project that challenges the existing power structure will provoke a response from those in power. Choosing collective courage means leaning into the strength of our communities and preparing to meet that resistance together, despite the odds.

It may be harder to build strength in a collective than retreat into the supposed safety of isolation, but the collective is our power. We can work to trust each other in a society that makes us unsafe, to confront our suspicion and our fears of one another. We can join with other members of the community despite our differences, working and grieving and celebrating together. We can do the hard work of crafting a strategy that integrates different approaches and groups of people in the building of a cohesive vision for our future.

We must be clear about what we’re fighting for and against, so that we don’t end up fighting each other. When those in power try to pit us against each other, we resist because we know that we are stronger when we’re together.

Choosing collective courage means organizing from our roots: being so grounded in our experience and in our place that when we turn toward one another, we can see that we are not alone. It is understanding that we must begin by changing our reality close to home. It is choosing to do the work, together, right where we are.

entries.title: Community Broadband Networks
entries.summary: Access to reliable internet service has become a basic need in most of the world, yet many communities either lack service in their area or are priced out by corporate monopolies. Community broadband is a way for people rather than companies to own the means of accessing the internet, securing lower prices and faster service in the process.
entries.body:
Households throughout the world often rely on local government to provide them with access to basic utilities such as electricity, gas, and water. In the last two decades, many cities have added another utility to the list of services they provide: internet access.

Community broadband providers offer an alternative to corporate telecom monopolies. In this model, a community-based entity such as a local municipal body, a tribal government, a cooperative, or a nonprofit organization builds and may also manage a network, offering services to residents and businesses. This allows communities to gain control over internet access prices, policies, and critical infrastructure.

In 1994, the city of Glasgow, Kentucky, created the first municipal broadband network in the United States after their cable monopoly frustrated customers with poor customer service and by neglecting to modernize infrastructure in rural areas. When the municipal electric utility in Glasgow began building its own network, the incumbent cable company lowered prices by 75% in an effort to discourage the competition. The struggle gained national attention for the town. Since forming its own internet service provider, the city has been able to adapt the network to community needs and keep prices low.

Rural areas are not the only regions ignored by traditional telecom companies. In Detroit, Michigan, over 35 percent of homes are not on the internet, with a majority of those being low-income households. To expand internet access, community groups came together in 2016 to form the Equitable Internet Initiative (EII), which connected over 150 homes in its pilot year. In addition to providing internet service, the EII offers technology literacy workshops, trains community “digital stewards,” and is in the process of forming a worker-owned utility cooperative to manage internet services. While neighborhood initiatives such as these may not always provide the fastest internet speeds, they can offer connectivity for very little cost to underserved communities.

This kind of model can easily be normalized and applied in neighborhoods across the globe. In Sweden, for instance, where community broadband is widespread, municipalities can choose between enabling a for-profit company to provide fiber access that upholds the community’s agreed-upon broadband standards or creating a local government entity to provide access. Among rural areas in the United States, existing utility cooperatives that provide electricity are increasingly expanding their services to include broadband access.

While local specificities need to be taken into account, there are several possible funding models for community broadband networks. Some cities turn to loans and revenue bonds, which are then paid back through the revenues collected by the network. Alternatively, they can borrow funds from other departments in the city government. Establishing broadband networks gradually, rather than across an entire city at once, can also keep costs low for municipalities. Cities and cooperatives are sometimes able to access public and philanthropic funds to provide for underserved residents.

Community broadband networks are able to keep prices low because, unlike national telecom companies, they aren’t required to generate a greater profit year after year. Additionally, for a municipal provider, a lower cost of service means the city pays less to connect its public libraries, schools, police departments, and government offices. While in the short-term, large telecoms may use their power to lower prices and undercut a community-based option, in the long-term, research suggests that community networks offer improved cost and service. Corporations have, however, fought fiercely to prevent them from doing so. 17 US states have corporation-written laws that restrict community networks.

Reliable internet access is now a necessity for the vast majority of people worldwide. Municipal broadband offers a way to make this crucial service accessible to areas that a traditional provider might neglect—such as rural towns and low-income neighborhoods—and to put its control into communities’ hands.

entries.title: Community Land Trust
entries.summary: A community land trust is a model of land or hous- ing ownership that isn’t run for profit but for the public good, for the benefit of families and commu- nities. Through collective control of land, a commu- nity can decide how they want to use it.
entries.body:
Community Land Trusts (CLTs) are a powerful way to protect affordable homeownership by taking land and housing out of the hands of profit-driven market forces. In societies that view land as something to be bought or sold, CLTs treat it as a shared resource to be stewarded for a social purpose. According to community organizer and scholar John Davis, “What the CLT does better than any other organization … is to preserve affordability when economic times are good and protect its homes and homeowners when times are bad. In the scorched landscape of the [United States’] national mortgage crisis, CLTs are almost alone in reporting few defaults and even fewer foreclosures.”

In a CLT, housing and other buildings are under “dual ownership.” The CLT is a nonprofit entity that owns the land, while families (or a cooperative association, or developers) own the buildings. The CLT signs a long-term lease with the building owners for the use of the land. Through restrictions put on these leases, the land trust puts a cap on the resale price of homes and requires that homes be sold to lower-income families. Government subsidies can be used to bring down the price of the homes and put them within reach of low and moderate-income families. These subsidies are attached to the homes, so they stay affordable for future generations of buyers.

As nonprofit organizations governed by community members on behalf of a social mission, CLTs are more likely to be committed to their community’s agenda and vision—supporting the stability and welfare of their neighborhoods—compared to single-family or investor owners. Most CLTs require that CLT houses be occupied by their owners, meaning they cannot be an investment property.

CLTs can be started as stand-alone non-profit organizations or as programs, subsidiaries, or spin-offs from existing non-profits. Funding a CLT requires a creative combination of government and private grants, loans, and donations. Donations can be in the form of money, land, or legal and technical assistance.

There are over 250 CLTs throughout the United States. They began spreading in the second half of the 20th century, starting with organizers in the Black liberation movement in the late 1960s. Considered by many to be the first community land trust, New Communities Inc. was founded by leaders in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to provide for Black families who were getting kicked off their land by white farmers in Georgia. In spite of their effectiveness in stabilizing and empowering communities and protecting low and moderate-income families, CLTs in the United States represent a very small fraction of housing, accounting for only about 10,000 units.

Land trusts can also be found around the globe. In Kenya, the Tanzania-Bodeni Community Land Trust developed in response to local housing needs and seeks to address urban settlement problems. The women-led Maria Auxiliadora housing project in Bolivia adapts the CLT model to build a community for low-income women and families. The Martín Peña Channel Community Land Trust (Fideicomiso de la Tierra del Caño Martín Peña) in Puerto Rico provides housing for a community of nearly 30,000 people. CLTs have also developed in European countries including England and Switzerland.

CLTs are changing with the times. Communities and governments have taken advantage of the flexibility of the strategy. While there are “classic” features to a CLT, it is an adaptable model that allows a community to incorporate the things that are important to them. Issues such as geographic area, how the land is used, affordability, lease provisions, and governance structure can be determined through community planning processes.

With local and national governments establishing CLTs to meet affordable housing goals, there is a risk that some new CLTs are not truly grounded in their communities. CLTs also face the challenge of having to secure funding up-front for land and homes, in addition to getting the support of the families and communities who will use the land and housing. This significant up-front effort to organize people and resources is an important consideration in pursuing CLTs over other forms of affordable housing.

The CLT model calls on landowners to work for the greater good rather than the greatest financial return for the individual. It treats land as a shared resource and housing as a fundamental human right.

entries.title: Community Media Association of Honduras
entries.summary: In June 2009, the democratically elected president of Honduras, Manuel Zelaya, was arrested and forcibly removed from the country on the order of the Honduran Supreme Court by the Honduran Army...
entries.body:
In June 2009, the democratically elected president of Honduras, Manuel Zelaya, was arrested and forcibly removed from the country on the order of the Honduran Supreme Court by the Honduran Army. In the months and years that followed the coup d’état, thousands of journalists, opposition politicians, human rights activists, and others were detained, disappeared, or murdered by the new regime. Media coverage of this violence was virtually non-existent, since even during Zelaya’s presidency, Honduran media was solely controlled by a few wealthy conservative families and intentionally excluded voices critical of the government installed by the coup.

This tumultuous political landscape led to the formation of the Community Media Association of Honduras (AMCH, or Asociación de Medios de Comunicación Comunitarios de Honduras in Spanish). The AMCH is made up of approximately forty groups and organizations throughout the nation, including alternative media groups, activists, indigenous groups, young people and more. It aims to facilitate conversations with the National Telecommunications Commission of Honduras (CONATEL) to challenge the limited broadcasting landscape in the country.

In Honduras, one must purchase a license to start a media company. After the coup in 2009, licenses could only be acquired through an auction system controlled by parties loyal to the government. This arrangement prevented large portions of the Honduran people from starting media companies, specifically excluding peasant groups, human rights organizations, young people demanding democratic change, and Indigenous and Garifuna peoples (descendants of 18th-century African shipwreck survivors). The result was that a small number of companies owned most of the radio and TV stations in Honduras—a broadcast monopoly.

A 2011 report on the events surrounding the coup, created by the government as part of the Accord for National Reconciliation and Strengthening of Democracy in Honduras, concluded that the broadcast monopolies bore significant blame for the social crisis, and recommended democratizing access to the radio frequencies, television, and the internet.

In response to the wave of national discussion that followed, the AMCH brought together local and regional collectives to demand change. In August 2013, the regulating authority approved the AMCH’s proposal to make it possible for community groups to acquire media licenses. As of January 2017, 25 community radio stations in different parts of the country are in operation, and two television stations have been approved. Prior to this, only five community radio stations existed in the entire country.

Community media grants visibility to decentralized grassroots resistance and social change. In the San Antonio neighborhood of the town of El Taragual in western Honduras, a Lenca indigenous community has been fighting a law passed by the government that would divide up their land into plots. For them, radio is a necessary tool for educating the community about the adverse effects and conflicts that this parceling would cause. Emeterio Pérez, the leader of the neighborhood where the radio station originated, joined a group of coffee and grain farmers between the ages of 80 and 100, who committed to donating a portion of their wages to the radio station’s Steering Committee. They donated one work day per week, and a group of women sold homemade bread, nacatamales and other treats to support the station. On May 3, 2015, with a year’s savings and the technical support of AMCH, the Taragual community put a radio transmitter on air with the Voice of Life program on 106.7 FM. One year after speaking into their microphones for the first time, the station’s management committee had built alliances with key players in the neighboring cities of Gracias, San Rafael and La Union.

Today, the committee is attempting to legally register with the Indigenous Association for the Integral Development of El Taragual, which would grant them governmental recognition of their community radio frequency. The AMCH is providing technical training and legal support for this effort.

Through supporting community efforts and providing resources to formalize local broadcasting, the AMCH slowly works towards building a democratized media landscape that provides a variety of cultural and educational listening options throughout the country.
entries.authorBio: Antonio Molina is a long-time Honduran journalist and the founder of the AMCH. Antonio Molina has survived two assassination attempts because of his work.

entries.title: Community Safety
entries.summary: People who have experienced violence and abuse from police and within their communities have ad- opted creative ways of addressing their needs for safety. Movements for community safety address violence without relying upon police or prisons.
entries.body:
Individuals and groups experiencing systemic oppression on the basis of race, gender, sexuality, disability, and other factors are often the most vulnerable to violence. Many of the systems and institutions that promise safety and security contribute to racial and sexual violence, as well as other forms of domination and abuse. As an alternative to relying on these institutions, people are creating community safety efforts grounded in their own neighborhoods and networks of people they know to help protect and heal from harm.

Around the world, women of color, particularly those who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender, have been at the forefront of creating groups and movements to protect their communities from violence, including the violence of police and other government institutions. A growing network has been forming to share experiences and techniques for community safety. Within the United States, the Oakland-based group Creative Interventions collected stories of how people intervened to prevent or stop family violence in their everyday lives. They also supported interventions by friends and family members of immigrant women experiencing domestic abuse, and produced a handbook of resources for anyone to use, informed by what they learned. In New York City, the Audre Lorde Project’s Safe OUTside the System Collective, meanwhile, created strategies based on community building and organizing to prevent racist and homophobic assaults on LGBTQ+ people of color in their Brooklyn neighborhood.

Their efforts often begin with developing ways to respond to interpersonal violence, which expand to strategies for preventing violence, intervening when harm occurs, and transforming the beliefs, patterns, and social and economic conditions that serve as root causes of violence. Some call this approach “transformative justice”—the work of not just addressing a specific instance of harm but also uprooting the underlying causes. Taken together, approaches for responding to interpersonal and state violence have become the basis of comprehensive visions for what it would mean to have truly safe communities.

Efforts to cultivate community safety often emphasize four goals: safety, healing, accountability, and transformation. To pursue these goals, practitioners start from the recognition that people experiencing harm tend to turn first to the people who are closest to them. Community safety can begin with those in relationship with each other, rather than by turning to the police or other government institutions such as the child welfare system. To make this possible, practitioners build their knowledge and capacity to pursue safety outside of state systems using storytelling, collective organizing, and skills trainings, among other methods. Some communities create new structures and cultures for safety by ensuring that they have resources and skills to meet their own needs. In Nairobi, Kenya, young people connected with St. Johns Ambulance have undergone first aid training so that they can administer help in emergency medical situations. This strategy has been especially important for groups in places where calls for medical assistance, including mental health support, could also bring armed police officers.

In addition to developing short-term responses and strategies, fostering safer communities entails a long-term commitment to challenging systems of oppression such as racism, sexism, homophobia, and transphobia that fuel abuse and violence. It involves cultivating value systems and ways of being that affirm the worth and dignity of all people. A community accountability process, for instance, might not only result in protection and support for a survivor of intimate partner violence, but also social, economic and mental health support for the person responsible for the abuse. Community safety is intimately connected to a vision of a world in which freedom from harm does not involve violent institutions like prisons, jails, and detention centers. Grassroots efforts to establish community safety facilitate the building of knowledge and skills so that people have the confidence to participate in liberatory violence prevention, intervention, and response.

Many groups of people who share the same apartment building, place of worship, or workplace have not established values, principles, and commitments to support the safety of their most vulnerable members. But that does not mean it is too late to start. All communities have the capacity to help the people in them experience safety.
