entries.title: Community-owned Sports Teams
entries.summary: Community-owned sports teams share manage- ment responsibilities, ownership, and profit with a team’s stakeholding supporters.
entries.body:
Around the world, a combination of mismanagement, lack of regulations, and inequitable wealth distribution has driven sports fans to feel increasingly disconnected from the affairs of their favorite teams. In the UK and elsewhere, football clubs and other sports teams have largely transitioned out of local ownership and into the hands of corporate owners with no real connection to the area and few interests beyond turning a profit. These enterprising, wealth-seeking owners or ownership groups buy a team for its business potential, only to sell it off a few years later at a higher price. As clubs have suffered financial losses under this model, their local supporters feel that this practice is unsustainable and that it diverges from the true interests of the fans. In response, supporters around the world have led efforts to collectively buy back their teams.

Community ownership allows teams to be managed by the people who are most invested in their success. Typically, community ownership structures include both a large membership and an elected governing board. Elections take place regularly to keep the board accountable; each member gets one vote, no matter how much money they’ve invested. In some clubs, board members may appoint a non-elected general member to the primary governing body to fill gaps in the skill set. For example, in a board of older supporters, it might be necessary to bring on a younger person to do youth outreach.

Membership fees and costs involved in becoming an owner of a team are kept low to encourage a broad and inclusive membership. The UK football club AFC Wimbledon, for instance, is majority-owned by a supporters’ trust with approximately 3,000 members. All members can access a website where they can share questions and opinions with other community members and the board. The club reinvests all revenue into itself according to an agreed-on code of ethics.

One frequent criticism of supporters’ trusts is that members equate their team’s success with the fulfillment of their own narrow financial self-interest. But in fact, the individual is not the center of a community-owned club model. Rather, many of these trusts are registered as community benefit (CB) societies, requiring them to prove that they primarily serve community interests, not those of their members. In the UK, an officially designated CB can pay a small dividend to its individual members, but it is usually no more than 2 percent above the interest rate.

Any existing assets are protected by an asset-lock clause, which prevents members from voting to privatize the organization or to distribute wealth outside of it.

In Germany, community-owned club regulation is different. All football clubs are majority-owned by their fans, following a 50+1 model, which stops wealthy corporations and individuals from controlling the teams. Greater regulation prevents clubs from filing for bankruptcy, and a strict licensing system weeds out clubs that are not properly tracking their finances. Similar supporters’ trusts have been implemented in Spain, too.

In the United States, there is a single community-owned American football team: the Green Bay Packers. When the team faced financial difficulties in the 1920s and 1930s, it sold stock to the community to keep itself from going bankrupt. That model persists today, and the team is a publicly owned nonprofit corporation with over 360,000 individual shareholders. Shareholders have voting rights and can participate in annual owner meetings, but their stock cannot appreciate in value and there are no season ticket privileges.

Community-owned teams can struggle with marketing and expanding their fan bases, as well as attracting funding. Another challenge is attracting volunteers on match days—but people are more likely to volunteer for a club that they have a stake in than one that is privately owned. This is just one advantage that this model affords in comparison to private ownership. Having a collective of people who are invested in the club long-term allows it to build better relationships with local partners and ensures greater moral and financial accountability in club governance. Successful supporters’ trusts have core governing policies, delegated authority, business knowledge, and fans who elevate the interests of the collective above those of the individual.

Community-owned sports teams, in contrast to their privately-owned and profit-driven counterparts, contribute to people-powered economies.

entries.body:
Youth in the Philippines face many challenges regarding their sexual wellbeing. Rates of teenage pregnancy and HIV/AIDS are rising, and high rates of violence and extreme poverty prevent youth from making healthy choices and completing their education.

85 percent of the Filipino population is Catholic, which means that Catholic teachings provide the dominant discourse on sexuality. An 18 year, highly politicized struggle led to the national Reproductive Health and Parenthood Act in 2012, which guaranteed access to contraception, maternal health, sex education, and fertility control. Since then, continued opposition from both religious leaders and politicians has prevented adequate funding of reproductive-health programs and severely limited their implementation across the country. Many Filipino youth have limited exposure to and experience with issues of sexuality, human reproduction, and anatomy. They’ve had little to no education about how to protect themselves from sexually transmitted infections and unwanted pregnancy. When unplanned pregnancies happen, young people face a great deal of pressure to marry. This often ties them into a cycle of poverty that can be very difficult to overcome. Sexual abuse, exploitation, and incest are infrequently discussed and, for the most part, young people lack the knowledge and tools for sexual safety and negotiating sexual relationships.

In 2013, Aimee Santos-Lyons, a Filipina immigrant to the US, and her husband Rev. Joseph Santos-Lyons from the US Universalist Unitarian Association (UUA) began holding a series of sexuality education workshops for Filipino youths with the national Unitarian Universalist Church of the Philippines (UUCP) team based in Dumaguete, Negros Oriental, in the Visayas region. The program was developed to be culturally relevant, utilizing local examples, popular education methods, and interpretation and translation work in Tagalog and Visayan languages. This work built on the sexuality education program of HASIK, a feminist organizing group based in Metro Manila that works with urban poor women and girls.

In an effort to expand the workshops nationally, the Rev. Jory Agate from the UUA collaborated with Rev. Rebecca Quimada Sienes from the UUCP to design and lead a Filipino adaptation of the Our Whole Lives (OWL) program. The OWL program first began in the US during the 1960s, when the UUA realized that the youth in its congregation needed guidance around sexuality. It created a secular, science-based curriculum that spoke to the sexual realities youth were experiencing. It provided sexuality education guided by ethics, safety, and responsibility to the community. Over time, with the help of the United Church of Christ, the OWL program has expanded to serve people of all ages. There are thousands of OWL trainers in the United States, and the curriculum is used by religious and secular groups alike.

To bring OWL to young people in the Philippines, the UUA raised money through international networks, relying upon the groundwork laid by the Santos-Lyons’s earlier workshops. Local workshop leaders aimed to center Filipino culture and norms, carefully adapting the OWL curriculum to ensure its relevance to the cultural and economic context of Filipino youth today. Trained peer facilitators assisted with delivery of the material and small group facilitators fostered conversations in participants’ own languages. Workshop leaders created mechanisms to circumnavigate traditional Filipino deference to authority figures in order to encourage more input, feedback, and questions from youth.

Since Filipino Unitarian Universalist congregations are small and rural, a week-long workshop was held at the church’s headquarters in Dumaguete, to which youth from various congregations were invited. To mitigate the privileging of white, Western views of sexuality, the program included guest speakers from the region. Local leaders from the health department led a presentation on contraception, three community members identifying as LGBTQ participated in a panel on sexuality, and an external agency led a day of gender equity and non-violence work with the male participants.

One goal of the workshop was to enable youth to take home and into their peer communities key principles of sexual health. Leaders encouraged the students to remember seven core components of a sexually healthy relationship, which represented the foundational values of the program. When the workshop’s success was later evaluated using a survey, these tenets were participants’ most significant takeaway, along with newfound acceptance of the LGBTQ community and a commitment to using contraception.

Leaders recognized the limited reach of this one-week workshop. The young participants could only absorb so much information from their first experience of comprehensive sexuality education. Additionally, the workshop only reached a tiny fraction of the Unitarian Universalist youth in the Philippines. For greater change to occur, these programs need to be available much more widely. In the process, however, they must retain their cultural specificity, connecting a global effort to the languages, norms, and concerns of the places where they spread.
entries.authorBio: Rev. Agate is the former ministerial development director at the Unitarian Universalist Association (UUA). This chapter also has contributions from the Rev. Sarah Gibb Millspaugh, co-author of the Our Whole Lives curriculum for young adults.

entries.title: Conflict Kitchen
entries.summary: Believing that the quickest way to a person’s heart is through their stomach, Conflict Kitchen sought to promote peace and build cross-cultural understanding by introducing people to the food and culture of places with which their government is in conflict...
entries.body:
Believing that the quickest way to a person’s heart is through their stomach, Conflict Kitchen sought to promote peace and build cross-cultural understanding by introducing people to the food and culture of places with which their government is in conflict. Based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and the brainchild of artist-activists Jon Rubin and Dawn Weleski, Conflict Kitchen used a simple takeout window framed by a colorful facade to serve up the cuisine, and celebrate the culture of a succession of countries, including Iran, Afghanistan, Cuba, North Korea, Venezuela, Palestine, and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

The takeout window functioned as a platform for public dialogue, and the food line became a space for hungry Pittsburghers to engage with people and places the media consistently distorts and misrepresents. The takeout counter was staffed by chefs and public artists trained to facilitate conversations about the featured country. Each food wrapper was printed with personal profiles of people who live in the country being celebrated, as well as articles on the country’s food, art, religion, culture, and government.

To extend the experience beyond the takeout line and further encourage cross-cultural dialogue, Conflict Kitchen also organized public events that centered around food. Pittsburgh locals and Iranians in Tehran shared a meal via webcam in a virtual, city-to-city dinner party. Both groups made the same Persian recipes, then sat down to eat together. Other events have included informal lunch hour discussions on food and politics, dinners with invited speakers, and live cooking lessons through Skype.

In November 2014, a series of death threats forced Conflict Kitchen to close down for nearly a week. In response to the threats and allegations of being anti-Israel, the directors of Conflict Kitchen emphasized that their purpose is to hold a loudspeaker to the voices and historical experiences of people from across the world—Palestinians and Palestinian-Americans included. The backlash they received is proof that this type of work is necessary.

Conflict Kitchen offered the public many points of entry, from the taste of a new dish, to interactions with employees or fellow customers, to the interviews printed on the food wrappers, and the intimate meals with people far away. Cultural exchange was central to the project; the organizers prioritized facilitating a space for locals and people overseas to express their respective point of view.

The webcam meals between Pittsburgh and abroad provided a temporary glimpse of what it can mean to share cultures, politics, and, of course, food. By creating a zone of open dialogue and cross-cultural understanding for at least one meal, Conflict Kitchen made a world where we listen to each other and draw our own conclusions seem possible. It used food as a vehicle for cross-cultural understanding—and also provided delicious takeout.

entries.title: Cooperative Education
entries.summary: Cooperative education builds the skills, consciousness, and culture of everyday people to grow and govern social and economic democracy. It teaches us to unlearn dominant values of individualism and greed and uplifts the sacred and interconnected nature of all people.
entries.body:
Cooperatives are not a silver bullet, but through member co-ownership and co-governance, they foster skills and culture that build more robust practices of local democracy. Cooperative education is therefore foundational for a more inclusive future. Building democracy requires teaching democracy, and ensuring that all people have access to the lessons of past experience in running democratic economies.

The exclusion of cooperative curriculum from formal business schools around the world pushes the cooperative sector to the sidelines. Of the 30 most prominent business management textbooks, only three mention co-ops, all in negative or neutral light. In some ways, this shouldn’t be a surprise. Most business schools are largely funded by wealthy alumni and multinational corporations, who don’t stand to benefit from the growth of the cooperative sector.

It wasn’t always this way. Before World War II, cooperatives were commonly found in textbooks. In the United States, the Department of Agriculture helped to establish centers to support cooperative development at state colleges, and such centers still exist at Cornell University, the University of Missouri, the University of Wisconsin, and elsewhere. Even Stanford University was founded in part on the premise of advancing education about cooperative economics, although this wish of its founder has been mainly ignored.

To address the lack of cooperative education, Saint Mary’s Business School launched the first cooperative business program in North America. Approved in 2002, Saint Mary’s Masters of Business Administration (MBA) allows students to enter business education through a cooperative lens, gaining fluency in mainstream business content while simultaneously critiquing it and cultivating an ability to build and run alternatives.

Full-fledged university programs in cooperative business are new to North America, but they draw inspiration from a global network of co-op educators. Kenya, India, and the Canadian province of Quebec all boast meaningful co-op sectors backed by formal cooperative education in universities. As a growing movement, new voices are helping to evolve and mature the field of cooperative education. Cooperative education can look different in different settings. Many universities in the United States still offer a cooperative center within a business school or a certification program that allows students to learn strategies for cooperative workplaces and collaborate with local co-ops. Some schools, like EdVisions Cooperatives and the Friends Institute, are run as cooperatives. Other organizations, like the Rocky Mountain Farmers Union, offer children’s summer camps that teach cooperative leadership skills.

Cooperative education is also happening through efforts to form or reorganize universities as cooperatives. Operating a university as a cooperative allows students to live and experience values of democracy and civil participation, and, in this way, contribute to one of the purposes of higher education. Cooperative universities recast students and faculty as active participants in democracy, increase their personal investment in the institution, and challenge the modern university’s profit motive. Mondragon University, for example, operates as a workers’ cooperative. Students earn their tuition through working within co-op businesses within the university, which together enable the university to operate, while faculty invest in the university and receive surplus funds as a salary.

In addition to fostering social and economic democracy, cooperative education matters for a variety of practical reasons. One example is accounting. Traditional accounting systems are built to help managers and owners track, manage, and maximize profits for shareholders. But cooperatives serve the needs of their communities and are expected to balance financial sustainability with other goals like job creation, access to quality goods and services, and ecological restoration. Without protocols to track these broader goals, narrow systems for capitalist accounting can easily distort the core intentions of a coop. An unfortunate trap is that the MBA graduate with the wrong accounting tools can destroy the culture and value of a cooperative because they aren’t tracking and accounting for the right things.

The field of marketing is also an evolving discipline within cooperative education. Investor-driven businesses are structured to “buy low and sell high,” using cheap materials and labor and selling at the highest prices that customers will pay (voluntarily or not). At the same time, mainstream marketing trains consumers to connect personal identity and value to the things they buy, while ignoring harm to workers, the environment, or even to themselves. This kind of marketing doesn’t make sense for the co-op sector. If you’re part of a community-owned grocery store, what does marketing look like? Do you mimic traditional grocery stores that place candy at children’s eye-level so parents can’t check out without a fight? How might marketing for cooperatives create healthier and more responsible consumer patterns while ensuring customer loyalty and sales? Marketing and accounting, along with new approaches to human resources and governance, are among the most exciting innovations that cooperative education can bring to the private sector.

While Saint Mary’s University’s MBA program has now gained international recognition and attracted students from several countries, it faced notable challenges as the first program of its kind. It took years to secure a student pipeline to meet the school’s financial needs. The sector faces a vicious cycle: without co-ops, cooperative MBA programs struggle for viability. And without formal cooperative education, co-ops struggle to reach scale and market-share.

As the viability of formal cooperative education depends on market and regulatory conditions, the broadest task ahead is to inspire public belief and demand in a vision for a cooperative, just, and democratic economy.

entries.title: Cultural Sovereignty
entries.summary: People and communities have the right to express themselves. We protect and draw from our traditional cultures while ensuring that everyone is able create culture together.
entries.body: Whether we are dancing, singing, painting a mural, kicking a football, praying for rain, or gathering to honor our dead—our cultures are who we are. Culture tells us where we came from, where we are, and where we can go. Cultural sovereignty means we are in charge of how we embody, remember, and shift our cultures. It enables our many different ways of understanding and existing in our complex world to survive. Unlike white supremacy and other ideologies that are about preserving cultures of dominance, cultural sovereignty is about honoring our differences; navigating the discomfort, tension, and conflict that comes from encountering different cultures; learning to speak one another’s languages; and creating new ways of being together that build on our histories rather than destroying them. Our cultures tell us to meet our neighbors, to face our fears together, to listen. The art, culture, and meaning we make is our defiance of the forces that try to take away our humanity. We create to be human. We create because we are human.

entries.title: Debt Abolition
entries.summary: Over centuries, popular uprisings and indebted poor people have advocated for the abolition of debt and won. At a time when billions of people are harmed and oppressed by debt, the time has come for an international “jubilee” of debt forgiveness.
entries.body:
In most mature capitalist societies, people are required to go into debt in order to access basic education, housing, and healthcare. Borrowers become beholden to lenders, who then use debt obligations to control and coerce whole communities. The same process that happens on a community and individual level also happens at national and global levels. Wealthier nations wield debt obligations over poorer nations, compelling them to sell public utilities to private companies, slash social services, and enable the exploitation of their natural resources.

Today, global debt equals more than 3.5 times the value of the entire global economy, and it is growing.Yet history shows us that unjust debt can be abolished.

Movements calling for the cancellation of debts are growing. After the 2007–2008 foreclosure crisis and recession in the United States, a group called Strike Debt (now The Debt Collective) organized a “Rolling Jubilee,” which raised donations by crowdfunding, bought $32 million in outstanding debt for a fraction of its value, and forgave all of it. In recent years, mass protests against systemic racism and police brutality have led to calls to buy back debt in Black communities. During the 2020 global pandemic, social movements worldwide called for a mass cancellation of rent.

These movements have deep roots. The idea of periodic debt forgiveness appears in many religious traditions—most famously the Hebrew Bible’s “jubilee,” a law stipulating that all debts be canceled every seven years. Islamic law has long held that charging interest on debt is immoral, and it strictly forbids usury.

The tactic of buying back debt can yield results. By 2019, the group behind the Rolling Jubilee won $600 million in student debt discharges for 28,000 former students of Corinthian College through its debtors’ union. The Debt Collective found that these debtor organizing tactics to dispute and ultimately cancel debt were highly effective at making meaningful change in debtors’ lives.

Sonya Renee Taylor, a Black author and activist in the United States, spearheaded the #BuyBackBlackDebt initiative in July 2020. This decentralized mutual aid campaign is a way of “mending the relationship between Black people and white people,” she said. “It is about ending the relationship of extraction and benefit at the detriment of Black people’s lives, opportunity, wealth, and resources. It is about balancing karmic debt, spiritual debt, energetic and relational debt—so that we can figure out how to be in a right relationship with one another.” The mechanics of the project are simple: Taylor calls on white individuals to reach out to Black friends, colleagues, and family and offer to buy back some or all of their debt. To date, the project has bought $100,000 in debt through the participation of nearly 200 contributors.

Political movements are also aiming to challenge the global inequities created and sustained through debt. One grassroots effort, the Jubilee Debt Campaign, calls on the Global North and powerful global financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to support a debt amnesty that would eliminate debts owed by countries in the Global South, especially those whose wealth was stolen through colonization. This campaign recognizes that exploitative policies by institutions and nations that benefited from colonization have continued to oppress post-colonial countries by subjecting them to predatory indebtedness.

The Jubilee 2000 movement took important steps to shed light on one of colonialism’s current manifestations: the injustice of high-interest debt owed to countries and corporations in the Global North by countries in the Global South. Between 1998 and 2015, the campaign won $130 billion of debt cancellation for 18 lower income countries, including Ecuador, Burkina Faso, the Philippines, and Argentina. Already, those countries and others had resisted paying the debts owed to the IMF and World Bank for decades, and audits later revealed that much of the debt was illegitimate and violated international law.

What does abolition mean for people and countries forced to live with the burden of debt? The urgent health and economic crisis caused by COVID-19 pushed countries in Latin America and Africa into impossible decisions: pay back debt owed to the Global North or provide healthcare for their populations. People in the US faced similarly dire choices, often forced to decide between paying off their mounting debt from medical bills and education or affording food and housing.

Debt isn’t just about money. Debt is a power imbalance— often along racist and classist lines—that can mean the difference between life and death.

entries.title: Democratic Participation
entries.summary: People have control over the decisions that affect their lives. They have the right, ability, and responsibility to participate in building and protecting their communities.
entries.body: Democracy is a way of putting those who are affected by decisions in charge of making them. By giving people the power to manage their homes, communities, and relationships with the earth, we have a better chance of meeting everyone’s needs—not just the needs of a few powerful people. Achieving a healthy democracy requires us to connect with each other. That means we have to overcome the forms of isolation and disconnection we experience in the household, workplace, or neighborhood, or even on a national or global level. Democratic participation can look like workers organizing to take over a factory that has closed down, landless people living and farming on land where nothing has grown for decades, a neighborhood assembly deciding how their share of the city budget will be allocated, or a community deciding how to protect each other without involving police.

entries.title: Democratize Ownership
entries.summary: Our communities practice direct ownership and control of the things that affect our lives.
entries.body:
Ownership can have many meanings. owning a house comes with different rights and restrictions than owning a business, or an energy grid, or a patent, or the rights to a song. But one way or another, ownership confers the right to decide how something is managed and how any surpluses are divided and shared. The people who own something are generally also those responsible for stewarding it. If it is a company or organization, its operations are directed by its owners. Most things are owned either privately—by individuals, corporations, or nonprofits—or publicly by governments. But not everything can or should be owned. A solidarity economy seeks to expand the commons that nobody can claim to own for themselves. Capitalism, however, seeks to make as many things as possible into private property. Ownership can be done democratically, but under capitalism it most often is not.

We can change that.

Democratic ownership is when the core stakeholders in an entity control it together—as opposed to just a few people calling the shots. In a solidarity economy, democratic ownership and control allows us to determine the future of our lives, businesses, public utilities, the land, and everything else around us. When we are organizing in our communities, we must ask: Who should have the power to control this project or business? Who should decide how the profits are shared and how much the workers are paid? How should those decisions be made?

Which community members are impacted? How can they be involved in important decisions? What process would allow stakeholders to govern together in the service of our community?

Throughout this book, we spotlight a variety of examples and models of democratic ownership. There are many different ways to do it depending on the situation and the particular needs of the community.

Some forms of democracy are indirect. For example, in the United States, anything that is owned by the federal government is technically somewhat democratic, since US citizens elect their government. However, it’s a stretch to say that many federally-owned projects are democratically controlled; most do not enable the communities they impact to participate in their governance. That’s why, as a general principle, we prioritize local and direct forms of democratic ownership whenever possible. A solution that isn’t accountable to the communities it serves is no solution at all.

entries.title: Design Global, Manufacture Local
entries.summary: The rise of the internet age has seen the cre- ation of a digital “design commons”: a vast pool of knowledge and blueprints—for everything from farm equipment to malaria drugs—that is freely accessible to communities around the world, for use in local production and economic development.
entries.body:
Imagine a community of farmers trying to find more sustainable and effective ways to produce. Through prototyping, they begin to develop equipment specifically suited to low-cost organic farming. As they experiment with designs and test equipment, they refine their knowledge of what yields results for their community. Instead of keeping the fruits of their intellectual labor to themselves, they decide to share them with the world, publishing their designs online for any internet-equipped farmer to adapt to their local context.

“Cosmolocal production” is a term for the process in which globally shared knowledge and designs enable communities to meet their needs locally. The growing knowledge commons includes designs for farm equipment, medicine, food-processing tools, and renewable energy tech. The three main motivations that drive cosmolocal production include livelihood, problem-solving, and sustainability.

First, cosmolocal production has the potential to catalyze a livelihood revolution. For instance, L’Atelier Paysans is a cooperative that conducts farm equipment prototyping and design workshops throughout France, then shares its designs freely. Farm Hack is an association started in the northeastern United States that does similar work. Shared designs for tools like irrigators and cultivators can dramatically lower the costs of equipment that might otherwise be too expensive for small-scale entrepreneurs. This model, applied not only to farming but also to other industries, can revolutionize how people earn a living and provide for one another.

Cosmolocal production is also about problem-solving through production at a small scale. The international humanitarian relief organization Field Ready uses portable molds and 3D printers to support the recovery efforts of disaster-hit communities across southern Asia. Here, specialized medical equipment—or even basic tools like buckets to fetch water—can take weeks or months to arrive at a disaster zone. Field Ready’s approach moves production to sites of disaster to address the problem without delay.

Similarly, Open Source Malaria uses shared knowledge and community contributions to develop malaria-fighting drugs, which can otherwise be prohibitively expensive for people in poor countries. The Open Insulin Project in Oakland, California has adopted a similar approach to insulin production in the United States, where the drug is exorbitantly expensive due to price gouging and predatory patenting. What if these and other medications, once proven effective, could be produced by any sufficiently resourced lab in any country?

The third main contribution of cosmolocal production concerns transforming the destructive logic of industrial production into something regenerative, something that can drive a transition to emission-free production, carbon drawdown, and local control. Netherlands-based company Precious Plastics, for instance, designs machines that recycle and upcycle plastic waste into new products. It has cultivated an international community of designers and volunteers to develop the systems, and its machine blueprints can be freely downloaded so that any locality can build its own solution to the plastic crisis. In the Maharashtra area of India, Solar Urja freely distributes its design for a cheap, repairable solar lamp that can replace dirty-burning kerosene lanterns. In conjunction with Solar Urja’s rollout of the new lamps to villages, repair centers have been established to fix broken ones, creating local employment opportunities. Additionally, a cooperative run by local Indigenous people produces solar panels for the lamps.

Global challenges like the climate crisis are too urgent to allow profit-oriented intellectual property regimes to hinder progress. Patents on critical technologies can take decades to expire, and most people cannot afford to pay excessive royalties for the technologies that are fundamental for planetary survival. Open access to knowledge and design can enable communities to adopt low- or no-carbon technologies with minimal obstacles. When designs are shared, anyone can be a participant, a contributor, and an agent of change in creating a better world.

entries.title: Develop Community Leaders
entries.summary: We share leadership and knowledge across communities and generations.
entries.body:
This is a long journey. All movements for transformative change require many generations of leaders sharing their knowledge, wisdom, and power.

One of our most important jobs is to build the capacity of the generations that will come after us. This principle is about reproductive labor—the work required to nourish the people who are our future. How do we pass along what we learn? How do we make it easier for the people and communities who will follow in our footsteps?

Developing community leadership means creating the space to share stories, wisdom, and resources with others. It requires the humility not only to share but also to receive. It means asking what elders and youth might add to conversations that people in their 30s and 40s would otherwise dominate. It means asking why people may leave the community, and if we can do anything to support them to stay. If we open ourselves to the possibility that we also have something to learn, we invite the emergence of a deeper truth: regardless of our age, where we come from, or what we have done, we are all teachers, and we are all learners. When we approach leadership development as a two-way exchange, we allow everyone involved to become better versions of themselves.

We should also recognize that leadership development protects us from the system we are up against. Those in power have a long track record of attacking anything they perceive to be a threat to the status quo, including our leaders. That is why a movement full of many capable leaders is more resilient than one that depends only on a few key individuals. If any one person is too essential to a piece of work, it’s a threat to the work itself. We can all create ways for learning to happen across generations of leadership so that our organizations develop institutional memory and so our work can continue for the long haul. Capitalism is a global system. When we share knowledge and skills across borders, we protect each other and speed up the development of solidarity economies as a force that can withstand attacks.

Another way to think about leadership development is in cycles: the cycle of an individual human life, of the planet’s life, and of our movements’ lives. Each of these cycles depends on us to pass along knowledge and wisdom. We should not let individualism prevent us from understanding the ways in which our lives depend on each other and on those who came before us. We are never all alone and we are never starting from scratch.

We are all elders and ancestors in training.

entries.title: Energiewende
entries.summary: On April 15, 2023, Germany shut down its last nuclear power plant...
entries.body:
On April 15, 2023, Germany shut down its last nuclear power plant. For over six decades, Germans had been getting up to a quarter of their energy from nuclear plants. Over the years, the political will to phase out nuclear power often waffled, highly dependent on popular pressure. The 2023 phaseout was not inevitable: it was a hard-won milestone in Germany’s transition toward a safer, more democratic energy system.

In 1971, Germany’s government adopted its first environmental policy program and formed the German Advisory Council on the Environment. Environmentalists in the early 1970s had pushed for holistic changes in the system, including an overhaul of nuclear energy efforts as the implications of nuclear power became part of public conversation. Activists and farmers occupied a site intended for a new nuclear reactor in 1973, drawing much public attention to the movement. The occupation proved successful, but oil shortages caused by the Yom Kippur War—and, later, the Iran-Iraq War—created a renewed interest in nuclear energy.

Germany’s Green Party, founded in 1979, won its first parliamentary seats in West Germany’s lower chamber in 1983. Its elected members brought with them the notion of “Energiewende”—literally meaning energy transition or energy change—which called for a transition to a renewable energy system controlled by local communities.

A newly popularized understanding of climate change brought about a 1987 Green Party proposal to drastically reduce carbon emissions in the decades approaching the 2000s. At the same time, renewed opposition to nuclear power developed in 1986 following the Chernobyl nuclear plant disaster in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, and this opposition successfully pressured the German government to agree on a nuclear phaseout date. But, just when it seemed that the phaseout would happen, a conservative government rolled back plans in 2010.

Then came the Fukushima meltdown of 2011. The anti-nuclear movement surged once again, and the government responded to the massive pressure coming from the people, again re-establishing a nuclear phaseout date.

Today, the fight for clean energy continues in Germany. Nuclear is out, but in the face of new crises, the German people, the German government, and industry interests are again engaged in the push and pull of deciding the fates of fossil energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The Energiewende calls not only for green energy but also for a democratized energy system. Renewable sources can be owned by individuals, municipalities, and communities. This redistributes power over the grid through a bottom-up approach led by energy activists and community leaders.

Opposition to the Energiewende primarily stems from the coal industry, particularly mining trade unions. As a stable and relatively cheap form of energy, coal is widely supported by Germany’s industrial base. Jobs in the renewable sector are far less protected by unions and tend to lack reasonable worker contracts, and the transition requires an energy surcharge for consumers.

For the Energiewende and German climate activists, there have been significant setbacks. After the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020, the clean energy movement took a hit in its ability to organize demonstrations and campaigns. Then, when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine in early 2022 and Europe mobilized to pull away from Russian energy sources, there was a renewed effort for increasing development of new gas contracts and infrastructure. As Europe and Germany in particular face an energy shortage, in large part due to the invasion and sanctions on Russian energy, there has been a big push from powerful institutions like the European Commission to transition to natural gas as a bridge technology.

But the crisis is an opportunity. “Energy policy is a highly controlled, elite controlled policy field,” says Tadzio Müller, longtime climate activist, political scientist, and researcher. It took time, but it was public pressure from the German people that resulted in the nuclear phaseout. Despite setbacks and delays, “we re-established the principle that social movements can demand phase-out dates for dirty technologies,” says Müller, referring to a 2038 phase-out date for coal in Germany.

The Energiewende lives on, aiming to curb carbon emissions and create a carbon-free, renewable grid by 2050. But its implications run deeper. It stands for a future of decentralized, community-owned power as people claim ownership of renewable energy sources.
entries.authorBio: Daley is a writer and digital media creator whose work centers lived experiences from the American South. entries.title: Equipo Maíz
entries.summary: El Salvador’s civil war and state-sponsored death squads terrorized the nation during the early 1980s...
entries.body:
El Salvador’s civil war and state-sponsored death squads terrorized the nation during the early 1980s. Among the atrocities were the mid-Mass assassination of Óscar Romero—the Catholic archbishop of San Salvador who loudly condemned poverty, torture, and other rampant injustices—and the subsequent murders of 42 civilians at his funeral. Spurred by those events, a group of educators founded Asociación Equipo Maíz in April 1983.

Although many civilians were involved in armed conflict, the Equipo Maíz team believed that education, information, and analysis were needed to understand and challenge the social, political, and economic forces that led to the country’s unrest. The group, using minimal resources and meeting in community settings, started teaching poor Salvadorans about the issues affecting their daily lives, thereby providing a route for people to transform their social realities.

When the group was initially formed, its founders struggled to agree on a name. After a few years operating as Equipo de Materiales Educativos Populares (Popular Educational Materials Team), the liberation-focused members craved a name that encompassed the mission’s breadth. In practice, the group was not solely issuing instructional documents; it was teaching and mobilizing the Salvadoran people. Names like Cebadera (a common shoulder bag carried by peasants that is filled with animal feed) were considered before someone suggested honoring maíz (corn), the life-giving crop for the Mesoamerican peoples that is the building block for traditional tamales, tortillas, and economies.

Because Equipo Maíz arose during the civil war, its outreach and educational efforts were concentrated within El Salvador. But over time, word of the group’s popular-education methods spread and gained traction throughout Central America. This led Equipo Maíz to collaborate with numerous organizations, sharing its printed materials, workshop outlines, and training guides with organizations in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Mexico.

Equipo Maíz’s founders aimed to promote inclusion, foster creativity, and provide a path to liberation through knowledge. “Popular education is about using the wisdom of the people for community transformation,” said María Elsie Orellana, a Salvadoran women’s activist who has participated in Equipo Maíz workshops. It is not about one-off training sessions; rather, it is a process, brought about by necessity, that encourages the wholeness of participants while also building communities and their capacities. “Organized communities find the solutions to their own problems,” added Zulma Tobar, a coordinator for Sister Cities International. These communities, in turn, create a larger network of solidarity and creative resistance against oppression and human rights violations.

Equipo Maíz ensures all of its teachings are accessible and relevant. During the war years, some of the earliest workshops focused on themes from the Bible as a way to analyze social realities. This enabled members of the general public, most of whom were familiar with the Bible, to draw upon their existing knowledge as a path to complex discussions about topics of common interest. Popular education takes many different tangible forms, inspiring theater-style programs and other hands-on activities to engage learners of all levels.

Today, Equipo Maíz continues to hold educational workshops for communities about locally important topics. Additionally, it acts as a folk-academic publisher, authoring and releasing educational books on more than 60 topics, including climate change, ecology, gender equality, neoliberalism, peaceful protest, national history, and more. By providing its services to community groups that advance public power and social justice, Equipo Maíz counters the resurgence of far-right authoritarianism in El Salvador and across the region. While many citizen groups access its educational services free of charge, some entities—such as local municipalities or their international sister cities— are asked to pay.

Equipo Maíz’s outstanding achievement is its ability to produce publications in a language accessible to the people it serves. It creates educational and communication materials that democratize knowledge for different communities, such as historical and cultural documents and informative posters on sexuality. The publications seek to better understand the fundamental goals and effects of the economic and political decisions made by governments in the region, which has allowed human rights defenders to expand their political participation.

Equipo Maíz is governed by a representative democracy, in which the board of directors is elected every two years by an assembly comprised equally of workers and supporters. Those leaders are tasked with shepherding the organization, setting priorities, strategizing, and overseeing the four employee teams: education, sales and marketing, design, and printing.

Today, Equipo Maíz strives to incorporate younger generations, especially students, into its efforts of educating and empowering communities. Through accessible study of pressing challenges, Central Americans have the tools to sow greater equity and justice.

entries.title: Equity and Justice
entries.summary: Everyone has access to the same rights and resources, and together we are responsible for guaranteeing that access.
entries.body: Equity is not possible without a radical redistribution of wealth and power. Justice is not possible without healing harm and restoring the communities that were destroyed to create wealth in the first place. The ongoing harms of wars, prisons, and pipelines prevent healing from the past as it continues in the present. This means we must create new systems and structures to replace the violent and extractive ones we currently have, systems that ensure that every community has access to what it needs—from safety, food, housing, and healthcare, to education, transportation, and culture. We can call this abundance: a recognition that, collectively, we have enough. We can also call it abolition: an acknowledgement that our society is controlled by systems that are incompatible with equity and justice, and a commitment to remaking our world, together.

entries.title: Food Sovereignty
entries.summary: Food sovereignty is the right of communities to access healthy and culturally appropriate food and to have control over agricultural and food production systems. More than just access to food, it means being able to choose our food and to participate in producing it.
entries.body:
More and more communities today have little or no say over how their food is produced. With the rise of multinational agribusiness corporations, farmers are locked in a race to the bottom, competing to sell their products to middlemen at ever lower prices, while consumers continue to face rising food prices. Additionally, with more than 50 percent of the world’s population now living in cities, growing and gathering food is no longer part of daily life for most people. Many people around the world depend on aid for their food, which is often of poor nutritional quality and culturally inappropriate.

The concept of food sovereignty concerns communities’ rights to have autonomy and control over their food consumption, production, and distribution. But there are barriers to accessing food, like cost and availability, and the ability of people to produce food, which relies on having land and knowledge. The food sovereignty movement first gained popular attention in the mid-1990s through the efforts of La Via Campesina, an international network of farmers formed to defend peasant agricultural practices and to address the insecurity that farmers experience globally. The movement gained greater momentum in 2007, when the International Forum for Food Sovereignty was held in Mali. There, the Declaration of Nyéléni establishing a definition of food sovereignty was written and signed by representatives from over 80 countries. From the beginning, the concept was political. Then and now, it challenges widespread trade and agricultural policies, as well as the powerful interests that benefit from them.

There are many examples of initiatives that show us what food sovereignty looks like. Community-supported agriculture (CSA) programs, for instance, are based on a mutual commitment between producers and consumers to share the risks and rewards of agriculture. The CSA concept exists around the world under many different names and arrangements, shaped by the unique needs of the local farmers and consumers.

In Japan, the CSA model first emerged as the teikei system. Teikei, which means “cooperation,” is a system in which community members contract a farmer to grow for them for a season. The payment given to the farmer is not based on the crop yield, but rather reflects what the farmer needs for the season. For instance, a group of 100 community members had each member pay 1 percent of their annual income in exchange for 1 percent of what the farmer was able to produce that season. Teikei members also contribute the labor to the farm, including doing intensive tasks such as weeding, harvesting, and delivering produce to members’ homes.

As the concept has grown and spread around the world, CSA programs have drifted away from their original ideal of food sovereignty and toward consumer demands, with farmers often offering customized share sizes and making consumer participation in growing, harvesting, and distribution optional.

Another powerful initiative that supports food sovereignty are the cooperatives of small-scale farmers who band together to pool marketing, administration, and logistical labor and costs. At their best, these cooperatives enable farmers to reduce their costs and challenge large corporations head-on, while retaining local ownership, culture, and values.Yet these cooperatives, like CSAs, run the risk of compromising with the market and losing their community focus in pursuit of large-scale production.

At the national level, the battle for food sovereignty has brought together organizations and individuals to lobby governments to adopt holistic food policies. Food Secure Canada was formed as a coalition of local initiatives in 2001 under the banner of food security. In 2009, the coalition’s framework shifted to food sovereignty, which led to a national campaign to lobby the government for more inclusive food policies.

Food sovereignty must be grounded in local practice, but effective organizing and collaboration between grassroots organizations has led to the formation of international organizations such as the International Planning Committee on Food Sovereignty (IPC). The IPC has successfully introduced reforms and brought food sovereignty principles to the table of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. The IPC has changed how food security is discussed at the international level, bringing stakeholders to the table, such as peasant farmers, who were previously excluded in these policy meetings.

In the face of frequent temptations to compromise with the status quo, the principles of food sovereignty provide an essential North Star for the farmers producing our food, the communities striving to nourish their families, and everyone in between.
entries.authorBio: Do is owner-farmer- operator of a small urban farm in Vancouver, Canada, and co-founder of FarmCity Co-op, a producer cooperative of urban farmers. She holds a PhD in agricultural economics from Tokyo University of Agriculture, where she studied large-scale cooperatives in Japan.

epigraphs.quote: Food Sovereignty puts those who produce, distribute and consume food at the heart of food systems and policies, rather than the demands of markets and corporations.

entries.title: Free/Libre and Open-Source Software
entries.summary: Transparent software written by and for the people can help us avoid corporate exploitation of our pri- vacy, data, and money.
entries.body:
In a world where so much of the economy is based on private ownership, the rise of free/libre, opensource software (FLOSS) as a central part of the digital economy represents a striking act of resistance. At the core of FLOSS is the belief that people should control the technology they build and use, and that technology is a commons that works better when shared. The underlying code must be “open source”—meaning that anyone can access, examine, and verify it. For example, when developers claim a piece of software is secure or does not surveil its users, others can inspect the code and come to their own conclusions. FLOSS is also typically available free of cost, so it opens doors for communities that cannot afford to pay for expensive corporate software.

With FLOSS, users can “fork” the code—copying it and creating their own tools out of it. Some licenses, particularly those that go under the banner of “free software,” require that all adaptations of the code be shared under the same kind of license. The result is a non-proprietary digital commons—a pool of interrelated tools that no single company or person can claim exclusive ownership over and in which no single entity can constrain innovation by limiting access to the software’s code. An example of how this works is that, while Microsoft and Apple tightly control the releases of their operating systems, there are hundreds of free GNU/Linux “distributions,” customized to various user preferences and needs through diverse FLOSS communities. The competitive influence of FLOSS also helps to drive down the price of proprietary software. In Latin America, where FLOSS is widely used, a legitimate, licensed copy of Microsoft Office only costs $10, down from hundreds of dollars previously. Further, activist-led cooperatives (like MayFirst.coop) and collectives (like Riseup.net) can use FLOSS tools to provide services to movement groups without relying on corporate services.

Proprietary software generates profit not only through sales and subscriptions but through controlling user behavior and extracting user data. For example, while Facebook may be free to use, its terms of service allow it to use or monetize any content a user generates on its website without compensation or consent. Uber profits from the labor of drivers who have no way of knowing how the underlying algorithms that calculate payment for that labor actually work. In contrast, FLOSS projects disclose their algorithms and data collection practices, making companies that build products using FLOSS much less likely to engage in questionable business models. Although FLOSS began largely among hobbyists working during unpaid time, developers can increasingly earn income from the work they do, including by providing technical support, customization, and computing power to the people who use their software. They may also receive income from the crowdfunding, grants, or investment that are given to a project in good faith before it begins. With crowdfunding, people are often happy to lend their support when project developers can clearly explain a compelling vision of meeting a community need. This means that crowdfunded projects are more likely to be designed to meet community needs from start to finish. Grant funding works well for projects that serve the public interest. Increasingly, software companies are also paying their employees to contribute to FLOSS projects that their products rely on.

Still, many FLOSS projects experience challenges with sustainability over the long term. Although the FLOSS movement is well established, corporations undermine FLOSS projects in many ways, such as by encouraging features and improvements that suit their own needs and preventing efforts that could compete with their proprietary products. In some cases, such as Google’s Linux-based Android operating system, FLOSS tools have been used to enable widespread corporate surveillance. There are also frequent legal challenges to FLOSS; most often, this occurs when proprietary software uses FLOSS components and violates the license when they charge people for that software. Finally, relying on corporate hiring practices and hobbyists with free time means that FLOSS projects have struggled to attract contributors with diverse backgrounds, identities, and income levels. Keeping the commons truly shared and accessible requires constant vigilance and intentional effort.

As corporations increasingly use FLOSS software in products for clients engaged in surveillance, policing, and weapons development, many FLOSS contributors are organizing to demand higher ethical standards. The Ethical Source Movement seeks to build on the achievements of FLOSS by requiring users to adhere to international labor and human-rights standards. Others feel that such restrictions would ultimately harm the software commons by adding overly complex constraints.

Given its subversive ethos with respect to the dominant capitalist logics of privatization and profiteering, it is easy to mistake FLOSS for a small or marginal movement within the software world. But more than 90 percent of the software that runs the internet is FLOSS. Much of this software is well-known and widely used, like the Firefox web browser, the Android mobile operating system, and GNU/Linux, which itself has hundreds of different spinoffs. The power of a digital commons has become clear. Increasingly, the struggle underway is about whether FLOSS will ultimately serve ordinary users or corporate interests seeking to co-opt it.

FLOSS has many layers. It is a legal definition that challenges copyright. It is a method of open, transparent, and collaborative innovation. Most importantly, it is a culture for creating trustworthy software that respects its users and contributes to a digital commons for all.
entries.authorBio: Knodel is the CTO at the Center for Democracy & Technology in Washington, DC. Knodel takes a human rights, people-centered approach to technology implementation and cybersecurity policy advocacy.

epigraphs.quote: Free software means that the users have the freedom to run, edit, contribute to, and share the software. Thus, free software is a matter of liberty, not price.

entries.title: GreenWave Regenerative Ocean Farming
entries.summary: In 1992, at the height of industrialized fishing in Newfoundland, the cod stocks collapsed and 30,000 people were out of work overnight...
entries.body:
In 1992, at the height of industrialized fishing in Newfoundland, the cod stocks collapsed and 30,000 people were out of work overnight. Boats beached. Canneries emptied. As a commercial fisherman, I was face-to-face with the reality that there would be no jobs on a dead planet, and went on a journey of ecological redemption.

After oyster farming on Long Island Sound for almost a decade, it all came to a screeching halt in 2011 and 2012 when Hurricane Irene and Hurricane Sandy destroyed my farm. My farm and livelihood had become a canary in the coal mine for a climate crisis that arrived a hundred years ahead of schedule. Our fishing community needed another way forward.

Ocean farming is a trade both old and new, a job rooted in thousands of years of history, dating back to Roman times and Indigenous clam walls in the Pacific Northwest. It is also a way to synthesize the good and refuse the bad of industrial practices. We desperately needed a strategy based on one hard and fast rule: grow only zero-input species that won’t swim away and don’t need to be fed.

The design morphed into a vertical underwater garden: hurricane-proof anchors on the edges connected by horizontal ropes floating six feet below the surface. From these lines, kelp and other kinds of seaweed grow vertically downward, next to scallops in hanging nets, mussels held in suspension in mesh socks, oysters in cages on the seafloor, and then clams buried in the mud bottom.

These crops are regenerative—they breathe life back into the ocean. Shellfish and seaweeds are powerful agents of renewal. A seaweed like kelp is heralded as the culinary equivalent of the electric car. Oysters and mussels filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, removing nitrogen, a nutrient that is the root cause of the ever-expanding dead zones in the ocean. And these farms function as storm surge-protectors and artificial reefs, both helping to protect shoreline communities and attracting a range of aquatic species that come to hide, eat, and thrive.

This regenerative ocean farm design is replicable, affordable, and easy to build—it requires $20,000-$50,000, access to 20 acres of ocean, underwater rope scaffolding, and a boat. Once finished, it churns out a lot of food: up to 250,000 shellfish and 65 tons of seaweed on a mature 20-acre farm.

The regenerative ocean farm model is scalable. There are more than 10,000 plants in the ocean and hundreds of varieties of shellfish—we’ve barely begun to scratch the surface of what we can grow. And the demand for these crops is not dependent solely on food; seaweed can be used as soil amendments, animal feed, biomaterials, and more.

These crops hit the climate sweet spot—requiring no fresh water, fertilizer, or feed while creating economic opportunities for coastal communities. Ocean farmers can partner with the ocean to simultaneously create jobs, feed the planet, and fight climate change. According to the World Bank, a network of ocean farms equivalent to less than 5 percent of US waters can have a deep impact with a small footprint, creating 50 million direct jobs, producing protein equivalent to 2.3 trillion cheeseburgers, and removing the carbon equivalent to 20 million cars.

In 2014, I co-founded GreenWave with Emily Stengel to replicate and scale regenerative ocean farming. GreenWave works to spur collaboration and innovation with a global network of farmers, entrepreneurs, and researchers, all hell-bent on building community-based climate solutions out at sea.

GreenWave works with ocean farmers to replicate the model throughout North America and beyond to build a blue economy that ensures we all make a living on a living planet. The goal is to train and support 10,000 ocean farmers by 2030 to build community-based climate solutions out at sea that yield positive environmental and economic impact at scale.

When more than 8,000 aspiring farmers signed up for GreenWave’s training program, the organization pivoted their strategy to expand their reach and jumpstart the industry. GreenWave launched the Regenerative Ocean Farming Hub in April 2022, a free online resource including a suite of seed-to-sale courses, more than 80 how-to videos, interactive farm design tools, and an online community for aspiring and active farmers to connect and propel the industry forward.

In addition to training and technical assistance, GreenWave supports small- and medium-scale seaweed farms through climate subsidies; market cultivation across food, agriculture, biomaterials, and other industries; as well as the development of farmer-owned kelp seed hatcheries, dock-side processing, and storage infrastructure.

With ocean agriculture still in its infancy, we have an unprecedented opportunity to build a food system from the bottom up. Together we can avoid the mistakes of industrial agriculture and aquaculture, farm for the benefit of all, not just the few, and weave economic and social justice into the DNA of the blue-green economy, all while creating millions of jobs and feeding the planet.
entries.authorBio: Smith is the co-executive director of GreenWave and owner of Thimble Island Ocean Farm. He is a commercial fisherman and award- winning author who is widely recognized for his pioneering developments in regenerative ocean farming.

entries.title: Guifi.net
entries.summary: In the rural mountain communities outside of Barcelona, Spain, fiber optic lines run across the land— from east to west and north to south...
entries.body:
In the rural mountain communities outside of Barcelona, Spain, fiber optic lines run across the land— from east to west and north to south. These lines supply internet access to the region’s farmers and villagers. The access they provide is thanks to Guifi.net, a telecommunications network that is governed democratically by the members it serves.

Guifi.net began in late 2003 to solve a specific problem in the village of Gurb in Osona County: little to no internet access. While urban centers in Spain were already connected, most rural villages lacked access. In Gurb, the only place in town with the internet was the town hall. This was because, under Spanish law, internet service providers (ISPs) are required to provide service to every town. For-profit ISPs could fulfill the minimum legal requirement by providing internet to only the town hall in rural villages like Gurb. Facing constituents who were angry that their representatives had internet access while they did not, elected officials welcomed the Guifi.net solution with open arms.

Starting as a single connection across rooftop antennas, Guifi.net then expanded and installed more nodes that could send and receive WiFi signal among them, sharing connectivity throughout the network. Eventually, in 2009, the network added fiber optic lines. Now, it has established over 36,000 working nodes, connecting not only Gurb but many other villages to WiFi. The network creates a common pool of bandwidth to which neighbors can contribute and from which they can draw, and this continues to grow as more participants join. Members receive bills that separate how much of their payment goes to construction and operational costs and how much gets reinvested into the network.

Guifi.net is explicit in its anti-capitalist motives. Its model disrupts the traditional telecommunications economy by fostering a collaborative economy and a commons. It rejects exploitation of user communities and favors a sustainable, mutually beneficial network infrastructure. The project sees internet and telecommunications access as a human right and aims to provide connectivity for groups who are traditionally excluded.

The infrastructure and services provided by Guifi.net are funded by donations, loans, subsidies, and member payments. The project also brings in money through the Guifi.net Foundation, which was founded after Guifi.net received the National Telecommunications Award from the Catalan government in 2007.

Unlike many for-profit companies, speculative and extractive practices are explicitly forbidden by the organization. To protect the network against exploitation, Guifi.net is a direct democracy where governance occurs through participatory meetings. It has three groups of stakeholders: public interest, altruistic, and in-return. The public interest group comprises the administrative bodies; the altruistic group is made up of volunteers and donors who do not seek repayment; the in-return group seeks some benefit for themselves either by offering services for fees, or fees for services.

Guifi.net isn’t the only network of its kind. Similar telecommunications networks include the Freifunk network in Germany, or FunkFeuer in Austria, a citizen-led provider that taught Guifi.net how to use its technology. Beyond this, there are other communities in diverse locations, from Slovenia to rural villages in Mexico, who are actively developing their own wireless networks.

In today’s world, internet access is not simply desirable but is essential for exercising other important rights and for accessing a wide range of further resources. It supports freedom of expression, education, communication across boundaries, and connects people to the information they need to defend their rights around housing, land, energy, and so much else. The countless rural communities who, under capitalism, lack internet access because supplying it is not profitable for ISPs, do not need to wait any longer. Like Guifi.net, communities can take steps to understand how these networks work, reach out to community members and international partners, and build mesh networks of their own.

entries.title: Health Mutuals in Mali
entries.summary: More than two decades ago, the chief physician of the Center for Community Health in the rural community of Nongom-Souala in Mali noticed the center’s services were largely unused by the region’s over 10,000 inhabitants...
entries.body:
More than two decades ago, the chief physician of the Center for Community Health in the rural community of Nongom-Souala in Mali noticed the center’s services were largely unused by the region’s over 10,000 inhabitants. Nongom-Souala is primarily home to agricultural workers in the cotton industry, who struggle to afford healthcare, especially in the winter after harvest season when they are short on cash. To remedy this, the center’s chief started Cotonniers de Nongon Souala (MUT-CO NONGON), a healthcare mutual that was the first of its kind in rural Mali.

The idea is simple: a mutual is a form of community insurance where members pay a regular fee with the understanding that the funds will help any member who falls ill. Membership fees are between 1,000 and 2,500 CFA francs a month (equivalent to $2 to $5) plus an annual fee of around 3,000 francs, depending on the mutual, and cover 70-80 percent of healthcare costs.

In the last 25 years, healthcare mutuals in Mali have grown exponentially as a mechanism for providing universal access to care. In 1998, the Malian government established the Union Technique de la Mutualité Malienne (Technical Union of Malian Mutuals), a federated structure for mutuals. Presently, it includes 115 mutuals of which 108 are exclusively health mutuals that together provide for 35,000 people.

Most health mutuals arise for reasons similar to MUT-CO NONGON: people living in poverty suffer disproportionately from health problems, which in turn exacerbate poverty through lost wages and the costs of care. Mutuals attempt to intervene in this cycle by improving poor people’s access to healthcare and being responsive to local needs. In Mali, health mutual members can afford to utilize twice the amount of health services as the national average.

Unlike private health insurance companies, health mutuals only serve one community and are run by their members. All members are part of a general assembly that elects the board of directors to make decisions. Mutuals often have no employees, ensuring all fees go to the membership. While corporate insurers prioritize profits, mutuals can put their members first. The rise of the mutualist movement in Mali has increased access to healthcare for workers in agricultural and informal industries, which represent 78 percent of the population. In 2010, the Malian government began co-funding 50 percent of mutual membership fees for these workers and continues to support mutuals through government grants. Mali remains the only country in Sub-Saharan Africa to have a legislative and regulatory framework for mutuals. Mutualists hope that eventually they will be able to provide access to healthcare for everyone in the agricultural and informal sectors, and they continue to advocate for Mali to establish a universal form of healthcare.

entries.title: How do we care for our people as we take action on the side of life and adapt to a changing world?
entries.summary: Human civilization is out of balance with nature...
entries.body:
Human civilization is out of balance with nature. For centuries, industrialization and global capitalism have polluted the air, burned down rainforests, and wiped-out countless species of plants and animals—warming the climate to levels that endanger much of life on earth. The impacts of this ecological devastation are significant and only getting worse, and they tend to hit hardest in communities least responsible for the damage: people who are forced off of their land; who are living near dirty-energy factories and suffering high cancer and asthma rates; whose agricultural harvests are devastated by drought, flooding, and erratic growing seasons; or whose access to healthcare makes them more vulnerable to global pandemics. Those who justified this destruction in the name of economic growth are learning too late that there is no economy on a dead planet.

In our lifetimes, we will determine the fate of our species and millions of others through the decisions we make about the climate crisis. A lot of choices have already been made, but there are also many others awaiting us that matter.

So what do we do with this responsibility? How do we take action on the side of life, for ourselves and for one another? How do we end centuries of ecological destruction while at the same time protecting our communities from the impacts of a changed climate? Indigenous communities at the frontlines of climate chaos have been leading the way to creative solutions rooted in ancient wisdom. Over and over, they show us that the corporate capitalism and the overconsumption that got us into this mess will not get us out of it, and that change will come from grassroots movements and communities.

“Relentless consumerism is unattached from rationality or from the pursuit of balance between our needs and what nature can provide,” says Ayala Lindabeth Dias Ferreira of the Brazilian Landless Workers Movement. “The sense of time for nature differs from that for capital.” What does this mean for our solutions? How do we reconnect human needs with what nature can provide?

We must also ask ourselves how to govern our communities to navigate unfolding crises locally and regionally, while communicating and coordinating globally. Environmental impacts do not respect borders, and so we must work together across them with a sense of shared responsibility and mutual care and respect for one another, on nature’s time. We must put our support behind those experiencing the worst of the impacts, knowing that their fate is bound up in ours. And we must demand that those responsible for the crises pay for the solutions.

Because the problems facing the earth and atmosphere are so big, change will not happen overnight. The impacts of a destabilized climate are already here and will continue for centuries to come. We can meet the despair that comes with what is dying with the hope that comes with the possibility of new ways of defending life. We don’t know what the future holds, but we do know that solutions grounded in care and cooperation will help us mitigate the crisis, adapt to the impacts, and claim meaning and joy in our lives.

entries.title: How do we create and adopt new technologies without deepening inequalities?
entries.summary: Technology is often framed as an almost magical, unstoppable force...
entries.body:
Technology is often framed as an almost magical, unstoppable force. We’re either told that technology will solve all of our problems, or that technology will take our jobs, robots will rule the world, and all we can do is learn to live with it. How else could we understand this relationship?

Technology is a tool; its value depends on how it is applied and its impacts on society. Humans have created increasingly complex technologies to solve problems. But sometimes one person’s problem is another person’s solution. Whether we’re talking about shovels, tractors, smartphones, or spaceships, technologies can help us or they can work against us. Like everything else, who owns and controls it matters. How can we ensure that technology is driven by community needs and not corporate profits? How do we make sure new technologies include everyone, and not just the wealthy and powerful? Not all technology is necessary. When does it make sense to choose not to develop that next piece of military technology or corporate-controlled AI—and how do we make those decisions together in a democratic way?

Alfredo Lopez, a founder of May First Movement Technology, a cooperative membership organization that advances “the strategic use and collective control of technology for local struggles, global transformation, and emancipation without borders,” considers technology to be valuable when it is controlled by people—not by profit-hungry corporations. Decentralized and democratic ownership challenges the exploitation that we find in tech hubs from Silicon Valley to Singapore. For Roger Baig-Viñas of Guifi.net, a grassroots telecommunications network that brings internet access to previously unconnected communities in Spain, good technology is that which is accessible to a greater number of people while also serving to promote the exercise of other civil and human rights, such as free expression and open access to knowledge. Participation is critical; people and users must be included in decision-making processes and understand the implications and consequences of different technologies.

We can’t expect technology to solve social problems for us. Often technologies that seem to solve problems in one area can create other problems elsewhere. Solar panels and electric batteries, for instance, require mining rare metals and minerals in ways that harm communities and the earth. We must pay attention to the impact that our technological choices have on the world we’re trying to build, and we must ensure that the communities most impacted by technological change have a seat at the decision-making table. When communities control their technology, they can challenge monopolies and the unintended consequences that are rampant in big tech. We can begin by building on the work of organizations that show us that technology can be as diverse and creative as we are, and can be employed to serve the interests of everyone.
