entries.title: How do we move beyond incremental reforms to real changes that transform the system?
entries.summary: Our solutions need to meet the scale of the problems our communities are facing...
entries.body:
Our solutions need to meet the scale of the problems our communities are facing. But how? These problems are so immense and interlinked that it can seem like fixing something in one area just creates another problem somewhere else. One of the most frequent critiques of the solidarity economy is that anything we build won’t be powerful enough to contend with the economic power of multinational corporations burning the planet and exploiting workers.

It’s true that a single project—or even all of our projects put together—won’t bring about the solidarity economy our communities need. But the point is not to add up all of our projects or deploy a single global solution. The point is to cause a sea change, a shift in culture that can transform the world. We are not alone in this. As builders and cleaners, teachers and artists, healers and scientists, planners and engineers, we can channel our collective brilliance into imagining and creating a livable future. We are growing our solutions within and alongside powerful movements that are mobilizing millions of people to put an end to oppressive regimes and claim sovereignty over their land and livelihoods. We are connecting and weaving our solutions, creating networks where our cooperatives and community projects can work together and support one another. If we do all this, we can create a whole that is much greater than the sum of its parts.

We feel pressure to compromise and accept policies that improve things for some without addressing root causes. Or we replicate solutions from elsewhere without considering the specific context that allowed the solution to thrive in the first place. How do we resist the impulse to compromise and demand what we actually need? How do we create solutions that are both visionary and designed to confront the root causes of harm in our communities?

We need to discern between what moves us closer to the world we want and what might co-opt or undermine our vision. Some solutions are ready to be tried elsewhere. Some compromises are worthwhile. Some political reforms might not get us to where we need to go but change something about the underlying rules of society, making transformative change more possible. The philosopher André Gorz spoke of “non-reformist reforms”—seemingly small achievements that point toward, not against, more radical change. On the other hand, some projects might have all the right intentions—and even look transformative from the outside—but in reality make problems worse, contributing to gentrification and displacement, exploiting the people they are meant to serve, or setting communities up for disappointment by having unrealistic expectations. We must turn our attention to the details of the projects we are building, while simultaneously thinking bigger. We must get better at learning from the times that our projects don’t live up to their commitments, or even cause harm.

Transformative change requires us to envision thriving local economies in relationships of balance and reciporcity with each other and the rest of the living world.

entries.title: How do we relate to government and state power in growing solidarity economies?
entries.summary: Governments can support or undermine our efforts to build solidarity economies...
entries.body:
Governments can support or undermine our efforts to build solidarity economies. State support for solidarity economies can come in the form of enabling policies and public investment. In some places, the cooperative movement is deeply embedded in government through political parties and tax law. In others, colonial and oppressive governments have repressed solidarity economies because community self-determination weakens top-down control. Almost everywhere, public policy gives advantages to capitalist ownership at the expense of collective power. We can push governments for the policies and resources to support our efforts and we can grow solidarity economies autonomously, without resources or support from the state.

We must relate to government and state power as it is, even as we organize for it to be something else. We can form alliances with governments and the people in them. We can align ourselves with politicians to build our power, and we can cultivate our own people to seek office. We can also work outside of government, designing solutions that do not require its participation or that even escape its notice. If we consider the solidarity economy as part of a “dual power” strategy, which calls for building alternative institutions (like cooperatives) and counter institutions (like political groups and federations) to defend those alternative institutions, we can challenge the state’s control of society and shift power toward new forms of self-governance.

Government is only one kind of governance—which is, broadly, how we make decisions about how to use our collective power and manage our common resources. In the world we’re working toward, democracy happens everywhere, not just in the politics surrounding governments. We decide how powerful and centralized governments should be, and what kinds of democracy we can practice within them. When we practice democratic governance in our daily lives, we have opportunities to learn about how to make those decisions, and to acquire the skills and perspective we need to self-govern.

Finally, the governance of our communities today is shaped by nation-state borders that privilege multi-national corporations and the Global North. We envision solidarity economies in a world organized instead by bioregional and ecosystem boundaries, with governance by and for those affected by the decisions we make—governance that can meet the needs of the land, the water, and all creatures who live here.

entries.title: How do we relate to the borders drawn by colonialism and empire, and to peoples’ need to move across them?
entries.summary: Borders are enclosures—just like fences or property lines, they impose artificial limits that restrict movement and turn collective resources such as water and energy into commodities that can be bought and sold...
entries.body:
Borders are enclosures—just like fences or property lines, they impose artificial limits that restrict movement and turn collective resources such as water and energy into commodities that can be bought and sold. Borders represent claims of power over land and of the right to exploit it. They have been especially useful for colonizers, who invented them to seize and extract land and resources and to divide people who might fight back.

We don’t often pay attention to the things that are allowed to pass through borders with little or no difficulty. The people who create borders usually move freely across them, as do corporate assets and the money of wealthy people. Migrating birds and deadly viruses pass across borders more easily than most people can. Displaced and poor people are often kept from moving freely by force. The hoarding of basic resources inside a country or region—while those outside suffer violence and ecosystem destruction—also creates a need to move. Migration has always been a fact of life, but the scale of forced migration due to war, poverty, and climate change is accelerating and destroying families and communities every day.

Unlike borders, boundaries are not inherently violent. Neither is migration. Boundaries are necessary for individuals and communities to claim their identities and self-govern. The boundaries we want honor life and invite change, while preventing extraction, privatization, and exploitation. Migration is a natural part of that change and creates opportunities for cultural exchange and for expanding our collective understanding of what it means to be human. The migration we want honors and seeks reparations for the theft of land and culture from Indigenous peoples, while also honoring and seeking healing for people living in diaspora.

As Michelle Mascarenhas of Movement Generation says, “Today, our communities are bound by borders created by nation states. As we shift to ways of meeting our needs in right-relationship with the living world rather than by taking it all, the containers for governance will shift from borders to boundaries. We can see the boundaries that the living world creates in Indigenous peoples’ territories that also relate to watersheds, foodsheds, and tradesheds. When those impacted by decisions are the ones making them, our governance will better take into account the needs of the land, water, air, and creatures of that place.”

Can we resist the borders maintained by force and honor the boundaries set by Indigenous peoples and communities? Can we resist forced displacement and support freedom of movement? How can our solutions redraw our maps of the world?

entries.title: How do we scale up solidarity economy ideas and solutions?
entries.summary: Capitalism says that bigger is better...
entries.body:
Capitalism says that bigger is better. What kinds of scale do we really aspire to? Yes, if we want to meet the needs of everyone in our communities, we need our grassroots solutions to grow beyond one place or community. But does scale mean large, powerful organizations with global reach, or does it mean networks of many small projects, powerfully organized? When does it make more sense for projects to stay small or local, and when should they be bigger? How should we support and plan for projects to evolve as they scale?

Nancy Neamtan, a founder of Le Chantier de L’économie Sociale, a membership organization that exists to promote and grow Quebec’s solidarity economy, talks about coordinated enterprise as a crucial aspect of scale—if multiple organizations work toward a collective goal, scaling up our efforts becomes more attainable. In a business that is struggling, owners can easily lose sight of their social mission as they make compromises to stay afloat. But if that project is part of a larger network, it can lean on others for support in hard times, and more easily expand and take risks when there are opportunities.

For Hanan El-Youssef, who served as director of strategy at the International Cooperative Association, including all members in governance processes should be considered a way to achieve scale, not an inhibitor of it. Thoughtfully adopting new digital tools like online voting and discussion can build widespread commitment in ways that closeddoor meetings among elites cannot. Julia Ho, of Solidarity Economy St. Louis, finds that scaling up becomes more possible when an organization repurposes tools that already exist in a community grounded in values and history; participation will spread more easily when it is based on what people already know.

There are a number of tools people have employed to manage the operation of solidarity economies at a larger scale while keeping real power at the local level.

One of these tools is the formation of federations, or umbrella organizations that are owned and run by smaller, more local groups or organizations. This happened in the English cooperative movement during the 1840s, when consumer-owned cooperative stores joined to form a national federation. The federation purchased and even manufactured goods for the stores at lower prices than they would pay on their own. They had national power together, grounded in local ownership. This model has been successful across the world.

Another pathway to scale is through networks. Networks are often democratic and participatory and tend to be less hierarchical and centralized than federations. Groups can usually come and go as they please, as long as they meet the core values and criteria of the network. Whereas a federation works best with a clear, specific purpose, networks excel at connecting diverse independent projects to support various collaborations. Networks are excellent ways for clusters of businesses and organizations to coordinate across sectors of the economy.

Finally, whether we’re talking about federations or networks, it’s important to note that we’re not only talking about economic coordination.Yes, these forms of group governance help our solidarity economy enterprises reach larger economic scales. But they can do much more. Successful networks and federations make it possible to build collective political power beyond the scale that any one project could reach alone. They can also help solidarity economy groups form alliances with other social and political movements. By coming together across sectors and movements, we can assert our power in ways that can change laws in our favor, like changing the tax code to make it easier to convert existing businesses into worker cooperatives. Some cooperative federations even form their own political parties that develop platforms and candidates for office.

Ultimately what’s needed for effective economic and political coordination will differ from community to community, but if we want to change society, we have to find ways to coordinate and share power across locations, sectors, and movements.

entries.title: How do we stop depending on violent systems to make us safe?
entries.summary: Police, militaries, and prisons were not created to make people safe...
entries.body:
Police, militaries, and prisons were not created to make people safe. They were created to protect wealth and property through force. They were created because the only way to maintain an unjust distribution of resources is with violence.

When have you felt safe? What conditions came together to create that sense of safety? For many of us, our imagining and experiences of safety do not include images of armed officers and barbed-wired walls. Safety is the care and support of our families, friends, and communities; it is a nurturing environment in which it is okay to feel all the joy and pain and contradictions of life; it is access to health, food and water, and beauty.

War, policing, and prisons are built on an assumption that people are disposable. Solidarity economies are built on the opposite assumption: that life is inherently sacred, and we can’t throw anyone away. This means we need other ways to resolve conflict and keep our communities safe.

In a world where there is enough to go around, why are we plagued by conflicts over land, water, and power? Many conflicts have at their roots a small number of massively wealthy and powerful people who stand to benefit at the expense of everyone else involved. Millions fight and die for their causes. Could these same millions change the structures of power and find different solutions to our problems? War, policing, surveillance, and incarceration are all tools for expanding and maintaining empires, large or small, by dominating people and pitting them against one another.

So how do we bring about other ways of keeping our communities safe?

There is no one answer. We’re talking about building a different culture, where we actually believe that the lives of everyone around us matter. Even if they have different values. Even if they have different ways of existing in the world. Even if they have caused harm. There are no shortcuts to this culture shift. Our task is the long, hard work of building communities rooted in care and respect for our common humanity. In this, abolitionist movements are leading the way to a world beyond police, prisons, and incarceration. We can learn so much from the long histories of these movements about how to transform conflict, and how to end and heal from violent systems, in our households, neighborhoods, and nations.

The root causes of much of the violence in our world today lie in an economic and political system that needs people to be poor. Solutions that restore economic control and ownership to our communities have the power to attack these roots, and ultimately make a safer world for all of us.

entries.title: Incarcerated Worker Co-ops in Puerto Rico
entries.summary: In most countries around the world, penitentiary systems are centered around punishment, not rehabilitation...
entries.body:
In most countries around the world, penitentiary systems are centered around punishment, not rehabilitation. That focus means that the people released from prison often re-enter society with few marketable skills, little money, and trauma from the years lost and the dehumanizing treatment they sustained while locked away. For those coming home to poverty, the likelihood of re-entering prison increases considerably.

Millions of people are incarcerated around the world, and many of them are subject to prison slave labor. This is a form of exploitation in which prisoners work grueling or dangerous jobs for corporate clients or the government. It is common for incarcerated workers to earn almost nothing, or a small fraction of the minimum wage, for their labor.

Incarcerated worker co-ops offer an alternative. Unlike prevailing systems of justice based on retribution, which expect a prisoner to suffer for their crime, incarcerated worker co-ops “return economic agency to those who are caged, giving them control over their livelihood and work experience,” says Jessica Gordon Nembhard, a US Cooperative Hall of Fame inductee and professor at John Jay College in New York City. Engagement in a cooperative enables incarcerated people to regain their dignity, while contributing to their families and communities in multiple ways. It also reduces recidivism, or the likelihood of a person returning to the criminal-justice system after leaving.

There are incarcerated worker co-ops in Italy, Canada, and Ethiopia, among others. On the Caribbean island of Puerto Rico, it was incarcerated people who started lobbying in 1999 for co-op education and the right to operate their own businesses in prison. They teamed up with the Puerto Rican League of Cooperatives and petitioned to change the law that had long barred them from running a co-op. After winning the right in 2003, they formed the artist’s cooperative Cooperativa ARIGOS. ARIGOS secured a contract with the Puerto Rican Department of Corrections, whereby the business pays 15 percent of its profits in exchange for production space and utilities in prisons such as electricity and internet. In addition, the co-op covers all costs for security and travel whenever its members need to go offsite to sell their art, especially at other co-op events around the island. After ARIGOS, more co-ops have formed in Puerto Rican prisons.

Through a co-op, incarcerated workers can gain some control over their working conditions and an ability to improve the dignity of their work. Income earned can be distributed as remittances to family members back home. The remainder is then paid out upon their release from prison, to help get their lives on track. By the time they are released from prison, co-op members will have developed employment-ready trade skills in carpentry, pottery, sewing, horticulture, or even solar technology. They also pick up other skills like problem solving, teamwork, and decision making, along with general knowledge of cooperative business practices. As a result, they are better prepared to either seek traditional jobs or collaborate with others to establish new co-op enterprises outside prison.

Of the dozens of men who have participated in Cooperativa ARIGOS and then been released from prison, only around 5 percent have been rearrested. The average recidivism rate in Puerto Rico, on the other hand, exceeds 50 percent. (For context, the United States has one of the highest recidivism rates in the world, at about 76 percent, and Norway has one of the lowest rates at 20 percent.) Equipped with new skills, social connections, and funds, co-op members have a better chance of succeeding upon their release. The ARIGOS model—and other programs that champion the dignity of prisoners—can be applied to existing prisons to aid in the transition away from punitive systems and toward prison abolition.

“When you’re in jail, the correctional department doesn’t care whether you’re doing better, whether you’re learning. They don’t care what you do. Just do your time and go home,” said Alan Vicéns, a former prison co-op member in Puerto Rico. “But this beautiful co-op system gave me theory and practice. It made me a better person,” he continued.

Despite the many benefits of such a system, there exist various barriers to its expansion. Certain laws, including those that prohibit entrepreneurship among incarcerated people or prevent the mere formation of co-ops in prisons, need to be changed. Prison administrators are constantly rotated in and out, often corresponding to each election cycle, so they need to be educated about—and convinced to endorse—the cooperative system. Though some of the public has yet to be convinced, the positive results of incarcerated-worker co-ops demonstrate the importance of efforts to enhance prisoner autonomy and dignity.
entries.guidesBio: Vicéns was the fifth president of ARIGOS co-op and an incarcerated person. Nieves Plaza is a marketing manager and former cooperative educator with more than 20 years experience with the cooperative model, always aimed at social responsibility and community work. She is a Chaplain for the incarcerated persons in Bayamón and Arecibo Penal Institutions. Gordon Nembhard is professor of Community Justice and Social Economic Development, in the Department of Africana Studies, John Jay College, City University of New York, and she is the author of Collective Courage: A History of African American Cooperative Economic Thought and Practice.

epigraphs.quote: The prison co-op is a positive thing, from the education it provided me to its values and principles. It has given me possibilities.

entries.title: Informal Settlement Networks
entries.summary: Residents in informal urban settlements are form- ing organizations and networks to demand their human rights and improve their quality of life.
entries.body:
The industrialization of cities in the global South has spurred economic growth. But that growth often does not appear in the incomes of the poor and working-class people whose work makes industrialization possible. Governments, both local and those providing aid from abroad, consistently fail to address the needs of these groups. Refugees, survivors of environmental disasters, and people who have been displaced due to discrimination by race, class, and other identities find shelter in informal settlements in countries including India and Kenya.

While informal settlements, or slums, are characterized by overpopulation and a lack of basic amenities like sewage systems, they are home to vibrant communities. When these communities organize themselves into networks at the local, national, and international levels, the settlements are able to share knowledge, collaborate, and create strategies for building power and meeting their needs.

Savings groups provide one of the building blocks for these networks. Here, community members pool together their money to form a fund that can be drawn from to support projects and meet needs in the community. In South Africa, one fund has loaned money to more than 2,000 members for business and livelihood projects, and it has a 95 percent repayment rate. But these savings groups do more than just pool money. As one member of a Liberian informal settlement network reported, “They collect people and build a critical mass. When the savings groups are networked, federations are born.”

For example, in Kenya, 15 to 20 women might form a network, supported by a small amount of funding that enables them to train and work together. Their network would then become part of a city-wide federation of other small networks. Each local group or settlement chooses its leaders—chair, secretary, and treasurer—and then creates teams: a finance team, a data team, and a documentation team (which trains young people to collect data through GIS, gather stories, and contribute to a blog). The leaders of each of these local networks congregate every three months in city and county forums to discuss challenges and decisions. Reports from local meetings are delivered by a representative of each county at the national level. At the national level, a working group of 12 people are selected according to their skills for partnering with governments and officials.

Informal settlement networks raise the voices of people living in slums, making their lived experiences and realities the basis for change. Instead of a top-down approach, the residents of the settlements decide what projects are most important for addressing their needs.

One of the primary needs facing informal settlements is secure housing tenure. Just about every informal settlement around the world is dealing with constant evictions and the immense harm these cause to residents. By organizing together, informal settlement networks can fight back.

In Nigeria, large-scale evictions in Lagos and Port Harcourt inspired the Nigerian Federation to support community-led mapping and profiling of informal settlements. They collected data from every informal settlement in both cities and used GPS boundary maps and geo-tagged information about the utilities (water, electricity, etc.) to make the informal settlements visible and support community members organizing to prevent evictions. At the same time, an allied NGO called the Nigerian SDI Alliance used multimedia to shine a public spotlight on the crisis.

Women are at the center of many of these settlement networks—negotiating for space, organizing for the right to stay, and building necessary infrastructure. Women often organize the savings groups and hold leadership roles that reflect their knowledge as shapers of their communities and as those who are most negatively affected by poor conditions in the settlements. The data they gather is used in negotiations with local governments, and the money and resources they pool are used to meet acute needs in emergencies. Peer-to-peer learning occurs as one group of women trains the next on savings collection, data aggregation, and negotiation tools.

These networks connect settlements locally and around the world. One of the primary connectors of settlements globally is Slum Dwellers International, an organization made up of more than 30 federations (or networks) of informal settlements in Latin America, Africa, and Asia which supports learning and collaboration across national and regional borders. Federations working to stop evictions in India compare their experiences with those of federations in Kenya. Data collection methods are adapted from one settlement to another. Local leaders attend meetings with government officials in different parts of the world to share strategies for success.

Informal settlement networks are an important example of the grassroots power that poor people can have when they come together to provide for one another and demand what they need.
entries.authorBio: Daley is a writer and digital media creator whose work centers lived experiences from the American South.
entries.guidesBio: Patel is the founding director of SPARC India, one of the co-founders of Slum Dwellers International (SDI) and former chair of the SDI Board. Muturi is the chair of the board of SDI and a national community leader with Muungano wa Wanavijiji, the Kenyan slum dweller network affiliated to SDI.

entries.title: Islamic Finance
entries.summary: 1,400 years ago, Islamic scholars recognized the fragility of economic systems built on interest and categorically forbade it...
entries.body:
1,400 years ago, Islamic scholars recognized the fragility of economic systems built on interest and categorically forbade it. They reasoned that money alone is not productive, so simply lending it should not produce more of it. Instead, value should increase or decrease according to people’s real-world productivity. At this time, Judaism and Christianity also opposed the charging of interest, but only in Islam has this legacy survived to the contemporary world in any widespread fashion.

Increasingly, people are realizing the global economy needs alternatives to dominant practices of interest-charging and debt. Economists have found that as people and businesses take on more and more debt they don’t invest as much in people, innovation, and other things essential to a healthy economy. Despite this evidence, policies and business practices around the world still favor debt-based financing and the interest that comes with it. But the longstanding tradition of Islamic finance reminds us that other ways of doing finance are possible.

While Islam welcomes loans, it uses debt as a form of redistributive finance, rather than as a profit-making tool for the already-wealthy. Islamic economics puts emphasis on mechanisms that foster widespread ownership through shareholding and risk-sharing. It encourages partners who take on some risk to share in the profits and losses. Mudaraba, for instance, is an Islamic finance instrument dating back to when Islam’s founder, Muhammad (peace be upon him), entered a partnership with his later-wife Khadija; she provided the capital and he provided the skill and labor, and they both shared the risk. When investors and participants share both risk and return, there is no incentive for dangerous financial projects such as the exchange of a debt for a debt or “shorting”—which helped produce the 2007–2008 global financial crisis by enabling investors to profit when borrowers don’t pay back their loans.

Fair trade, socially responsible enterprises, and shared investments make up the backbone of contemporary Islamic economics. Islamic tradition also recommends a wealth tax known as zakat on idle assets—those not generating revenue but requiring maintenance costs—which reflects an expectation that rich individuals and companies should circulate wealth in the economy rather than putting the burden on those dependent on an income. This tax then becomes a source of interest-free capital for future entrepreneurs.

Much of what is practiced in global financial markets today contradicts the values of Islamic finance. In the predominant forms of capitalist economics, interest-bearing debt is an integral feature. For most individuals and businesses, the only way to access capital is by taking on an interest-bearing debt. This makes borrowers beholden to lenders who, rather than sharing risk, profit from the interest on the loans and take possession of collateral offered against them. This allows lenders to increase their wealth regardless of the outcome and pushes borrowers into financial turmoil. Today, usury—the practice of lending money at extremely high interest rates—is a major contributor to wealth inequality.

It is difficult for alternative financial practices to function alongside and compete with dominant financial practices of today’s global capitalist system. Most of the Islamic financial sphere has side-stepped fundamental Islamic principles in order to maximize profits. This means there aren’t many working examples that can demonstrate the true potential of an Islamic finance model. But some entrepreneurs are working to change this.

After civil war broke out in Yemen in 2015, a London-born Yemeni named Faris Sheibani opened Qima Coffee to introduce Yemen’s specialty coffees to the world, using the company as a vehicle to improve the livelihoods of local rural communities sustainably. Modest loans played a vital role in Qima Coffee’s growth. With the help of flexible three-year payment terms, Qima Coffee became the largest specialty coffee exporter in Yemen, now working with 2,500 farmers across the country and selling to 26 countries globally. Sheibani went on to set up the Qima Foundation to direct the success of the coffee business toward serving Yemeni communities by making loans to local enterprises. In the spirit of Islamic finance, instead of imposing fixed repayment terms, Qima encourages entrepreneurs to move toward profitability before a 12-to-36month repayment period begins.

One could compare Qima Foundation’s interest-free loans with microfinance—small loans extended to unbanked communities. But most microfinance initiatives that have arisen in recent decades are rooted in conventional capitalism and interest-based practices. Qima offers an innovative approach through an incubator program based on the same age-old forms of support and financing that Qima Coffee received on its own journey.

There are aspects of the internet economy that are well-suited to be managed according to the principles of Islamic finance. Rewards- and equity-based crowdfunding, for instance, is a financial tool centered on communities pooling money rather than interest. But currently the model is rife with abuse. Most crowdfunding platforms don’t hold their campaigns to any ethical standards. As many as 9 percent of Kickstarter campaigns fail to deliver a single reward to supporters, enabling the campaigners to pocket their crowdfunding wins. The absence of guidance or education has resulted in a 64 percent failure rate for crowdfunding campaigns across the various platforms that host them. Since large crowdfunding platforms are financed by venture-capitalists, their business models privilege creators who can raise large sums at lower cost, through ripe access to resources, capital, and networks. This is a disservice to social enterprises led by women and people of color who are more likely to lack such privilege.

Inspired by the tradition of Islamic finance, UpEffect emerged in London in 2016 to address the failures of modern finance to empower and equip entrepreneurs addressing today’s most pressing problems. Through rewards-based crowdfunding, campaign management, and strategic consulting, UpEffect helps enterprises engage in real economic activity, avoid misaligned investors, and raise capital directly from customers to grow revenue. In contrast to the average industry success rate, UpEffect’s crowdfunding coaching model has led to a formidable 95 percent campaign success rate for social entrepreneurs. 70 percent of UpEffect campaigns have been female-owned and 65 percent have been led by people of color.

In 2017, actuarial practitioner Raza Ullah co-founded Primary Finance in London, a cooperative reinventing home buying by creating ethical alternatives to traditional mortgages. Its product enables home buyers and investors to enter into equitable partnership arrangements that form a virtuous cycle of risk-sharing and shared ownership. Home buyers are able to purchase a home by making monthly payments similar in cost to a traditional mortgage, but without any burden of debt. Meanwhile in Chicago, Muslim community organizer Hoda Katebi co-founded Blue Tin Production, a sewing cooperative run by refugee and immigrant women to address the fashion industry’s reliance on sweatshops, which, in turn, normalizes violence and exploitation. Profits are shared and distributed equally among the members every quarter, and all the members (minus one) are stitchers. Through organizations like Primary Finance and Blue Tin Production, the long tradition of Islamic finance converges with other traditions to promote inclusivity and solidarity in our economies.

Projects like the above demonstrate how financing instruments can enable shared ownership and equitable capital distribution on the path toward a more just economy. Alongside other global traditions, Islamic finance shows that efforts to imagine alternatives to economic exploitation go back a long, long time.

entries.title: La Coperacha
entries.summary: In 2005, a group of independent journalists collaboratively produced a magazine entitled El Coyote Itinerante (The Traveling Coyote in English)...
entries.body:
In 2005, a group of independent journalists collaboratively produced a magazine entitled El Coyote Itinerante (The Traveling Coyote in English). The magazine explored local and regional issues of identity, culture, and community values. Through constant interaction with their communities—particularly in Coyoacán, a village south of Mexico City—the journalists discovered a trend. People throughout the country were working to transform their economic realities through business models such as cooperatives and collectives. Most of these initiatives did not receive media coverage, though, and seemed absent from public knowledge.

What they uncovered led them to form a digital media cooperative, La Coperacha, in 2012. The cooperative reports full time on Mexico’s grassroots democratic economic and social agenda. Its goal is to publicize successful local and regional efforts toward social transformation and gain both media attention and formal recognition for such efforts. The material La Coperacha covers is diverse and interconnected, documenting collective artmaking, free and cooperative technologies, efforts to defend land from unsustainable exploitation of natural resources, and the political and environmental impact of these topics and others. The cooperative’s website features written articles, video, audio, and other media.

As a cooperative, La Coperacha is democratically governed by its journalists, whose cohesion and discipline leads to solidarity and trust within the group. The cooperative model allows them to work in an environment governed by values like democracy and participation, which closely mirrors the values that guide the content the group produces. A core team of regular journalists executes daily administrative tasks like project management and finances, in addition to their own reporting, while contributors occasionally supply additional content.

La Coperacha receives funding from a few different sources. Other media and communication co-op projects provide some financial support while advertisements from social enterprises in La Coperacha’s publication provide additional revenue. The group also draws funds from awards and collaborations with local governments or organizations to cover certain issues. As with any media organization, though, financial sustainability is one of the greatest challenges and La Coperacha is always seeking new opportunities for funding partnerships.

La Coperacha is prolific. The worker-owners have produced over 2,500 pieces of journalism, 185 radio episodes on public radio, and five radio series. They have won the National Prize for Journalism twice—first in 2011, before officially organizing as a cooperative, and again in 2018 for the radio series Manantiales en Resistencia, which documented local and regional efforts to challenge problematic policies of the National Water Commission.

Manantiales en Resistencia is a prime example of the stories La Coperacha creates. The series uplifts the stories of Zapotec, Cucapás, and Totocanas communities in Guanajuato and Tecámac who fight for the right to water and its sustainable management. La Coperacha’s reporting makes space for stories that profit-driven media companies won’t or don’t normally cover. They both practice and write stories about democratic innovation, popularizing collective processes and community sovereignty through both their organization and their journalism.

La Coperacha also provides accessible resources about collectives and cooperatives throughout Mexico, from artisans to coffee co-ops to medical groups. Their efforts to disseminate this information began long before the media group organized into a cooperative. In 2007, La Coperacha had a webpage offering information about local cooperatives for conscious consumers and “cooperation among cooperatives.” With the formation of the G50 Network of Cooperatives, La Coperacha created an official digital directory of Mexico’s co-ops.

The organizations that make up the G50 network are an important part of La Coperacha’s mission. Groups must apply for certification as a G50, but once they are approved, they receive recognition and a profile with their mission, services, and contact information on La Coperacha’s website.

La Coperacha is working to expand reporting in isolated areas of Mexico that receive little to no media coverage. This commitment to inclusion and focus on community-based solutions defines La Coperacha as it continues to publicize efforts for social and environmental justice, cooperatives, and the solidarity economy.

entries.title: Land Justice
entries.summary: All people have a right to permanent and secure land tenure as the source for many of our most basic needs. Through tools such as reparations, rematriation, easements, and land trusts, we can share the land fairly among the human and non-human citizens of planet Earth.
entries.body:
The theft and private hoarding of land is part of the DNA of racial capitalism. Around 60 million hectares of the Global South is gobbled up by transnational corporations annually. In the United States alone, over 95 percent of the farmland is white-owned and increasingly corporate-controlled. This is the result of the violent expulsion of Indigenous people from their homelands, as well as the systematic exile of Black and Brown people from their land through government discrimination, lynching, redlining, and corporate land grabs. Colonial powers have imposed private property throughout much of the world, changing people’s relationship to land to one of property, as opposed to Indigenous understandings of land as a family member and a shared commons.

“To us in Africa, land was always recognized as belonging to the community,” said Julius Nyerere, the first president of Tanzania. “Each individual within our society had a right to use the land, because otherwise he could not earn his living and one cannot have the right to life without also having a right to some means of maintaining life. But the African’s right to land was simply the right to use it; he had no other right to it, nor did it occur to him to try and claim one.”

Millenia-old Indigenous land sharing tools like the huza cooperative system of the Krobo in Ghana and the matrilineal clan-based collective land ownership outlined in the Kayanerehkowa (Great Law of Peace) of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy demonstrate that private enclosure is not an inevitable phenomena. This essay discusses five legal tools that build on Indigenous wisdom and can support the work of land justice.

A land trust is an organization that holds land or conservation easements to protect properties for a public or environmental purpose. The first community land trust, New Communities Inc., was founded in 1969 by Black civil rights activists who had been violently attacked for their voter registration work. They purchased 5,700 acres of land shared among 500 families and established residences, cooperative farms, and a community center.

Building on this legacy, the Northeast Farmers of Color Land Trust, established in 2017, has been working to purchase 2,000 acres of land over the next five years to return to Indigenous, Black, and Brown farmers and land stewards. This land will be permanently protected through the legal mechanism of agricultural and cultural easements.

A property easement is a legal agreement where the title to a parcel of land remains with the landowner, but another person or organization is given use rights for a distinct purpose. While easements for conservation, agriculture, and utilities are most commonly known, the Native Land Conservancy (NLC) of the Mashpee Wampanoag is pushing forward the newer idea of cultural easements. Indigenous peoples’ rights to use their homelands for gathering, ceremony, burial, fishing, and wildcrafting can be restored using a cultural respect easement, which guarantees permanent access to the land even if ownership changes hands.

After recognizing where land has been stolen, rematriation is profoundly and simply an act of giving the land title back, with particular attention to the leadership of Indigenous women and trans people. The Sogorea Te’ Land Trust rematriated its first property in Huchiun territory, Bay Area, California, a traditional village site named Lisjan, which is now home to ceremonial grounds, gardens, emergency water catchment, and youth programs. Settlers can give their property deeds to native land trusts or directly to tribal entities, as in the case of the Ponca tribe accepting the return of their land along the Trail of Tears in 2018.

Near the end of the US Civil War, Rev. Garrison Frazier and 20 other Black Baptist and Methodist ministers met with Union General William T. Sherman to request allotments of 40 acres of land for each freed Black family in an area independent from whites. Fazier and the ministers explained, “We feel it very important that we obtain HOMES, owning our own shelters, and the ground, that we may raise fruit trees, concerning which our children can say, ‘These are ours.’” The Union agreed to give these allotments, but the famous promise of “forty acres and a mule” as reparations to former slaves was broken, and reparations were instead given to the plantation owners for their lost “property.”

The call for reparations continues today, through the work of the Movement for Black Lives and the Truth and Reparations project. Reparations has the potential to return 36 million acres of land to dispossessed Black people via public trust, and would guarantee cessations of harm, compensation of damages, and the restitution of livelihood and dignity.

Land justice, however, is not just a matter of changing who owns the land—it means recognizing that the earth cannot be owned by humans. We are guests on this planet, the younger siblings of creation, and we need to infuse our relationship to land with commensurate humility.

entries.title: Landless Workers' Movement
entries.summary: The Landless Workers’ Movement (Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, or MST) began to build its power in Brazil during a period of military dictatorship...
entries.body:
The Landless Workers’ Movement (Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, or MST) began to build its power in Brazil during a period of military dictatorship. Though officially founded in 1984, the group’s formation began in the early 1980s, as the rural poor came together to fight back against displacement from their land by powerful landowners and the rampant human rights violations that came with it.

The tumultuous political landscape of Brazil following the 1964 military coup (backed by both the US government and the Catholic Church) paved the way for extreme concentration of wealth—in particular, by perpetuating the concentration of land ownership which had marked Brazil since colonial times. This made Brazil a frontier for the growth of global capitalism, growth that excluded, displaced, and further impoverished rural people. Modernization of agricultural practices through widespread mechanization put farmers out of work and prevented them from renting land or even participating in sharecropping. The rural poor, now landless, began organizing throughout southern states of Brazil to demonstrate their right to work on the land. They occupied lands that sat unused, building tents and cultivating crops and livestock. Eventually, through pressure and negotiation with the government, many of these occupations became “agrarian reform settlements” in which the peasant families received formal rights to remain on the land. As the occupations spread and participation grew, their power increased to assert the ideals of democracy and push against the military dictatorship.

Occupying unproductive land has become the MST’s trademark. Its efforts led to the amendment of the Brazilian constitution in 1988 to say that land must be used to fulfill a social function. This means that the land must not only be used for the private interest of its owners, but also for the public interest, including being reasonably productive, making fair use of natural resources, and observing labor laws. This gave the MST an historic and transformative legal basis for its occupations.

The movement’s structure enables the direct and collective participation of everyone involved. Through delegating tasks and encouraging participation in collective decision-making processes (which are open to all families in the MST), the movement ensures strong bonds among its members. MST activities also help shift agricultural production toward agroecology, which is practiced in many agrarian reform settlements secured by the movement; in fact, the movement has become the largest producer of organic rice in Latin America. The MST estimates that it has helped 450,000 families secure formal land rights in agrarian reform settlements. Hundreds of thousands of families have participated in its more than 2,500 occupations.

Despite legal protections, the MST’s land claims continue to be threatened. The mid- to late-90s and early 2000s were particularly violent. In Pará in 1996, military police killed 19 landless workers in the Eldorado dos Carajás Massacre. An additional 69 people were wounded, with two dying from their injuries. Later, between 2020 and 2022, Brazil hit new historic records of violence in rural areas. State violence against the movement is ongoing as the MST faces continued displacement and human rights violations.

The MST is not the only movement in Brazil with goals of land reform. Other groups such as the National Confederacy of Agrarian Workers held a similar vision but implemented different strategies in their approach, such as forming labor unions. The MST, though, is set apart by its on-the-ground mobilization of farmers. The MST’s ideology is based largely on the idea that participants’ struggles and experiences—not the concessions of governments— are the path to progress.

Though land reform is still the MST’s focus, the movement has expanded to include a wider range of activities. These include interventions in education, health, human rights, and international relations. Local chapters gain support from their communities through educational projects, selling farming goods they produce, and reporting on human rights violations. More recently, the MST started promoting the so-called “Agrarian Reform Markets,” which give peasant families a chance to showcase their products to large urban audiences who are encouraged to support the movement. The MST rejects the uncritical consumerism and exploitation of Brazil’s capitalist class, particularly the exclusion and oppression of rural people. The movement advocates for a new agricultural model that finds balance and harmony between the needs of the people and the need to protect the environment. It challenges big agribusiness and proposes replacing capitalism’s social, economic, and political failures with a model that better serves the needs of the people and of the earth.

entries.title: Legislative Theater
entries.summary: Legislative theater is a participatory, community- based tool for proposing and enacting legislative and policy changes at any level of government.
entries.body:
In 1992, Augusto Boal, the creator of Theatre of the Oppressed—a set of practices that empower people to change society using theater techniques and games—was faced with a dilemma. His theater work was an international sensation. Centers for the Theatre of the Oppressed were up and running in both France and Brazil, and people all over the world were practicing his ideas. At the same time, he was facing pressure at home in Brazil to run for city council in the city of Rio de Janeiro. Faced with a choice between the two, Boal decided not to choose. Instead, he combined the two possibilities and passions into one—and legislative theater was born.

To those who say that theater is nice but has no tangible outcomes, legislative theater may be the answer.

Legislative theater involves a short play about a particular issue or set of issues that ends in a crisis that the audience is invited to help solve by taking the place of one of the characters on stage. Audience interventions are followed by a brainstorm and discussion of policies or laws that could solve the problems that came up in the performance, or that could help bring about some of the solutions “spect-actors” (the engaged audience) had offered during the performance. In some iterations of legislative theater, mock legislatures debate bills drafted based on the laws or policies previously suggested in the theater exercise.

Boal’s election campaign literature explained his rationale: “I want to make politics but I don’t want to change my profession—I am a man of the theater! For me, this was always possible and now it is necessary: Theater is political and politics is theater.”

Boal was one of 42 city councilors elected from a field of 1,000 candidates. Over the next four years he developed the methods of legislative theater, forming 19 permanent Theatre of the Oppressed companies in Rio, which led to the introduction of 30 pieces of legislation, 13 of which resulted in legal changes.

The version of legislative theater Boal developed while he was a city councilor was an ideal arrangement that has proven difficult to match since. In his case, the elected official was the main convenor of the process, and was therefore in a position to act on the recommendations that emerged. In other cases, without one or more elected officials directly involved in the project, or without a firm and genuine commitment to the project from elected officials, it may be harder to achieve such results. Therefore, it is advisable to seek out legislators who are willing to play a role throughout the process, including fighting for the resulting recommendations in the actual legislature.

Like all Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed practices, legislative theater trusts the wisdom of the audience, and provides them an opportunity to try out their ideas on stage to see how they might work in real life. Legislative theater simply takes that process one step further, making a direct connection between the ideas generated in the theater and the legislative process, which so desperately needs creative approaches to problem solving.

entries.title: Limited-Equity Housing Cooperatives
entries.summary: A limited-equity housing cooperative is a form of shared housing in which many individuals or fam- ilies jointly purchase housing, often a multi-unit home. Instead of owning a particular unit within it, each party owns a share of the property as a whole, which expands access to home ownership for lower-income people.
entries.body:
In many countries, home ownership is a time-tested path to financial security. But today, rental costs in urban centers across the globe continue to rise at a rate faster than income, making it nearly impossible to save enough for a down payment on a house. Expensive down payments and the skyrocketing cost of urban real estate have pushed home ownership further out of reach for many on low to moderate incomes. Communities need a model which serves the housing needs of these income groups over time. There is an accessible alternative to a lifetime of high rent payments to landlords: limited-equity housing cooperatives (LEHCs).

Buying housing as a group presents many advantages. The most obvious is that buying a share in a housing cooperative costs less than buying an individual unit. Members of a housing cooperative have joint control over the governance of common areas like green spaces and playgrounds, and in the US, owners of a share in a co-op are entitled to the same tax deductions as homeowners.

Housing co-ops have a board of directors composed of member-residents which is responsible for overseeing the management of the property and planning for future renovations, much like a homeowner association.

A limited-equity co-op is one in which the resale value of shares is limited. This means that if someone decides to leave the co-op and sell their share, they will receive the purchase price plus interest which is capped at a certain amount. Limiting equity helps to keep homeownership accessible to low- to moderate-income families by protecting share prices from the speculative market. Most members end up paying the equivalent of 5 to 10 percent of the unit’s total cost for their initial share as opposed to the 20 percent down payment generally required to get a mortgage.

Not all housing co-ops impose restrictions on resale value. In fact, most co-op housing units are sold at the market rate. Some only restrict resale value until the first mortgage is paid off, which normally takes 30 to 40 years. Limited equity allows co-op residents to reap the benefits of home ownership, while also keeping housing affordable for generations to come. Many limited-equity co-ops have income restrictions, where membership is restricted to lower-income applicants to prevent wealthier buyers from crowding others out. Laws and regulations supporting LEHCs vary from state to state and country to country.

In the 1960s and ’70s, LEHCs experienced explosive popularity in major US cities like New York, Washington, DC, and San Francisco, thanks to a broad range of financing options including low interest rates and affordable loans for prospective builders of new co-ops. However, after their first mortgages were paid off, many LEHCs transitioned to market-rate cooperative housing. The number of accessible, limited-equity co-ops in the United States has dwindled.Yet the model still shows its promise. In 2005, a building slated for demolition in the Chinatown district of San Francisco became the center of a long, difficult fight for a limited-equity housing opportunity. The San Francisco Community Land Trust, Asian Law Caucus, and Chinatown Community Development Center teamed up to buy the building and transform it into a cooperative. The tenants were able to avoid eviction and are now owner-residents of their limited-equity co-op.

Establishing a LEHC entails a lot of heavy upfront costs and efforts such as buying land, funding new construction, and navigating housing code and laws. The journey from idea to occupancy is normally about five years, which can deter those who might benefit the most from being part of a co-op. To make matters worse, traditional banks often refuse to finance blanket mortgages to groups of lower-income people because they perceive them to be high-risk borrowers.

In the United States, when the size of a LEHC is above 20 units, it usually requires a professional management company. In larger co-ops, the board members need training in governance, financial planning, management oversight, and conflict resolution. In effect, the resident board members are overseeing a sizable ongoing business and stewarding a multimillion-dollar asset. The turnover of board members means that the latter need continuous training to ensure their capacity keeps up with the organizational and corporate needs of the cooperative.

The limited-equity model is most common in the United States, but housing cooperatives with many different structures and models have developed and proven viable all over the world. Furthermore, this idea of established institutions creating housing opportunities can be seen in several other countries such as the Philippines, India, Turkey, Egypt, and Singapore. In Italy, housing cooperatives are managed by four national groups. Social housing cooperatives throughout the country provide accessible homes for the elderly and for people with disabilities. Over 200,000 people in the Emilia Romagna region of Italy live in housing cooperatives.

In some places in Scandinavia, 15 to 20 percent of all homes exist in some form of housing co-op. Two national organizations in Sweden, HSB (founded by consumer cooperatives) and Riksbyggen (founded by the construction trade union movement) leveraged their access to land and assets to become the two main developers of the nation’s co-ops. Prior to 1991, national and local government policies enabled the development of municipal or limited-equity housing cooperatives in Sweden through the provision of land at below market price and loans below market interest rates. By having prospective members fund capital accounts, HSB and Riksbyggen raised the capital to provide their members with access to affordable housing. With their resources, these national organizations set up housing units and then transferred management responsibilities to the cooperative. In Sweden, applicant members of HSB must fund a deposit account with the organization to be in line for a new co-op apartment. The funds of these 120,000 non-housed members are a key supplier of funds for HSB to build new cooperative apartments.

In Uruguay, Federación Uruguaya de Cooperativas de Vivienda por Ayuda Mutua (FUCVAM) brings together over 500 mutual aid housing cooperatives comprising more than 25,000 families across the country. Their model is built on five core principles: solidarity, democratic participation, self-management, mutual-aid, and collective ownership (i.e. limited-equity). Founded in 1970 to unite and build the power of the housing cooperative movement, FUCVAM has shaped housing policy across Latin America, supported the formation of housing federations, and, most importantly, provided access to housing for hundreds of thousands of people across the continent.

With the support of funding entities and government policy, LEHCs could bring the dream of permanently affordable home ownership to many more people. Coops like these also transform the dream itself from one of individual ownership, to co-owned and co-managed communities.

entries.title: Media Cooperatives
entries.summary: Corporate consolidation has combined catastrophically with the rise of targeted online advertising to degrade the quality and independence of journalism. In the resulting tectonic shifts, there are opportunities to build democratic media outlets that channel power to communities and workers.
entries.body:
Seismic shifts in how news is funded have plunged journalism into an extended crisis. As a result, movements and civil society have an opportunity to create a news ecosystem that is aligned with popular priorities. But this chance won’t last.

As tech platforms have cut deeply into advertising revenues, news organizations are more dependent on reader revenue, and this has given audiences more power. They now worry relatively less about corporate advertisers and relatively more about anything that could cause a wave of mass unsubscriptions. While this trend is broadly positive, the power of subscribers and donors remains mostly unrealized. A corporate representative can still influence coverage by conveying mild discomfort in a meeting about a multi-million-dollar ad buy. To match that, thousands of monthly donors would have to threaten to leave in unison.

The fact that these publications are for-profit means a big chunk of reader revenue is paying shareholders, not journalists. While no publication would exist without its readers, investors make the big decisions: hiring, firing, editorial mandates, and budgeting.

A truly accountable media economy needs readers to be actively involved in democratically shaping the news institutions they rely on. Media cooperatives, where workers and audience members collectively, proactively and democratically determine the direction of the organization provide an important example.

Cooperatives can take many forms, depending on their membership structure.

Worker cooperatives like Mexico’s La Jornada or Uruguay’s Brecha are democratically controlled by the workers. Consumer cooperatives like Germany’s Taz, England’s Bristol Cable or the NB Media Co-op in Canada are owned and funded by readers, who employ journalists to carry out the mandate. Multi-stakeholder cooperatives like Scotland’s The Ferret and Canada’s Media Co-op (of which this writer was a co-founder) bring reader-members, worker members, and sometimes contributors together on the board of directors.

In each case, members are involved in the big decisions. And when the model is successful, each media institution is more connected to the creativity and energy of its workers and readers. That can mean better coverage overall, resilience in times of crisis, and the ability to change leadership that is out of step with members’ needs. But a cooperative isn’t the only way for readers and workers to be represented.

In 2022, the Guardian pulled in nearly $100 million from online reader revenues—mostly monthly donations. A non-profit like the Guardian could, and should, have board seats reserved for representatives elected from its reader-donors. Readers should have a forum to discuss the priorities and standards of that institution.

Despite hopeful entrepreneurial rhetoric, reader-funded outlets are not growing fast enough to make up for the wreckage left behind by corporate media. To restore an economic basis for journalism—and create for the first time a vibrant and truly democratic media—bigger investments are needed. Government funding is a fraught subject, but it is possible to design such programs in ways that keep control in the hands of voters instead of bureaucrats or corporate actors.

On the scale of an individual reader, journalism is expensive. But if we think of it as a social institution on the level of schools or health care, it’s exceptionally cheap—about $20 per year, per person could double the number of journalists in any given country.

The challenge is to keep the interests and desires of each person connected to the value they create—whether by funding, reading or creating the news.
entries.authorBio: Oja Jay is a writer and organizer living in Val David, Quebec. Oja Jay currently serves as publisher of The Breach (breachmedia.ca) and executive director of Community University Television in Montreal. He is co-author, with Nikolas Barry-Shaw, of Paved with Good Intentions: Canada’s Development NGOs from Idealism to Imperialism.

epigraphs.quote: Whatever your first issue of concern, media had better be your second, because without change in the media, progress in your primary area is far less likely.

entries.title: Mutual Aid Finance in Montreal
entries.summary: Some people face difficulties getting loans because they are written off for being in debt, having bad credit, or lacking collateral...
entries.body:
Some people face difficulties getting loans because they are written off for being in debt, having bad credit, or lacking collateral. This is often tied to discrimination on the basis on their race, class, or immigration status. Instead of getting loans to help them build a business or return to school, they are denied and sent home empty handed.

Borrowers need access to lenders that understand their loan history, financial products that meet their needs, and repayment schedules that don’t punish them for having unpredictable income. Communities left out by banks and lenders need mission-aligned investors who understand that value is more than just profits and are willing to trust the borrowers and their communities.

Finance needs to be controlled by the people it is supposed to serve—or it can exploit them, as many “microlending” initiatives around the world have. Community-controlled finance is about building power. Consider an example from Quebec, a province known for its long history of cooperative entrepreneurship and innovation around social finance. MicroCrédit Montréal puts into practice the original ideals of the movement that shares its name. Aware of the potential risks of microlending, they have developed measures to avoid the cycles of extraction and exploitation into which some other microlending has fallen.

MicroCrédit Montréal emerged in 1990 from the Milton Park neighborhood, the site of important housing rights organizing that led to the creation of a multi-unit housing cooperative in the early 1980s. Organizers noticed the lack of investment in this mixed-income area, where affluent blocks are in close proximity to poverty. A committee studied this issue and created a local loan fund inspired by the 1977 Community Reinvestment Act in the United States, which outlawed certain discriminatory credit practices (like redlining) in low-income areas. Listening to the needs of the community, the organization now manages a business-loan fund for new entrepreneurs, and offers loan products for immigrants seeking local recognition of their foreign credentials. In both cases, MCM prioritizes lending to women.

Currently, over 70 percent of MCM’s business loans are extended to entrepreneurs of color, many of whom encounter barriers to loan approval, because they might lack local credit history, assets for collateral, or people to act as guarantors.

MCM’s Foreign Credential Recognition loans aim to end the common assumption that first generation immigrants must work low-wage jobs and hope that their children might do better. New immigrants to Quebec need to demonstrate their credentials to the Ministry of Education and professional associations. It can cost the equivalent of tens of thousands of US dollars to obtain official licensure. This type of loan helps fast-track the credential-transfer process so new immigrants don’t have to fall behind or sustain gaps in their professional work experience.

MCM analyzes every business project and meets with each potential borrower to listen to their needs and approach their venture from an informed perspective.

Marc Nisbet, who served as a loan analyst and business development coach at MCM, explains that applicants often express that it is refreshing to show up somewhere and be treated in a way that is aligned with their self-image, as entrepreneurs. “We could see it in their body language,” says Nisbet, “They would arrive with a defensive posture, that changed after we spoke with them for half an hour.”

MCM’s loan fund is financed by a mix of large and small investors, from the cooperative Desjardins Group to individuals willing to contribute at least $500 CAD. Anyone can support the program—the youngest investor was only eight years old. Investors receive interest payments of up to two percent and are updated about their investments and the capital pool twice per year.

MCM’s loans are repaid with ten percent interest—a rate far preferable to those of predatory lenders or credit cards, which on average charge 22 percent. MCM’s average loan is $6,000, up to a maximum of $20,000. All the fund’s earned interest is returned to the capital pool, which covers the interest paid to investors, as well as any losses. Then, that growing capital pool can go out into the community as new loans.

MCM’s employees, whose wages come from outside fundraising, support prospective borrowers throughout the entire loan-application process. A committee composed of volunteers and a member of the board of directors reviews completed applications; investors do not have a voice in that process. The majority-immigrant staff uses its knowledge of cultural practices around money to guide applicants. The board determines whether to approve or deny the loan, but entrepreneurs who have been denied can request an appeal to better understand the reasoning behind the rejection.

Although loans officially last up to three years, loan officers are flexible about life’s uncertainties and have the power to postpone loan repayments in some situations, in order to avoid placing borrowers in a situation where they are unable to repay.

What began as a local project has created spin-offs across the province, with 17 agencies under the umbrella of Micro Entreprendre. This is a model that depends on local knowledge and local power, but it can be replicated in many contexts.
entries.authorBio: Guico was vice chair of Cooperatives and Mutuals Canada until 2021. In her consulting practice, Guico focuses on updating local approaches to cooperative development to create space for new forms of labor and economic justice in today’s economy.
entries.guidesBio: Nisbet has over 15 years of experience in the social economy sector in the management of nonprofits, and is a part-time faculty member at Concordia University where he teaches community development. Krishnamurthy has worked in finance, banking, and the nonprofit sector, in addition to her firsthand understanding of immigrant integration, having moved from India to the UK and then to Canada.

epigraphs.quote: The trust that we grant through loans to people who face systemic barriers allows them to take their future in hand with dignity.

entries.title: Muungano Slum Dwellers
entries.summary: Kenya is a country of 54 million people, with roughly one in two living on less than $5...
entries.body:
Kenya is a country of 54 million people, with roughly one in two living on less than $5.50 a day, according to World Bank data. The capital, Nairobi, has a population of over four million and is a hub for economic migrants, young people, and displaced people from across the country who are looking for jobs and better opportunities. Urban population growth has expanded industry and education, but it has also created a need for housing and infrastructure that the country is not prepared to meet. The outdated system of urban planning employed in Nairobi is a holdover from British colonization, which continued into the 1960s. Today, over 50 percent of Nairobi’s population lives in informal settlements—or housing that is not recognized by the government—which make up less than two percent of the land mass.

Muungano Wa Wanavijiji—Swahili for “united slum dwellers”—is a Nairobi-based movement that emerged in 1996 in response to demolitions and evictions occurring in slums as a result of private development. Community members organized together and, through years of militant struggle, were able to stop the evictions and spark a movement that spread throughout Nairobi and then Kenya. Today, Muungano comprises over 100,000 people in 1,000 groups across Kenya. The movement has two main demands: secure tenure and access. “Secure tenure” means that every slum dweller, informal trader, and squatter should have a title and deed that recognizes their right to use the land. “Access” means every slum dweller should have access to clean water, health, basic services, and housing, among other human rights described in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.

Muungano reflects communities’ power to protect their rights, lands, and livelihoods as well as pushing for recognition of slums as important spaces not only for their inhabitants’ survival but also for the functioning of the city itself. The movement does not depend on external support. Instead, it emphasizes slum residents organizing themselves into networks that become part of city-wide federations.

In order to avoid stagnation within the movement, leaders are chosen at a community level rather than elected. This also keeps the movement from being used as a stepping stone for individuals seeking political power. In addition, Muungano intentionally develops women’s leadership, as women are at the center of communities and families and also suffer disproportionately from poor conditions in the slums. In Muungano, women are the leaders of data collection, savings, negotiating, and training.

In 2001, Muungano joined Slum Dwellers International, a global network of community-based organizations that mobilize urban poor people and slum dwellers. Through this connection, Muungano leaders learned the importance of data collection and mapping, and the need to strategically partner with the government. Although Muungano’s decision to work with the government has sometimes created tension, the movement has been able to leverage this relationship to access the services and information it needs. City officials have technical expertise and power to approve plans, and cities often own the utility companies, making them crucial partners in establishing both secure tenure and access to necessary services for slum dwellers.

Since its inception in 1996, Muungano has successfully shifted national policies around land and housing, gaining recognition for informal settlements, securing tenure in various parts of Kenya, creating housing projects, and securing access to services for thousands of slum dwellers. In 2003, Muungano established a finance vehicle, the Akiba Mashinani Trust (AMT), that can manage and hold assets for communities until those communities have the ability to manage them themselves. AMT also offers financial services like loans and savings for groups that might otherwise be excluded from the banking system and provides non-financial services like training, consultation, and technical assistance for Muungano members.

Thanks to the organizing of Muungano, more than 40,000 people have improved access to water and sanitation, and 7,000 homes and land rights to more than 140 hectares have been secured for Kenyan slum dwellers.
