entries.title: NDN Fund
entries.summary: NDN Fund is an indigenous-led organization which provides loans and investments to large-scale community and national development projects...
entries.body:
NDN Fund is an indigenous-led organization which provides loans and investments to large-scale community and national development projects. The fund is unique in scope and in structure: it seeks to invest in Indigenous communities while building Indigenous political power with the rallying cry: “Defend, Develop, and Decolonize.”

Starting in 2017, NDN Fund began with a vision to indigenize large-scale development, regenerative agriculture, food sovereignty, and equitable economic growth. Its parent organization, NDN Collective, is an advocacy organization for building Indigenous power. Creating the fund was a fundamental part of a strategy for transforming colonial economic practices through the application of Indigenous worldviews, knowledge, and perspectives.

NDN Fund is an emerging community development financial institution (CDFI), of which there are over a thousand across the United States. The community development sector has often played a paternalistic and colonizing role—or no role at all—in Native communities. There is a long and painful history of non-Indigenous populations seizing Native lands and imposing development models (including cooperative business models) on Indigenous communities across North America.

More recently, a dependence on federal funds has led to what former Managing Director Nikki Pieratos, a citizen of the Bois Forte Band of Chippewa, calls a scarcity mindset. Native Nations end up competing for scarce resources from the bureaucracy of the federal government—which throughout history has opposed and undermined Indigenous sovereignty and self-determination. The federal government’s investments often don’t align with the long-term vision of Indigenous communities; non-Native lenders, and the stakeholders they answer to, often fail to understand—and actively disregard—what is actually needed on the ground. When Indigenous communities look beyond government funding to commercial lenders, they encounter a predatory industry with high-interest rates and collateral requirements that exclude those who are not already wealthy. This industry has a history of extracting what little wealth remains in Native communities, which has led to community distrust of most outside lenders and funders.

The Fund provides an alternative route for Indigenous entrepreneurs by turning those extractive and paternalistic practices on their heads: it is run by Indigenous leadership, it gives decision-making power to Indigenous borrowers, and it practices an economics that aligns with Indigenous values.

What does an Indigenous economy look like in practice? The answers differ, of course, by community and context. The Minnesota Indigenous Business Alliance names eight values as being fundamental to building its understanding of an Indigenous economy: wisdom, humility, social responsibility, honesty, respect, equality, reciprocity, and love.

Guided by values like these, NDN Fund’s approach to project-based lending seeks to decolonize conventional financial practices. Firstly, tribal leadership has power over money, and the ability to control its own development—as opposed to the conventional model of top-down nonNative-led development. Secondly, lending is relationship-based, moving at the speed of trust—as opposed to transactional, volume-based operations. Next, NDN Fund practices a mindset of abundance over scarcity and incorporates this into its decisions. Finally, NDN Fund works to make its investments with nature and the wisdom of the land its ultimate guide, centering circular—as opposed to linear or extractive—economic relationships. All of these practices build on an Indigenous history of pre-colonial economics on Turtle Island, before capitalism dominated the continent.

This type of approach to development is rare for a financial institution. At NDN Fund, there is an ongoing practice of decolonizing “traditional” (read: colonized) underwriting and financing standards. According to Pieratos, “When we think of wellbeing, economic development is the cornerstone. But economic development for who? One of the most important and impactful things for Native communities is generational impact. To have a generational impact, we need to shift the way capital is flowing into communities.”

NDN Fund has already financed a number of projects through this decolonized lens: an eel aquaculture business in Maine, a Navajo-owned solar project in the Southwest United States, and a boat building company in Cordova, Alaska to support kelp harvesting. NDN Fund does not always require traditional collateral from the borrower and is creative in terms of what it requires to secure the loan. For instance, it has used equity shares and revenue sharing instead of requiring personal guarantees or asking borrowers to stake their homes or assets.

Another means by which NDN Fund seeks to “shift the way that capital flows” is through its sourcing of investment. Recognizing the restrictions that come with accepting federal dollars, NDN Fund has focused on bringing in flexible capital from private foundations, impact investors, and individuals. This has allowed it freedom in how it lends and who it lends to. With less red tape, it can structure project-based deals more creatively, create terms that work better for communities, and scale up the size of investments in a culturally responsive manner.

Defending Indigenous land rights is key to Indigenous sovereignty and, therefore, to developing strong Native economies through a decolonized approach. So, in addition to its development work, NDN Fund also builds Indigenous political power through supporting the return of Indigenous land with landback loans, such as the loan to Tzicatl Community Development Corporation for the purchase of land in Los Angeles to expand their language revitalization school.

That’s the power of “Defend, Develop, and Decolonize.” The three are interconnected, and one cannot happen without the others. NDN’s efforts in these three areas should be compelling not just for Indigenous peoples, but for everyone; as NDN President and CEO Nick Tilsen argues: “The liberation of Indigenous people is directly connected to the liberation of all people.” For NDN, to fight for Indigenous land sovereignty is to fight for collective liberation through movement building across all communities and generations.
entries.authorBio: McShiras is a fundraiser, storyteller, and business development strategist who has worked in student organizing, worker cooperative development, popular education, and impact investing, and currently serves as investment and fundraising director at the East Bay Permanent Real Estate Cooperative.
entries.guidesBio: Pieratos is a member of the Bois Forte Band of Chippewa and executive director of Tiwahe Foundation. She has over ten years of experience in community development finance, including by creating new models for resilient and regenerative lending and investing at NDN Collective. Pate is the managing director of NDN Fund, where she is responsible for the leadership, management, and growth of NDN Fund. She provides leadership in all aspects of the emerging Native CDFI.

entries.title: Participatory Budgeting
entries.summary: Through a local democratic process, community members directly decide how to spend part of a public budget. Participatory budgeting enables residents to work with their government to make decisions that affect their daily lives.
entries.body:
In 1989, the workers’ party implemented participatory budgeting in the city of Porto Alegre, Brazil, making it the first city in the world to have this. Participatory budgeting was intended to directly include citizens in government decision-making, after years of military dictatorship had excluded them. For nearly 20 years, as many as 50,000 people participated annually in making decisions on how to spend up to 20 percent of the city’s budget. In 2017, the practice was suspended by the newly elected Brazilian Social Democracy Party, which cited a lack of resources and a need to reform the process.

Despite the setbacks in Porto Alegre, participatory budgeting has spread to over 3,000 cities in Latin America, North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe since 1989. Most participatory budgeting processes involve the municipal budget in cities of all sizes, from ones with less than 20,000 inhabitants (e.g., Icapuí and Mundo Novo in Brazil, and Grottomare in Italy) to mega-cities like Buenos Aires, New York, and São Paulo. Participatory budgeting has worked in both rural municipalities (like Governador Valadares, Brazil) and completely urban ones (like Belo Horizonte), and in cities with both scarce and plentiful public resources. The process can be applied at any level of governance, including counties, states, housing authorities, schools and school systems, universities, and other public agencies.

Though each participatory budgeting process is different, most follow a similar basic structure: residents brainstorm spending ideas, volunteer budget delegates develop proposals based on these ideas, and residents vote on the proposals. The government implements the top projects and then begins planning and revising the process for the next time. For example, if community members identify recreation spaces as a priority, their delegates might develop a proposal for basketball court renovations. The residents would then vote on this and other proposals, and if they choose the basketball court, the city uses the funds they allocated to renovate it.

In fact, in the Kadutu community of the South Kivu province of the Democratic Republic of Congo, participatory budgeting led to renovations of basketball and volleyball courts in 2012. There, much of the process relies on mobile phone technology and SMS voting to ensure widespread participation. Throughout the province, participatory budgeting also led to the construction of nearly 60 new classrooms, a public health center, and public restrooms, along with the repair of a dangerous bridge.

Participatory budgeting relies upon both the political will of officials and community support. Someone with control over budget money (an elected official, agency head, or department director) must participate in the process and agree to let the public decide how to spend part of the budget. Participation from community organizations, particularly those working with marginalized groups, is necessary to engage people and push the process forward. The result is a process that is both top-down and grassroots.

Participatory budgeting does not require a new pot of money but a change into how funding decisions are made. Some resources are necessary to carry out the process, but this investment saves money down the road, as participants discover new ways to make limited budgets go further.

As with any kind of public participation, there is a risk that the individuals and groups with the most power will dominate the process. But this risk can be minimized by setting low barriers for participation, encouraging community members to both plan and lead the process, and doing targeted outreach to ensure inclusion of underrepresented communities.

Budgeting is a large part of what governments do. When community members decide spending through a public process, there are fewer opportunities for corruption, waste, or backlash. Ordinary people have a real say—and they get to make real political decisions. As a result, participatory budgeting tends to engage many people who are otherwise cynical about government. Politicians build closer relationships with their constituents, and community members develop greater trust in government. Participants become more active and informed citizens. Community members, staff, and elected officials learn democracy—by doing it together.

entries.title: Participatory Guarantee Systems
entries.summary: Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) facilitate the building of closer relationships among food producers and consumers involved in short sup- ply-chains by enabling for quality certification to take place on a local level. Organic producers and consumers use PGS to create healthy and resilient local food systems, to make organic certification more affordable and accessible, and to build trust and relationships.
entries.body:
The modern organic movement started as a response to industrial agriculture systems, with independent small-scale farmers choosing to sell their products locally and build direct relationships with their consumers. As organic began to grow as a sector, supply chains lengthened, meaning that the number of people and processes between the farmer and the family eating the food increased. Private, for-profit, third-party certification of foods became the norm. In many countries, including the United States, the use of the term “organic” is now regulated by the government and can only be used by producers with accredited third-party organic certification.

The organic sector is increasingly dominated by largescale agribusinesses that only produce one type of crop and long supply chains. Many small farmers are not able to manage the costs and paperwork requirements of third-party organic certification, and people living in areas where organic food is produced are often unable to access or afford that food.

Participatory guarantee systems (PGS) provide an alternative to third-party certification schemes that are specifically suited to local markets and short supply-chains. In a PGS, the producers, consumers, and distributors can define and enforce their own certification, based on the standards that are most important to them. Since each PGS is created by farmers and the communities they serve, the model is adaptable to local cultural values and community needs. For example, some PGS go beyond conventional organic certification standards to include a greater focus on issues like soil health, biodiversity, food access, or working conditions.

The International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM) maintains a directory of PGS initiatives worldwide and advocates for governments to recognize them. While many different forms are possible depending on the context, an initiative must contain the following elements to be recognized as a PGS: a shared vision, stakeholder (farmers and community members) participation, transparent standards and processes, mechanisms for building trust, non-hierarchical democratic structures, and an ongoing learning process. In 2020, the directory included 223 PGS initiatives in 76 countries serving more than 500,000 farmers.

Organic PGS initiatives are often linked to local market opportunities. In 2012, for example, a group of volunteers in Sri Lanka started a weekly market called Good Market, at which all farm products for sale had to be organically grown. One of the most common questions from early visitors to the market was: “How do I know this is organic?” Large organic exporters had third-party certificates for their tea, spices, coconuts, and tropical fruits, but small-scale farmers who grew organic rice, legumes, and vegetables couldn’t afford export-level certification. This imbalance worked against creating more sustainable, sovereign food systems.

In 2013, a local farm hosted a weekend retreat for producers and consumers who were interested in making organic certification more affordable and accessible. The group used the IFOAM Organic Norms and experiences of other PGS initiatives as a starting point, and then over time added additional standards and processes based on their requirements. For example, they decided that consumers should be able to participate in all farm visits, and they developed an assessment form with a “star system” so they could distinguish between farms that just barely met the organic standards and farms that were adopting regenerative practices to build soil and increase biodiversity. All materials were translated into Sri Lanka’s three local languages.

Farmers who are verified under the PGS are able to sell through marketplace events, local retail outlets, and organic delivery services. Local consumers tend to prefer PGS over third-party certification, not only because the products tend to be more affordable, but also because the process is transparent. They can find out what farm a product comes from and can partake in farm visits. Everyone involved feels a collective responsibility for maintaining this trust in, and the reputation of, the PGS. The consequences for non-compliance are clear. Farmers lose their organic-certification and are no longer able to supply through organic market channels.

While PGS initiatives are most common in local food systems, they can provide a low-cost, community-owned alternative to private third-party certifications in other sectors as well. PGS works in any context where community stakeholders agree on a core set of standards, a process for verifying those standards, and a transparent recordkeeping system.

entries.title: Policies for Cooperatives
entries.summary: Public policies are often designed for the benefit of profit-focused businesses and disadvantage co- operative enterprises. But legislation can—and in many places around the world already does—sup- port cooperatives and enable them to flourish.
entries.body:
Member-owned companies around the world are achieving great success in certain industries, from insurance and software to dairy and textiles. Studies repeatedly find that co-ops are as productive as—or even more productive than—their investor-owned counterparts. And they have proven more resilient than capitalist businesses during periods of systemic financial crisis. However, in most regions of the world, cooperatives comprise just a small fraction of all businesses. If co-ops are so beneficial, why aren’t they more widespread?

Government agencies, financial institutions, and the laws that spell out how enterprises must operate can help or hinder the cooperative sector, depending on how they are designed to understand cooperatives and promote their growth.

In many places, co-ops encounter financial and administrative obstacles that their investor-owned competitors don’t face. In markets designed to serve wealthy investors, co-ops can struggle to access the funding they need to flourish and grow. Conventional banks are often reluctant to give loans to co-ops that have a few members or have unconventional business models. To them, shared ownership can appear confusing or excessively risky. So-called impact investors rarely know how to work with cooperative startups and may demand a right to vote on and veto decisions in a manner that is incompatible with the interests of members. Therefore, co-ops often must seek alternative means of funding like subsidies, grants, tax exemptions, preferential procurement by public authorities, and more. Even regions that have laws allowing the formation of co-ops can make the process unnecessarily hard. For cash-strapped founders looking to create a business that prioritizes its social mission over its profit margin, these hurdles can be onerous enough to deter them from forming a cooperative.

Carefully crafted policymaking can help make co-ops a more accessible and attractive business structure. For instance, Italy has pioneered several strategies that make it easier to establish and grow co-ops. Italian law requires most co-ops to contribute a portion of their profits to solidarity funds, which are then used to support growth within the sector. There is also a separate legal framework that enables employees to pool their unemployment benefits and savings to buy shares in a traditional business when it is on the verge of closure and convert it into a worker co-op.

In the United States, a federal loan fund for rural electric co-ops in the 1930s enabled consumer-owned utilities to power most of the country’s farmland within a decade. In the 1970s, US Congress began providing tax advantages for owners who sold their companies to employees. During the same decade, the Swedish economist Rudolf Meidner proposed a model where a portion of corporate profits would go toward expanding employees’ ownership of companies and the economy at large. While not fully realized, his proposal—and the support it garnered from unions—galvanized the development of a more robust social safety net for workers in Sweden.

Other countries, such as Brazil and South Africa, take a more targeted approach to supporting co-ops through laws that require governments to prefer cooperative suppliers when buying certain things, like food and clothing for schools. In Bangladesh, national policies concerning rural development, women’s empowerment, and cooperative entrepreneurship seek to encourage women to form and contribute to cooperatives. To do this, the government disburses loans to members of women’s cooperatives and encourages saving through cooperatives. These policies have strengthened over 115,000 cooperatives with over 7.5 million members. In the US city of Cleveland and the UK city of Preston, “anchor institutions” like hospitals and universities enter into procurement contracts with co-ops, after competitive tender processes, which provide significant sources of regular income for the co-ops in the city.

Governments can also ensure that it is possible to incorporate cooperatives flexibly and creatively. Laws in Italy, Quebec, and France allow co-ops to have multiple stakeholders as members, pursue broad social interests (like employing folks from disadvantaged groups), and accept investment money from “supporter” members who don’t use the co-op’s products or services.

On the other side of the globe in South Korea, a law was passed in 2012 reducing barriers to co-op formation, most notably by reducing the number of required founding members to five. Within three years of its enactment, more than 7,000 new co-ops were registered—mostly by small entrepreneurs like freelancers and informal workers. Without this reform, thousands of people would not have benefitted from even the limited degree of job security that such co-ops provide.

A robust cooperative policy agenda need not be limited to cooperative law reform, but should also include economic policy on procurement, labor, securities, and competition. Governments can encourage business advisers, lawyers, and accountants to be educated about how co-ops work, so that they can help potential cooperative entrepreneurs navigate the financial and administrative hurdles to formation. Whether a co-op gets started through the pooling of worker or community member resources, or whether it is started with the help of funding from formal institutions and government support, policies have an important function in creating a favorable environment in which cooperative enterprises can thrive.

entries.title: Popular Education and Folk Schools
entries.summary: Folk schools and popular education processes provide opportunities for people most affected by injustice to build skills, participate in democratic learning, and gain tools for organizing.
entries.body:
Liberatory education supports people to build connections, learn freely, and organize to make change in their communities. Examples of liberatory education have arisen around the world out of peoples’ struggles—in the folk schools of Denmark, out of political repression across Latin America, in African liberation struggles, and during the Great Depression in the United States. Two related approaches to liberatory education are the methodology of popular education and the folk school.

The term “popular education”—and its early development in theory and practice—comes from Paulo Freire, a Brazilian intellectual and activist active in the mid-twentieth century. Popular education is a group process that brings people together to share and analyze their experiences, and come up with strategies for change. In the simplest terms, it means people getting together to learn something they need to know. Popular education rejects the system of experts and teachers transferring knowledge to students, only for that knowledge to be regurgitated for an essay or exam. This more rigid system confines even the most creative of teachers, who are held back by standardized curriculums and testing. In popular education, everyone involved is both a teacher and learner.

Folk schools, which originated in Denmark during the nineteenth century, were designed to provide people in rural areas with educational spaces to learn skills relevant to their lives. Inspired by the ideas of Danish poet, thinker, and pastor Nikolai Frederik Severin Grundtvig, these schools also taught citizenship skills that aided Denmark’s transition to democracy and encouraged lifelong learning outside of formal educational institutions.

Today, folk schools are located around the world and often provide both educational spaces and living and cultural spaces that allow people to gather and learn from each other, in a spirit akin to popular education. Their missions depend on the needs and culture of their local communities, so they often look and behave very differently from one another. Music and other cultural expressions are often central to how they share stories and raise spirits.

One of the most famous examples of a folk school is the Highlander Research and Education Center, located in New Market, Tennessee, in the United States. Founded in 1932 as the Highlander Folk School, inspired by Denmark Folk Schools, its mission was to “provide an educational center in the South for the training of rural and industrial leaders, and for the conservation and enrichment of the indigenous cultural values of the mountains.” Over the years, it has offered a variety of programs such as supporting labor organizers working across racial lines, civil rights leadership training in the 1960s, and intergenerational workshops. Its location at the intersection of the Appalachian region and the American South has led to a focus on regional issues such as efforts to protect the land from strip-mining and organizing against toxic polluters.

The methodology of popular education is central to Highlander’s approach, and generations of movement leaders in the US South and elsewhere have received training from Highlander to transform how their communities and movements learn and take action together. Interwoven with their commitment to popular education, Highlander practices related methodologies of cultural organizing, integrating community based art and cultural expression into everything they do; participatory action research, in which communities shape the methods and analysis of research that affects them; language justice, so that people can lead changemaking whatever language they speak; and intergenerational organizing. Highlander shares the theory and practice of these methodologies to encourage widespread use.

Highlander hosts community workshops, leadership and fellowship programs, and children’s justice camps. They support liberation struggles like the immigrant justice movement and the Movement for Black Lives. The work of Highlander can also happen in communities far away from Tennessee. One example is Project Upstream, which enabled unhoused people to become fellows in a program where they met, discussed their conditions with other unhoused people, and then worked to bring that information to government officials. The first year, the program identified the need for improving access to restrooms.

Other folk schools may operate differently, with a student demographic that aligns more closely with the ages of traditional university students. It is common for Danish folk schools—more than seventy operate independently throughout the country—to offer on-campus housing as well. But despite differences in target populations and course design, the basic tenets of folk schools remain the same. There are no traditional grades. Learning is rooted in students’ own motivation and interest. By providing a space for popular education, where everyone is an expert on their own life experience, folk schools allow people who experience oppression to gain tools for leadership and making change. Schools that empower their learners create more empowered communities.
entries.authorBio: Daley is a writer and digital media creator whose work centers lived experiences from the American South.

entries.title: Practice Freedom
entries.summary: We live our lives as acts of resistance to the destruction of land and life.
entries.body:
This book is full of powerful stories about new ways of organizing our economies, and there are many thousands of other examples globally. The reason we think it is important to tell these stories is because community institutions and democratic workplaces can be spaces where we can make different choices, choices that are about becoming free.

A beautiful solution is an act of resistance against the systems that dominate our people. Resistance is not just about marches, blockades, and protests; it is also about building the systems we need here and now for our communities to thrive. Resistance is setting up our own schools, our own housing complexes, our own factories in ways that reflect our values. It’s collective liberation in practice.

Living by our values and embedding these in our work doesn’t just happen, though. All of the solutions described in this book, from cooperatives to land trusts to communities of mutual aid, face pressure from existing power structures to perpetuate racism, classism, and heterosexism instead of cultivating relationships of interdependence and mutual respect. Building different structures is not enough. Practicing freedom means we work to understand how systems of oppression operate in all of our groups. We don’t assume that because we are trying to change the system, we are immune from recreating it.

Imagine a growing cooperative enterprise that has to compete with similar sized capitalist businesses to survive. It comes under increased pressure to adopt exploitative practices and take shortcuts in how it sources its materials. The business also becomes large and complex enough that the majority of members are not aware of the cooperative’s practices or of how management makes decisions. To overcome this, the cooperative’s members need to actively work to understand these pressures, come up with creative solutions, and commit to steering the co-op to make decisions that protect workers and the earth.

Working toward our collective liberation must be at the core of everything we do—otherwise, what’s the point? Above the success of any single cooperative project, we must prioritize the broader goal of transforming society for all of us. We must be that ambitious, because our ancestors are counting on us to continue the work they started, and our children will inherit the world we create.

The good news is that everyone—and we mean everyone—can practice freedom in their everyday lives, whether we are raising a family, cooking meals for our religious community, making art, delivering healthcare, or simply surviving in a system that doesn’t want us in it. The choices we make about how we do these things can always move us toward practicing freedom.

entries.title: Public Pharmaceuticals
entries.summary: By removing the profit motive, democratic and pub- lic ownership of pharmaceutical companies can lead to healthier outcomes for society and reclaim medicine for the common good.
entries.body:
The global medicines market is dominated by large private drug companies responsible for a decline in meaningful innovation as well as skyrocketing prices, recurring shortages, troubling safety issues, and corruption in the institutions that are supposed to regulate them. These trends are harmful to our health, economies, and democracies—and they are inevitable outcomes of an industry driven by profit-maximization.

So-called “Big Pharma” companies spend less than onefifth of their revenue on research and development, but half of their revenue on marketing. Many also regularly distribute more than 100 percent of profits to shareholders by selling off assets, taking on more debt, and downsizing production—inefficient and extractive practices in an industry we depend on for our health and wellbeing.

To get different outcomes, we need a different design. Democratic, public ownership of pharmaceutical institutions at scale would remove the profit motive and help reclaim medicine for the common good. Public ownership of pharmaceuticals can exist at any or all points in the supply chain, from research for new medications to manufacturing and distribution services. Since they are not beholden to shareholders and have some insulation from market pressures, they can focus on goals other than maximizing profits—like contributions to public health, scientific advancement, and local economies.

From Massachusetts to the UK, Thailand, India, and beyond, there are many existing examples of states turning to public ownership of pharmaceutical companies in efforts to combat high prices, medicine shortages, and political interference by multinational corporations.

Since 1960, Cuba’s entire pharmaceutical sector has been public. It produces both low-cost generic drugs and first-in-class discoveries, while providing thousands of good jobs and educational opportunities in the national economy. Known principally for its innovations—like the world’s first lung cancer and meningitis B vaccines—the industry also manufactures most of the domestic supply of medicine and shares its technology with numerous low and middle-income countries, lessening those countries’ reliance on Big Pharma to meet healthcare needs.

When properly resourced, Public Pharma can lower drug prices, reduce inefficiencies, and ensure broad, equitable access to new drugs. Public control of manufacturing, wholesale distribution, or retail pharmacies can serve as the basis for large-scale investments in public health, creating educational opportunities and decent jobs and increasing resilience in supply chains. South Korea, for instance, supports small and medium pharmaceutical companies with publicly owned manufacturing facilities, which generate local jobs and purchasing power that broadly benefit the economy.

Public Pharma can also assure that medications most essential to public health are prioritized for development. State-owned pharmaceutical companies in both Cuba and Brazil operate with explicit mandates to develop medications ignored by the market, like those for neglected tropical diseases, while Big Pharma companies prioritize medications that generate the most profit—often copies of existing products.

Public Pharma can contribute to the creation of a biomedical commons in which life-saving technologies, and the information needed to produce and improve upon them, are treated as collective resources for all of humanity. Large-scale public ownership and control of the benefits of pharmaceutical innovation, for instance, could help facilitate programs in which the wealth created by the industry could prioritize serving historically marginalized communities, rather than perpetuating neglect in the name of business imperatives. Public Pharma is a vital tool for reorienting the purpose of health care from profits to human needs.

Successful examples from around the world can inform the design and development of a robust Public Pharma sector for any country. Sweden’s state-owned Apotek Produktion & Laboratorier AB has found a niche in specialty pharmaceutical manufacturing, selling products to dozens of countries, and directing any profits it earns to its only shareholder: the Swedish state. China and India’s stateowned drug companies have long produced a significant portion of the world’s supply of active pharmaceutical ingredients. Brazil’s state-owned labs produce more than 100 essential medications that allow its national health service to offer free and reduced-price medications to low-income patients.

Around the world—even in the United States—public sector labs were historically responsible for the development of most vaccines. Insulin as a treatment for diabetes was developed in a public lab in Canada and the subsequent sale of the rights to produce insulin to private US manufacturers remains a powerful cautionary tale about the harm that can happen when privatizing public goods. Despite being a century-old drug, insulin prices in the US have skyrocketed in recent years as the three companies that control virtually the entire insulin market make small tweaks on their products in order to take out new patents and continually raise prices. This trend has produced a uniquely American epidemic of cost-related deaths because of people rationing insulin.

Because of the US’s outsized role in global trade talks and the utter dominance of its Big Pharma firms in the global medicines market, developing a public pharmaceutical industry in the US in particular would be decisive in global efforts to roll back Big Pharma monopolies and reclaim medicine as a public good. It would reduce regulatory capture and shrink corporate lobbying, opening up political space for much broader input into the priorities and outputs of this critical industry. With democratic, public-sector institutions innovating and producing medications at scale, Big Pharma’s interests would no longer dominate, and public institutions would have incentives to cooperate instead of competing in times of public health crises.
entries.authorBio: Brown is the director of health and economy at The Democracy Collaborative, where she advances economic transformation strategies that contribute to broad-based health and wellbeing. She is an expert on public sector pharmaceutical production and has broad interests in the political economy of illness and health.

epigraphs.quote: We don’t have to leave ourselves at the mercy of the most profitable sector on Earth to get the drugs we need. We must nationalize the pharmaceutical industry and turn the medicines millions rely on into public goods.

entries.title: Put Care First
entries.summary: Taking care of each other and our home is the basis of the world we’re trying to create—and how we get there.
entries.body:
Caring for ourselves and one another is how we stay connected to our humanity, to the source of our power and dignity, and to the web of life. It is the purpose of community. It is the purpose of a solidarity economy.

We want a world in which everyone has what they need to thrive, to be joyful and to be well. Prioritizing quality of life for all human and non-human life means putting care first.

We need to feel safe. We need permission and space to be ourselves and pursue our passions. We need to feel like the rules of the community are fair and applied equitably. We need to have control of our culture—our language, food, dance, music, and history—and our land. And our communities, not just health professionals and politicians, need the power to define what trauma, care, wholeness, and health look like for themselves, because they look different everywhere.

Under capitalism, care—including our health, time, passions, and the environment itself—has been commodified. As we create different kinds of economies, we can measure value in different ways in our businesses and communities, and we can use these measurements to inform how and what we choose to build together. If our economy values care, then it will also include policies and protections such as family and medical leave, minimum wages, overtime, comprehensive benefits, and more. We need to structure our economy so that everyone can access quality healthcare, education, and housing.

Putting care first also means recognizing the labor of caretakers regardless of job title or wage. So much care work is invisible and undervalued in a capitalist economy. The work of caring for an elderly parent, giving birth and raising children, helping a friend in need, or repairing what we have so that we don’t need to buy more new things, is seen as something outside of the economy—something that people should do on top of the “real work” of earning a living. As we build solidarity economies, we know that care work is essential to the health of our communities, and we have to treat it that way.

A society that doesn’t honor and value care is not a society worth building. As the world changes around us, we must be willing to do what it takes to keep taking care of each other even as things get harder and new needs emerge. This is both the basis of the world we’re trying to create—and an essential part of how we get there.

entries.title: Radical Grandma Collective
entries.summary: Radical Grandma Collective (RadGram) is an international and intergenerational organization that works in solidarity with communities in northeast Thailand to change the balances of power that extractive industries have disrupted, and to defend and restore the land those communities share...
entries.body:
Radical Grandma Collective (RadGram) is an international and intergenerational organization that works in solidarity with communities in northeast Thailand to change the balances of power that extractive industries have disrupted, and to defend and restore the land those communities share. The collective first began as a way to bring a small social enterprise centered around one community’s anti-mining activism to an international audience. Today, RadGram takes a multifaceted approach. It supports community-led restoration efforts through fostering social enterprise initiatives, leading educational programs, and directing financial resources to organizations and leaders guiding environmental, societal, and health restoration efforts.

Extractive industries have poisoned environments and fractured communities in northeast Thailand, as in many parts of the world. After pushing through an inadequate environmental impact assessment and excluding community members at every turn, Tungkum Limited mining company began gold mining in Loei Province, in 2006. The downstream effects culminated in land too toxic to farm, fish too polluted to eat, and water too contaminated to drink. The residents of six impacted villages embarked on a fight for their health and environment, forming the group Khon Rak Ban Kerd (KRBK), or People Who Love Their Hometown.

As in many movements around the world, older women have led the struggle from the start, and they are the source of RadGram’s name. They not only lead the charge through on-the-ground protests but use traditional weaving practices to fund their organizing. The weavers pay for KRBK’s legal fees and other costs associated with activism by selling woven scarves. For some of these women, protesting in person is not an option due to health and safety concerns, but weaving provides their entry point into the movement. For others, like movement leader Ranong Kongsaen (“Mae Rote”), weaving is another way to support the cause for which she already works tirelessly on the ground.

In 2016, the Khon Rak Ban Kerd weavers began collaborating with four women from the United States to form the Radical Grandma Collective. The collective has allowed the weavers’ work and business to expand to an international customer base through RadGram’s online store and attendance at various events. For the weavers, RadGram provides more than income—it helps preserve traditions while creating a new revenue source to offset economic hardship caused by environmental degradation.

In 2016, the military government suspended all mining operations. Tungkum Limited has since gone bankrupt, leaving behind a toxic mess. Currently, KRBK is pursuing representation in the government-led land restoration process. Many of the same tactics used to exclude community members from decision-making during the mining concession process are being employed in the restoration process. Thailand lacks a clear legal framework for restoration, and community members know that restoration efforts will not meet their needs if they are not driving it. Restoring the community’s power over how land is managed in their home is essential to restoring dignity after years of extraction. One tactic that KRBK has used in the summer of 2023 is to begin the restoration process on their own, alongside local government officials, school children, and US university students, by planting local tree varieties on one of the mountains contaminated by mining activities.

RadGram’s origins lie in the six gold-mine-impacted communities in Loei, but that is only one of several mine-impacted areas with whom the collective works today. In Dong Mafai District in Nong Bua Lamphu Province, activists of the Khao Lao Yai-Pha Jun Dai Forest Conservation Group are fighting for permanent stone quarry closure, restoration of surrounding mountains, and development of the area as a tourist attraction—on their terms. Using social enterprise activities to preserve their land, build income, and share their story with a broader audience, community members are organizing to bring tourism that supports the protection of the land in their area.

In the summer of 2023, RadGram hosted its first study abroad program, which taught US university students about mine-impacted communities in Thailand. During the multi-week program, the students visited both Loei and Dong Mafai to learn about the communities’ restoration efforts and environmental justice activism. Hosting students—and other outsiders—helps the community clearly articulate and organize further around their goals, amplifies the community’s stories to wider audiences, and generates new projects that align with the community’s vision for restoration. For example, students in this first two-week program drafted a sign explaining the Na Nong Bong community’s restoration principles to educate other visitors. The program allows students to have a broader understanding of extractive industries and their impact on people and the environment.

RadGram also partners with NGOs and individual activists to financially support frontline human rights defenders through direct grants. With this approach, the collective connects national and international organizing to local efforts. Beginning in 2022, RadGram established an emergency grants fund to help organizers who may need financial support urgently.

Communities depend on natural resources, and those resources should be managed by the people living there, not extracted by transient external industries. The toll of extraction and fighting against environmental degradation on communities has been tremendous. RadGram and many other organizations are supporting grassroots efforts to restore community power and dignity in managing their land.

entries.title: Recuperated Factories
entries.summary: Worker-led campaigns have seized the means of production, made decisions democratically, prevent- ed unemployment, and revitalized communities in the process.
entries.body:
Recuperation refers to when workers take control over their workplace and transform it into a worker cooperative, with decisions made democratically and profits shared among all. Although often motivated by national economic crises and the resulting abandonment of businesses by capitalists, recuperation can arise from a range of situations affecting a workplace, such as strikes or bankruptcies. Unlike owner-led conversions to employee ownership, recuperation is a process that comes from the bottom up, often against the wishes of the owning class. Recuperated factory takeovers have happened all over the world.

During Argentina’s economic crisis that began in 2011, workers prevented the permanent closure of dozens of businesses—from ceramics factories to luxury hotels. One of these businesses, the towering Hotel Bauen, opened in the late 1970s in the heart of Buenos Aires. It held status as a meeting place of the ruling class during Argentina’s ruthless military dictatorship. After the hotel’s indebted owners fired the staff and permanently turned off the lights in late 2001, a few dozen ex-employees and cooperative activists banded together to reclaim it. They staged an occupation of the hotel in early 2003, and immediately began talking about how to reopen it—only this time, under democratic control. They wanted to replace the hotel’s previous culture of competition, suspicion, and chronic instability with one of solidarity. Despite continuous harassment by powerful state representatives, the worker-owned Hotel Bauen grew to become a hub for progressive politics—providing space for community organizers, discussion groups, and artists.

In 2008, during the global economic recession, workers at the Republic Windows factory in Chicago protested layoffs by staging a sit-in strike—one of the first since they were made illegal in the United States in 1939. To the surprise of many, they won. But only four years later, the new owners laid them off. This time, a group of the now jobless workers decided to do something different. Working with an organization called the Working World, they bought their old factory and started their own business, New Era Windows Cooperative.

Meanwhile in Thessaloniki, Greece, workers began occupying a factory in 2013 after the owners declared bankruptcy and stopped paying wages. With the overwhelming support of their members, the workers’ union decided to repurpose the factory’s machinery to make ecological soap products for a new business, Vio.Me, which would be run by the workers. For nearly a decade, the workers have had to defend the property with physical blockades and nightly security shifts. They also have had to defeat annual attempts to auction the property to new ownership. Meanwhile the government refuses to acknowledge the workers’ attempts to formalize their ownership of the factory and has shut down electricity to the property in an effort to drive them out. Nonetheless, Vio.Me continues. As one of the workers said in a 2019 article in Unicorn Riot, “This factory is a factory that mainly produces dignity.”

For workers, recuperating a workplace usually begins by occupying it, but that is just the first step. A lot of learning and planning is often necessary before the business can get going again. Workers who were previously employed at the factory understand parts of the manufacturing process. But because former managers will have withheld certain information from them and separated workers into isolated assembly-line roles, workers often need to combine their experiences to reconstruct an understanding of what is involved along the production chain. In cases where the owner moved or sold essential equipment, new worker ownership must replace that equipment and establish relationships with suppliers of raw materials and anticipated customers. Unless members of the previous management team are part of the takeover, the workers might need to pursue training or find trusted advisers in the areas of bookkeeping, financial analysis, sales, human resources, and more.

As a group, it is important for the workers to collectively develop an understanding of entrepreneurial risk-taking, when to delegate tasks or grant authority, and how to define success. In situations where the business is embroiled in a wider economic crisis, the workers will need to be creative problem solvers, because banks often freeze accounts. If payments in the national currency are jeopardized, workers may need to organize compensation in ways that meet their needs without relying on money. Whether or not business is good, the workers must consider how much money to save for purchasing future raw materials and equipment.

Typically, legislation protects the previous owners of recuperated businesses, and authorities may forcibly evict, imprison, or repress workers attempting to occupy and operate them.Yet factory takeovers can mobilize support from surrounding communities, as well as from academics, activists, and pragmatic lawmakers. After all, an empty factory does not produce value in the form of jobs or taxes for the local municipality.

Existing labor unions and cooperative developers can help support the process whenever the opportunity to recuperate a factory presents itself; they should prepare ahead of time for how to do so. Additionally, policymakers should consider proactively establishing legislation that facilitates recuperation, especially to safeguard manufacturing jobs in their communities. But most importantly, workers must understand that they have the power to take back any community asset that lies empty, remains idle, or does not serve them.

entries.title: Reggio Emilia Preschools
entries.summary: Emerging after World War II from one of the most war-ravaged regions in Italy, Reggio Emilia is a teaching style and philosophy that enables young children to grow into complete people and develop the core capacities to participate in radical democracy throughout their lives.
entries.body:
Reggio Emilia is a system of education—a pedagogy—focused on preschool students. It embraces and encourages the unique curiosities of each child, grounding education in the needs and conditions of the surrounding community. Teachers, parents, community members, the classroom, and the local environment are all integral components to how a child learns to participate in the world in the Reggio method. But it goes one step further—recognizing how teachers and parents learn from their observations of and interactions with children.

The pedagogy gets its name from where it first arose: Reggio Emilia, a small city in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region. One of the wealthiest regions in Europe, almost a third of its economy flows through cooperative businesses, in industries such as agriculture, manufacturing, and finance. But it was not always this well-off. Immediately following World War II, Emilia-Romagna was one of the poorest, most devastated regions in the country.

Educator Loris Malaguzzi developed the system in response to the war’s devastation, as a way to inoculate children against fascism and similar nationalistic, depersonalizing ideologies. The original Reggio Emilia preschools were funded by local women, and as a result the community was highly involved in how the schools operated.

Today, there are many Reggio-inspired schools around the world, making this style of preschool a regional export. Naturally, their interpretations of the core ideas vary, since Reggio Emilia schools should be flexible and adaptive to the needs of the locality, its families, and the individual students.

According to Malaguzzi, Reggio-inspired schools should be organized to foster strong relationships among “three central protagonists”: children, teachers, and parents. These relationships allow them to influence and learn from each other, continuously. “Our aim is to make a school that is a place of research, learning, revisiting, reconsideration, and reflection,” he wrote in 1993. “We strive to create an amiable school where children, teachers, and families feel a sense of well-being.”

Reggio schools train students to participate in democratic and cooperative structures throughout their lives by turning the classroom into a radically democratic place. “Ensuring that every child feels a sense of security and belonging within the school enables each child to accept and participate actively in transforming situations that are part of learning experiences,” wrote Malaguzzi. “The group becomes self-sustaining, developing its own conversation, its own ways of communicating, acting, and thinking.”

The role of the teacher is different from more conventional schools as well. In Reggio-style schools, teachers behave as facilitators for learning, and a significant part of their role is focused on documenting the behavior of children and tailoring teaching styles accordingly. By documenting and thinking deeply about the progress of students, and then discussing broader observations among themselves, teachers practice an iterative process rather than an inflexible and repetitive one.

A popular book about Reggio Emilia preschools, The Hundred Languages of Children, explains that teachers “need to redefine their roles so that they are more than conveyors of knowledge and supporters of children. They are creators and sustainers of relationships; they are researchers; they must learn to follow children’s time and interests; they must sometimes think ahead, be the chief protagonist, invent, prompt, design, create, be the audience and the listener, the arbiter and judge, the author and scribe, the listener and recorder.”

Reggio Emilia preschools turn the classroom itself into an environment where children internalize the values of collaboration and democratic society even before having the vocabulary. These experiences prime children to be active participants in the world around them.

entries.title: Remunicipalization
entries.summary: Remunicipalization is when the management of utilities is brought back under public control. Some of the most important examples concern water, but remunicipalization encompasses regional and na- tional-level services from energy and transportation to internet access and education.
entries.body:
The remunicipalization of utilities is often a community response to dysfunctional governance by privatized utility suppliers and public-private partnerships between governments and private industry. The factors leading to water remunicipalization, for instance, are similar worldwide: poor service performance, under-investment in infrastructure, disputes over operational costs and price increases, soaring utility bills, environmental hazards, and lack of financial transparency. Their experiences of these common problems have motivated many communities and policy-makers to take services back into public control. Between 2000 and 2015, 235 cases of water remunicipalization occurred in 37 countries around the world, including in major cities from Kampala to Kuala Lampur and Bogotá to Berlin.

Though each case differs, remunicipalization brings benefits to local governments and citizens alike. Since remunicipalizing its water supply in 2007, Houston, Texas has saved $2 million annually while Paris, which remunicipalized in 2011, saved €35 million in the first year alone. Without the obligation of generating profits for shareholders, the publicly owned utilities companies don’t have to fight to reinvest revenues in improving the water systems—as have governments in both Dar es Salaam and Berlin.

Remunicipalization efforts can increase access to water for low-income households by making water policy more accountable to community needs. Arenys de Munt, a small town in Spain, has promoted social policies to guarantee the right to water for all its citizens since 2011, when the town successfully remunicipalized water services. The newly established municipal company Aigües de Arenys/ GUSAM reformed the tariff structure by providing a discount on the first 100 liters of water per person per day. The most vulnerable families—those earning less than a single minimum wage income—are guaranteed access to water.

Similarly, Medina Sidonia—another Spanish city with remunicipalized water services—has developed an innovative approach to ensure the provision of a minimum amount of water (three cubic meters per person per month) to residents experiencing financial difficulties. After remunicipalization, the city council has not only declared water a human right but is implementing a policy to make it an accessible reality.

Most cases of remunicipalization around the world have involved terminating private contracts, either before they were due to expire or directly after the expiration date. However, challenges can arise with the premature termination of a contract. If the contract is terminated before it expires, private operators can obtain compensation for the profits they would have generated. If municipalities claim a breach of contractual obligations, private operators often contest this in court. The government of Castres, France, for example, was forced to pay €30 million in compensation to private water empire Suez, even though its contract had been illegally signed by former Mayor Jacques Limouzy without proper consultation with the town council.

Beyond national litigations, investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions, which allow multinational companies to sue states, increase the risks for governments and citizens wanting to remunicipalize utilities. Multinational water companies use ISDS provisions to claim significant amounts of public money in compensation for canceled service management contracts, despite failing to meet their own obligations.

Many of the successful remunicipalization efforts around the world would not have been possible without the tireless mobilization of committed citizens. Berliners organized a referendum to demand that secret water privatization contracts be disclosed. In Uruguay, a referendum calling for a nationwide end to privatization eventually led to the remunicipalization of water and sanitation services.

Remunicipalization is about building better public services—more transparent, more accountable, more efficient, and more focused on people’s long-term needs. If citizens are willing to fight for remunicipalization and against privatization, it is because they believe that the public sector is better equipped to meet broader social and environmental goals than profit-driven private companies.

Remunicipalization strategies can be applied to other essential services such as energy, transportation, healthcare, education, and more. Hundreds of cities in Germany have remunicipalized energy services; several cities in Sweden have reversed private contracts in elderly care; and numerous cities in France have remunicipalized waste collection, transportation, and school meal services. In Spain, many services from public park maintenance to funeral services have recently been remunicipalized.

These efforts reflect a global recognition of the need for cross-sector strategies and alliances among citizens, workers, and local authorities to de-privatize essential services. People are rediscovering the value of public ownership for the common good.

entries.title: Restorative Practices Aotearoa
entries.summary: On the night of October 12, 2012, 20 Jewish graves in Auckland’s oldest cemetery were spray-painted with Nazi symbols and anti-Semitic phrases...
entries.body:
On the night of October 12, 2012, 20 Jewish graves in Auckland’s oldest cemetery were spray-painted with Nazi symbols and anti-Semitic phrases. The impacts of acts like these are often difficult to overcome, inflicting deep, lasting pain on affected communities. When one of the two people responsible volunteered to participate in a restorative justice process, it gained a lot of attention beyond Auckland.

Only 19 years old, one of the young people involved in this act had grown up among multiple homes without much family support. A tinkerer by nature, he had aspired to study engineering at university, but now that was unlikely to happen. The courts required that he perform community service and pay reparations for the damage he had caused. But additionally, he chose to engage with the Jewish Council of New Zealand. During these interactions, one of the senior members of the Jewish community admitted to the boy that, three decades earlier, he himself had desecrated a church—and had been carrying around the weight of that secret ever since. The restorative justice meeting gave this Jewish man the opportunity to admit his wrongdoing.

This restorative conference had many other outcomes, including allowing Auckland’s Jewish community to meet one of the people responsible for the desecration and be seen and heard by him, so healing could begin. But it also resulted in that same community offering mentorship and guidance to the person who had harmed them, once they understood that this was a crime of ignorance rather than of hatred. They invited him to Friday night Shabbat dinners. The elder who admitted to his own act of vandalism 30 years prior even offered financial support for this young person to attend university—a way to atone for his own past while opening up opportunities for someone without access.

This healing process was facilitated by Restorative Practices Aotearoa (RPA), an Aotearoa New Zealand-based network of providers founded in 2005 to facilitate restorative conferences. RPA has providers assigned to every district court in the country. They emphasize flexibility and responsiveness to the needs of all stakeholders in a process, while facilitating discussion and catalyzing community-wide healing. “We are accustomed to putting people into two groups: offenders and victims,” says Mike Hinton, RPA’s general manager. “That’s only about 20 percent of the story. Victims come with families. Families come with communities. Offenders, too, come with families and communities. It’s about engaging all of the people that have been affected by the trauma, the hurt, or the harm.”

Participation in restorative conferences is elective and separate from the court system. “Being completely voluntary is a cornerstone of this practice,” Hinton adds. “If a judge recommends it, then it is not voluntary.”

In another instance, a motorist accidentally killed a child in a road accident. He asked to speak immediately with the child’s family, but was told not to by the police and his lawyer. Later, during the restorative conference facilitated by RPA, the family was able to hear the man express his deep regret and pain about what had happened. He told them, “If it was up to me, I would be at your house the day after the accident because that’s the island way.” Where the formal justice system prevented healing, restorative practices enabled it.

Practitioners at RPA do not limit restorative practices to less serious crimes or young offenders, as often happens in other countries. Communities and organizations also use restorative practices outside the criminal justice system. For instance, Tawa College in Wellington established a tiered set of restorative practices to aid in communicative conflict resolution, resulting in a significant change in the atmosphere on campus and in outcomes across the educational institution. “The reality is that restorative practices are suitable for every case, at every level,” Hinton says. Imagine a world where, no matter the nature of the wrongdoing, the response is a collective effort toward healing.

entries.title: Right Relationship
entries.summary: We belong to each other. The world we are building must help us remember how.
entries.body: Our economies are built on stolen land, labor, and culture. Everything we build must work to end and help us heal from this exploitation and extraction, restoring balance in our relationships with one another and the earth. Our relationships are out of balance at every level; the clues for how to restore them are mostly found in the intimate and the local levels. Humanity as a whole has forgotten how to cultivate healthy relationships with the earth, yet every human being knows how to love a place, a tree, a familiar animal. The Global North has plundered the Global South, yet relationships of collaboration, mutual benefit, and learning exist in households, in neighborhoods, in companies with just trade practices, and in communities that engage in truth, healing, and reparations. The scale of the healing is vastly out of balance with the scale of the harm—we cannot hope to heal the earth by loving a tree, or to heal the harms of colonization by removing one statue of a colonizer. But we start there and we bring what we learn to our relationships everywhere.

entries.title: Rights of Nature in Ecuador
entries.summary: For as long as they have existed, the indigenous people of Ecuador’s Sarayaku region have inhabited a forest fed by water from the Andes mountains, which drains into the Amazon basin through the Bobonaza River...
entries.body:
For as long as they have existed, the indigenous people of Ecuador’s Sarayaku region have inhabited a forest fed by water from the Andes mountains, which drains into the Amazon basin through the Bobonaza River. They share an architecture of sacred tree canopies sheltering a rich undergrowth populated by millions of animals and insects. When an oil company invaded their territory in the 1990s, the people of Sarayaku were challenged to become the voices and last line of defense for their ecosystem. Their struggle helped shape their country’s constitution—and showed the world that nature, not just people, can have rights.

Compared to Ecuador’s population of over 14 million, the Kichwa of Sarayaku have a small population of just 1,200, but this didn’t stop them from mobilizing in defense of the earth. For generations the Kichwa of Sarayaku had watched as their closest neighbors, both Indigenous people and recent colonists, were subjected to violence and displacement by the state and the agents of extractive industries. Developers of oil wells, pipelines, large-scale mining, forestry, and hydroelectric stations used payoffs and threats to gain control over Indigenous lands in the region. When developers threatened their own lands, the people of Sarayaku chose to stay and fight rather than to accept displacement.

Grandparents would watch the children while young men and women patrolled the land, confiscating guns and explosives from oil company security and trained soldiers. For years they disrupted the best laid plans of the oil company and its enablers in the Ecuadorian military, ultimately leading to their withdrawal and a victory for Sarayaku on June 27, 2012, at the Inter-American Court.

Important to Sarayaku’s success was the community’s use of innovative media tactics to gain attention and keep the struggle visible to the public. When the internet was still young, the Sarayaku community took advantage of it to embarrass the government by publicizing their victories against the military on their own website. At the time, media outlets would not cover their actions. When radio stations would not carry their messages, Sarayaku activists directed their voices within earshot of broadcasters’ microphones, yelling to be heard, speaking of their spiritual calling and describing their connection to the life-giving rainforest. In 1992, they walked the land for a month, meeting with everyone along the way and making new allies, until they reached Ecuador’s capital, Quito, and demanded an audience with the president.

Sarayaku’s people used diverse tactics to protect their spiritual homeland. Their struggle was guided by sumak kawsay, a principle enshrined in their cosmology. Sumak means wholeness, beauty, a state of wellness that is complete and harmonious, while kawsay refers to life. In becoming teachers of sumak kawsay, they also became scholars of the legal frameworks imposed on them. In the first battle, they demanded titles to their land and were successful. When they learned that their ownership of the land surface did not prevent the state from selling off the mineral rights underneath it, they became experts in international law and found means to overcome this threat. They filed a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, then recorded evidence for seven years, updating the Commission continually, until it agreed to take their case against the state of Ecuador. In 2011 they won, securing a historic judgment against the state of Ecuador. Because the ruling was at the international level, Ecuador was forced to follow its own laws. Today, the people in Sarayaku still monitor the state for compliance.

Following Sarayaku’s lead, other Indigenous groups in Ecuador have started to wear traditional jewelry, makeup, and bright feather headdresses when they speak to outsiders, and are taking ownership over their connections to the animals and the plants and their roles as defenders. Amazonian women in particular are fighting to defend their ways of life, even when the male tribal leaders are bought off or made to bow to political pressure.

In 2008, Ecuador adopted a new constitution that borrowed language from Kichwa cosmology. The constitution, drafted by popular assembly, speaks of the shared purpose of sumak kawsay as an alternative to the global model of capitalist development. The concept underlies the entire constitution. The document affirms the intrinsic rights of the natural world, the Pachamama, and equates the destruction of Indigenous habitats with genocide. In reality, however, those who ratified the new constitution seem to have understood little of what they were committing to law. The national leadership soon went on to continue the extractive practices of previous governments.

The 2008 constitution was Ecuador’s 20th constitution since gaining independence from Spain in 1830. Following a chaotic political decade that saw three coups, economic crises, massive out-migration, and the rise of a new governing coalition in 2006, elections were held to choose representatives for a constitutional assembly, and this assembly dissolved the National Congress. More than 3,000 legislative proposals were submitted to the new assembly for consideration and debate. The rights of nature were championed by the president of the constitutional assembly, economist Alberto Acosta, and were understood to be critical to ensuring Indigenous support for the document. But no ombudsperson’s office was created to defend the rights of nature, so Indigenous nations themselves remain the staunchest defenders of these rights in Ecuadorian society.

In 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic decimated the global economy, Sarayaku was swept away by the worst flood in generations. Schools, houses, and crops were swallowed by the Bobonaza River. Despite the state’s failure to protect them, Sarayaku’s people are grateful to have retained their connection to the Pachamama. In recent years, they drew on their shared knowledge of medicinal plants to treat the symptoms of COVID-19. Their international allies have contributed to a crowdfunding campaign that allowed Sarayaku to rebuild—the din of hammering can be heard among the bird song and rooster crows. Today, new solar panels enable a satellite internet connection, keeping Sarayaku’s leadership in contact with the cities and their allies.

The people of Sarayaku know the state did not understand the language it enshrined in law in 2008, just as in 2007 it did not fully grasp the international commitments it agreed to when signing the UN Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous People, requiring Indigenous self-determination and informed consent. Today, the Kichwa continue to push for the Kawsak Sacha (living forest) proposal and for further legal safeguards for nature, the source of all life. To Sarayaku’s people, the task of educating those who would destroy their way of life transcends the boundaries of Ecuador and connects them to every living being on the planet.
