entries.title: Seikatsu Club Consumers’ Co-operative Union
entries.summary: In the mid-1960s, in response to rising food prices, a group of Japanese housewives started a buying club to purchase milk directly from producers...
entries.body:
In the mid-1960s, in response to rising food prices, a group of Japanese housewives started a buying club to purchase milk directly from producers. Not only did the club secure lower prices by cutting out the middleman, its members also gained fresher products. The group grew to become a consumers’ cooperative called the Seikatsu Club Consumers’ Co-operative Union, which today has hundreds of thousands of members.

In the 1960s, cultural and legal barriers prevented women in Japan from being leaders in their communities except in the family sphere, as housewives, daughters, or mothers. They were not even permitted to fill out an application with the government under their own name. Seikatsu Club challenged these traditional gender roles. It required women to apply for membership under their own names, and, more importantly, to become owners of a business. Seikatsu Club was an opportunity for many women to become active in the community. Today, 95 percent of its 420,000 members are women. Though the club’s founding members have aged, outreach to young parents has expanded the club’s demographic; it added 60,000 new members under the age of 44 in 2015 alone.

Until the early 1990s, most of the Seikatsu Club members were organized into small groups called han, which comprised up to eight people or so. In these units, members would collect money, place orders for milk and other items, and coordinate deliveries. The han was also a forum for members to express their views and wishes. By involving themselves in decisions around purchasing milk, the members grew interested in understanding the industry. They asked themselves why Seikatsu Club was able to lower prices and why mainstream milk was so expensive.

This process of inquiry and education led Seikatsu Club members to realize that they could sustain lower prices and consume higher quality milk by building their own processing facility. To raise the money necessary, the club issued bonds to borrow money from their members and established the first milk factory in 1979. Some wealthier members agreed to lend the cooperative even larger sums. After 10 years, Seikatsu Club was able to repay all the money it had borrowed.

Since then, Seikatsu Club has been solvent. Today it is able to finance new projects on the contributions of its members alone. Every month, each of the club’s members pays 1,000 yen (about $10). As of 2021, over the course of a year, this added up to about 48 billion yen (about $365 million).

As with other cooperatives, the Seikatsu Club is governed according to the principle of “one member, one vote.” However, the club has taken the ideal of participatory democracy to another level, seeking to make governance as community centered as possible. The largest body for decision-making is the general assembly, which meets annually and as needed. Beneath that are regional units called “primaries.” In big regions like Tokyo, the club has divided the structure into “sub-primaries” that have their own legal statuses and identities.

This decision-making structure ensures that every member has an opportunity to be heard. When the club is deciding whether to supply a new product, each primary or sub-primary has its own discussions. Eventually there is a convergence of opinion at the general assembly. Major decisions like the club’s five-year plan entail months (or even years) of deliberations before a decision is reached.

Today, Seikatsu Club is engaged in two primary activities in addition to the collective purchasing of products: mutual aid and renewable energy. As of 2021, Seikatsu Club had about 140,000 members enrolled in its co-op insurance plans, and an additional 50,000 in its new mutual-aid society, Hagukumi. In each of its regions, Seikatsu Club also operates long-term nursing care and childcare programs rooted in the cultures and needs of local communities. Following the Fukushima disaster of 2011, Seikatsu Club invested substantial resources to build wind and solar farms. In 2021, it generated 27,632 megawatt hours of clean energy, which it offered to its members for a price on par with fossil fuels.

Seikatsu Club also serves as an incubator for hundreds of small workers’ collectives—from bakeries to design studios—providing technical assistance and patrons for new businesses. Today, around 12,000 people are engaged or employed in these collectives.

The founding members of Seikatsu Club had a saying: “If you are cooking and you open the pan, you will find politics.” In order to sustain the beautiful and innovative alternatives it created, Seikatsu Club also had to work to change laws and policies. This was realized early on; since 1979 the club has run candidates for local assemblies through the Seikatsusha Network. Today, about 80 club members are elected at different levels of local governments.

Seikatsu Club is a model for consumers in Japan and throughout the world; for its members, it is a tool that allows them to do what they want to do—as long as they are willing to come together, listen, discuss, and decide on a common cause.

entries.title: Self-Employed Women’s Association
entries.summary: The Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) is a trade union of self-employed women workers—the first in India to gain legal recognition for self-employed women in the informal sector...
entries.body:
The Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) is a trade union of self-employed women workers—the first in India to gain legal recognition for self-employed women in the informal sector. Since its establishment in 1972, SEWA’s membership has grown from a few hundred women in Ahmedabad, Gujurat to almost two million women today. SEWA’s members span regions, languages, and sectors: they are fish vendors and clothes hawkers, home-based potters and bidi rollers; they are cattle rearers and salt workers, domestic cleaners and construction laborers. In many ways, the work of these women underpins India’s economic functioning: 64 percent of the nation’s GDP is accounted for by self-employed workers, and self-employed women are often also expected to perform household and domestic labor, in addition to earning income.

Despite the foundational role they play, women workers in India’s informal sector face deep-rooted and material discrimination on the basis of caste, class, and gender. Unlike workers in the organized sector, they don’t have access to regular employment, benefits, or welfare, and as a result often work long hours doing hard labor for little to no eventual pay. To make matters worse, it is often impossible for these women to demand fair wages or protect themselves from exploitation, because they lack realistic ways to take their employers to court. At its core, SEWA aims to organize women workers to collectively demand their rights, with an emphasis on two goals: full employment and self-reliance. Full employment, to SEWA, means ensuring that members also have the foundational rights of job security, income security, and food security. The emphasis on self-reliance stems from SEWA’s roots in the ideas of Mahatma Gandhi, and a firm belief that women—as individuals and as a collective— have the independence, resources, and decision-making abilities to sustain themselves and their families.

SEWA’s organizational structure underpins its pursuit of these two goals. It is an open organization, with minimal barriers to entry: although more than half of SEWA’s current member base is located in Gujurat, union membership is open to self-employed women all over India, with a low annual fee of five rupees. Further, SEWA operates through a combination of decision-making systems, with varying levels of direct and indirect control.

This is done in two ways: First, under the SEWA umbrella, informal workers formed hundreds of individual, economically independent cooperatives (of about 100 women each) and producer’s groups (of about 15-20 women each). These are largely governed through directly democratic procedures, with marketing, production, and processes determined by the relevant members. Second, every 200 members elect a representative to state- and national-level trade councils and program committees that together determine SEWA’s national priorities, ensuring that the direction of the organization is responsive to community needs without requiring excessive time or resources from individual members.

Through this structure, members have formed healthcare, housing, childcare, and farming cooperatives, as well as savings clubs, social security organizations, and educational institutions such as information technology training centers. The organizing of support services for poor women by poor women is a challenge, and capacity-building is a consistent focus of the organization. But the struggle has also created a powerful and resilient network, and deep-rooted organizational capacity across SEWA’s many initiatives.

SEWA’s strategy has two main components: struggle and development. The struggle is against a society and an economic system that holds back women through traditional systems of patriarchy, class, and caste. This struggle in turn fosters development, as learning to collectively resist oppression and fight for justice as a group of workers naturally leads into developing alternative economic and social structures.

The organization itself initially grew out of a partnership with the Textile Labor Association (TLA), which was set up with Mahatma Gandhi’s encouragement in 1918. While there were significant breaks with the TLA after the first decade, the Gandhian legacy remains SEWA’s guiding force. It follows the principles of satya (truth), ahimsa (non-violence), sarvadharma (integrating all faiths, all people), and khadi (promotion of local employment and self-reliance). These principles are closely tied with the needs and priorities of SEWA’s members and inform SEWA’s daily activities.

Groups of anti-caste and anti-capitalist activists have also pushed SEWA beyond the Gandhian legacy, toward adopting more clearly liberatory and anti-caste frameworks in its organizational mission and structure. In addition, as SEWA grows, its federated decision-making process has in some ways been strained by layers of representation, with some workers finding it difficult to raise concerns or have their needs prioritized within the structure. Rather than taking away from the path-breaking work of SEWA, these ongoing tensions represent an opportunity for SEWA to continue to redefine cooperation and collectivization. SEWA shows that large-scale cooperative organizations can have the flexibility and capacity to grow and adapt, thereby serving the changing needs of their members, communities, and the movement for labor rights and justice at large.

entries.title: Share Responsibility
entries.summary: We are responsible to each other and have shared responsibility for the whole.
entries.body:
How far does your circle of responsibility extend? To your household? Your neighbors? Your country? What is your responsibility to people on the other side of the world? What happens when we extend our shared circle of responsibility to include all of humanity, the earth, and life itself?

If we are to bring about broad social change, our circles must be so much bigger than they are right now. They must include people who have migrated to our communities, people who pray in different ways than we do, and people who hold different values and political perspectives. In a global economy, we have to pay attention not just to the people with whom we interact most directly and most often, but also to those who grow our food or eat what we grow, make the machines we depend on, or feel the effects of our decisions. We are human, so our circles will also include people who have violated community norms and caused harm, and those who they’ve harmed. Shared responsibility means we navigate this reality with practices that don’t throw anyone away.

Mutual aid, or working together to care for each other’s needs, is an expression of shared responsibility. There are times when we respond to the needs of others, and there are times when we are the ones in need. Communities are healthy when they welcome the contributions and value of all their members, not just a few.

When a cooperative business practices shared responsibility, it recognizes its impacts on the entire community and on the supply chain to which it belongs.Yes, it looks out for its members, but it also looks out for the land that it sits on, the community that shares this land, and the workers who extract or produce the materials that its business requires.

Sharing responsibility means that as we organize to build a better world, we don’t look away from the impact of the choices we make along the way. It also means that we pay attention to the choices others are faced with and support each other in making better options available for everyone. Grace Lee Boggs said, “You cannot change any society unless you take responsibility for it, unless you see yourself as belonging to it and responsible for changing it.”

entries.body: Elandria said: “Collective power is our communities’ ability to thrive. Power to me is a spiritual force that one has. It is what we are guided by.” Power sharing is an active process that requires trust. We must build the structures and relationships that enable trust and then we must work, every day, to maintain them. As the world around us changes—as regimes come and go; as we organize to claim positions of formal power; as floods, famines, or earthquakes shift the ground beneath our feet—we must already be figuring out how to work together. In a system based on hoarding power, choosing to build a world where power is shared will require us to work alongside unlikely allies, with whom we never imagined uniting to build a common future.

entries.title: Social Cooperatives
entries.summary: Through social cooperatives, people can care for each other within a framework of democratic con- trol and shared power.
entries.body:
In the 1980s, the Italian government implemented a range of austerity measures. These included reductions of government services in response to financial crises and the rise of an ideology that favored private business over the public sector. This left devastating gaps in the provision of critical services like healthcare and shortages in opportunities for people with disabilities. The country’s cooperative movement responded by adapting old models of economic democracy to new challenges. Cooperators created a new type of cooperative, one designed specifically to serve a public mission.

Many kinds of social cooperatives have emerged across Italy in recent decades. Coopselios, for instance, is a large co-op in the Emilia Romagna region that provides health and social services. InGalera is a Milan restaurant run by incarcerated people, while the Girasoli restaurant in Rome mainly employs members with Down syndrome. Social co-ops are engaged in a wide range of initiatives, from recycling to fostering relationships between native Italians and immigrants. Some specialize in supporting people struggling with drug dependency, while others provide home-based care for the elderly.

Whereas cooperatives traditionally have just one type of member—such as their workers or their consumers—social co-ops can be multi-stakeholder. Care providers and their patients, for example, can co-govern the organization together. And governance is key. Unlike other kinds of nonprofit organizations, social co-ops are controlled by the people who participate in them directly, not just the people who fund them.

The government of Italy formally embraced social cooperatives in 1991, when it passed a law that established the model as a distinct kind of legal entity. Most of the revenue for social co-ops now comes from government contracts. But operations are managed by the people providing and receiving services, not a distant government bureaucracy. This way, public services can involve a deeper sort of democracy than government elections. Over 10,000 social co-ops are operating in Italy today.

When social co-ops work the way they should, their workers and those they serve in the community have a seat at the decision-making table, either through direct assemblies or elected board members. This is especially important for groups of people who tend to be ignored or dismissed by traditional service providers and government officials. In social co-ops, they are at the center.

Social co-ops have spread beyond their roots in Italy. Governments in France, Canada, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere have passed legislation to support the formation of social co-ops following the Italian model. But even in places that lack supportive legislation, the ethos can still take root. For instance, charitable nonprofits can organize their governance so that workers and other participants are in control, not just funders. Businesses can do the same, ensuring that they are accountable to the public good, not just to private investors. And governments can prioritize cooperatives when they grant healthcare and public service contracts.

For all of us, the social co-op tradition can serve as a reminder that we can take care of each other without sacrificing democratic participation. The work of care need not be paternalistic; it can and should empower everyone involved.

entries.title: Social Solidarity Clinics in Greece
entries.summary: In the fallout from the 2008 global financial crisis, the Greek government implemented severe austerity measures in exchange for a bailout from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund...
entries.body:
In the fallout from the 2008 global financial crisis, the Greek government implemented severe austerity measures in exchange for a bailout from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund. Public health spending fell nearly 43 percent between 2009 and 2017, leaving hospitals severely understaffed and underequipped. Outsourcing of maintenance activities to private contractors and budget cuts hindering access to basic sanitation supplies impaired the quality of healthcare afforded to patients, and even increased hospital infection rates. As the government continued to pull funding from public health institutions, the cost of healthcare services shifted to patients. Hiring of healthcare professionals in the public sector froze, pushing many to leave the country in search of opportunities abroad, while patients were left overpaying for services that could take months to access.

Today, the healthcare system continues to fail to meet the needs of Greece’s many immigrants and refugees, who face a myriad of barriers to accessing basic services. In the wake of a 2011 hunger strike of immigrant workers demanding basic rights, healthcare workers (many of whom also belonged to social movements in northern Greece) began to discuss how they might meet the need for affordable, accessible healthcare services. One of the first solidarity clinics to be established was in Thessaloniki, the second largest city in Greece. It opened its doors in November 2011 and has cared for tens of thousands of people living in northern Greece without access to care.

Clinics such as this one recognize the ongoing nature of the migrant and refugee crisis and have created permanent autonomous structures to meet a widespread need.

The initial goal of the solidarity clinic was to provide care for people in Greece who had no social security benefits or rights to access the healthcare system—among other reasons due to their immigration status—who at one point represented as much as 30 percent of the population. The pressures of the system-wide breakdown of healthcare and the accelerating refugee crisis have combined to create an ongoing and widespread need for free and accessible healthcare.

Social solidarity clinics operate democratically in departmental and general assemblies. Decision-making occurs through consensus rather than voting. These clinics are also completely independent from the government. Their funding comes from donations and even the equipment used in the clinics is donated by members of the public or retired doctors. Donations come from local people and organizations, and organizations abroad with similar values and motives.

The clinics’ centering of patients sets them apart from traditional healthcare providers. Clinic staff members do not consider their work a form of charity, but a form of commoning—providing shared resources to those who need them. The staff see themselves as equal to their patients and even avoid the term “patient” in favor of “incomer.” To challenge the power imbalance between doctors and patients, clinic staff aim to treat those they serve as whole people who are more than their illnesses or healthcare needs. Additionally, psychologists and doctors collaborate to provide a wider range of services than what would be standard for the specific issue for which someone entered the clinic.

Two seemingly contradictory visions guide the clinics. One is of a future world in which these clinics are no longer necessary because the healthcare system properly serves people and provides quality care to all who need it. The other vision is of an improved healthcare system that is supplemented by social solidarity clinics, which will remain an important service for all people due to their autonomy, democratic structure, and community-building focus.

At their highest point between 2012 and 2016, about 40 solidarity clinics and pharmacies operated across Greece, communicating closely with one another and carrying out four national assemblies to share practices and talk about principles and goals. In a radically different political environment, about 10 of them are still in operation today. As of 2023, several of these clinics are participating in the establishment of a network of collaborative and social clinics across Europe.

entries.title: Southern Journeys Collective
entries.summary: Southern journeys collective is a worker-owned craft cooperative that provides income and an outlet for self-expression for Black women in the Black Belt of Alabama and Georgia and the Mississippi Delta...
entries.body:
Southern journeys collective is a worker-owned craft cooperative that provides income and an outlet for self-expression for Black women in the Black Belt of Alabama and Georgia and the Mississippi Delta. It seeks to celebrate and sustain West African and rural African American culture, spirit, and art through the creation of textiles.

Southern Journeys was founded with support from the Southern Rural Black Women’s Initiative, which conducted listening sessions among approximately 1,000 women throughout Georgia and Alabama Black Belt and Mississippi Delta counties in 2004. The women expressed a desire to own their own businesses and find work that would allow them to use their sewing and quilting skills while evolving the cultural and artistic traditions that represent an important part of their heritage.

Piece sewing, couture, and quilting are integral to the cultures and livelihoods of the African American South. The contribution of African American women to American art, fashion, and industry is undervalued. Southern Journeys seeks to recognize the meaning and value of these contributions by creating a collective platform that company members and sewers will benefit from directly.

For many of the sewers at Southern Journeys, the art of sewing is deeply collective, cultural, and personal. It reminds one woman we interviewed of her childhood, when her grandmother allowed her to dig through a trunk of fabric and create whatever she wanted. For another, sewing was not just a hobby, it was a necessity when she and her family were evicted from a sharecropper farm. Her mother sewed all of her clothes based on images in department store catalogs. Another member described sewing as a means of economic livelihood; she worked in apparel factories for years before they shut down or the labor was outsourced overseas. Many Southern Journeys sewers have been and still are part of community quilting bees where they quilt and sew collectively.

The collective’s techniques of piece-sewing, quilting, and weaving have roots in West African and Southern traditions. Members help to preserve these cultures and their art practices as they create their own pieces. They designed their products to incorporate and showcase traditional patterns, which they refer to by names like Jacob’s Ladder, Wheel of Freedom, Middle Passage, Blues and Jazz Remix, and African Garden.

The connections to West African culture were also made tangible through Southern Journeys’ relationship with a women’s collective in Ghana, from which it bought handdyed fabric, and the company’s ongoing commitment to purchase African textiles directly or from Black-owned businesses. Upcycled feed sacks and burlap, as well as hand-dyed fabrics, are all materials that give a unique quality to Southern Journeys’ products. The group is committed to sustainability; many pieces are made from reused denim, recycled fabrics, and vintage clothing. While many of the worker-owners had prior sewing experience at the start of the cooperative, the Southern Rural Black Women’s Initiative facilitated technical training for Southern Journeys members so they could create cohesive styles and collections.

Philanthropic organizations like the Kellogg Foundation and Mary Reynolds Babcock Foundation were instrumental in funding the technical assistance that helped Southern Journeys get started. A myriad of other groups and individuals contributed to the collective to develop in its early stages, and partnerships with retailers and cultural festivals across the United States allowed Southern Journeys’ crafts to achieve widespread recognition and reach.

Southern Journeys fulfills its promises of fair wages and meaningful work for its members through its organizational structure. It is a limited-liability company that functions as a worker-owned cooperative, drawing members from across three states. It is part of a long legacy of African American cooperative networks that provide necessary resources, economic opportunities, and community assets for marginalized communities. The cooperative also sees its work as a mode of community-building, generating shared prosperity and cultural value.

Southern Journeys honors achievements and events of the past while making space for creativity through crafting. The products are more than socially responsible consumer goods—they are an innovative form of self-expression, keeping cherished traditions alive.

entries.title: Sustainable Resources Management in Nepal
entries.summary: The forests of Nepal are essential for the balance of the region’s ecosystem, the health of the economy, and the livelihoods of local people...
entries.body:
The forests of Nepal are essential for the balance of the region’s ecosystem, the health of the economy, and the livelihoods of local people.

Historically, Indigenous people of Nepal participated in decentralized management of the forests, with codes ensuring that only local people used their resources and did so responsibly and sustainably. Many areas that are prone to erosion were conserved and protected with the active involvement of local people. Under the National Forest Privatization Act of 1957, people who relied on the forests for their livelihood lost their usage rights. But as the forests began to suffer from illegal exploitation, the government redistributed these rights, officially recognizing community forestry practices in the 1988 Master Plan for the Forestry Sector.

The programs implemented through this plan delegated legal management responsibility to the local people, which has ensured that they have access to forest goods and services for their basic needs. Such practices have grown through the implementation of community forestry programs in Nepal. Local people also have ample opportunity to participate in different types of skill-based training for the development and promotion of the forest. Because of this, the community forest program in Nepal is a source of national pride for conservation, protection, and sustainable management of the forest. Around 22,000 community forests covering more than 2.2 million hectares are managed by community users throughout the country. In total, about 35 percent of the country’s total population is directly involved in managing Nepal’s forests.

The concept of sustainability in the forestry sector has evolved from a previously limited understanding. Sustainability is now understood as multipurpose management of the forest in a way that doesn’t diminish and degrade the resources or services it provides to local people.

The results of this shift are evident: better forest conditions, increased community participation, new sources of income, and community development and institution building at a grassroots level. Community development activities support schools, health centers, and infrastructure including irrigation, roads, and bridges.

Scholarships for students from poor households and the active inclusion of poor and marginalized women have further contributed to the community’s achievement of sustainable development goals. According to the community forestry guidelines, 50 percent of Community Forestry User Groups’ (CFUG) total income is distributed to entrepreneurship development and women’s empowerment efforts, 25 percent is allocated to sustainable forest management, and the remaining 25 percent to social development. The participation of women in decision-making processes and sustainable resource-management activities is key to the success of the community forest programs.

Nevertheless, participants in community forestry programs still face challenges. To address these issues, the Federation of Community Forestry Users Nepal (FECOFUN) formed in 1995 to advocate for the rights of community forest groups throughout the country.

FECOFUN is a network established to ensure and promote the rights of community forest users through advocacy, lobbying, policy development, and networking at national and international levels. It works to uphold the values of inclusive democracy, gender balance, social justice, and biodiversity conservation. FECOFUN supports the process of forming user groups, preparing operational plans, and maintaining CFUG accounts. Additionally, it builds the capacity of local and district leaders and chapters. FECOFUN is now the authentic and consolidated voice of grassroot communities’ forestry rights and a political actor in democratizing natural resource governance in Nepal. Because of its extensive network—CFUGs are present in all 77 forest districts of the country—FECOFUN has become the official body for communicating forest and natural resource management policies, regulations, laws, directives, treaties, press releases, and research outcomes across Nepal.

FECOFUN also contributes directly and indirectly to the Sustainable Development Goals established during the 2015 United Nations General Assembly. Evidence demonstrates that community forestry has contributed to poverty reduction, environmental conservation, gender equality, primary education, and partnership for development. These outcomes are testimony that the community-based approach to resource management supports goals of environmental conservation and improves the wellbeing of communities in Nepal.

entries.title: Take the right risks
entries.summary: We all have different boundaries, and we support each other to experiment and take risks while taking care of ourselves.
entries.body:
How much are we willing to risk in our fight for a better world? In every situation and at every moment, we each have something different at stake. We each have different things to gain and lose, and different levels of vulnerability to the consequences of our actions and the actions of our community members.

Those who are privileged can take big risks without having to worry much about the consequences; others are seen by those in power as expendable. Collective institutions like unions protect us against individual risk, building the people power to allow us to stand up to injustice as one.

Knowing when and what to risk means being realistic about what is needed. Often, you can try something only once; if it is unsuccessful, the chance may not come again. If you are trying to organize your neighbors to start a food cooperative, but there are already several food cooperatives in the area, then this is probably not taking a “right risk” with your community’s resources.

Taking the right risks also requires recognizing that failure might be more harmful to some people than to others. The consequences of risks are often carried more heavily by people who are more likely to be harmed or criminalized by those in power on the basis of race, gender, class, religion, or sexuality. Those in privileged positions can choose to assume more risk, and privilege can be a valuable tool when leveraged strategically in support of the collective. For example, in a group starting a collective enterprise, those with more money might take on financial risks like guaranteeing a loan.

Taking the right risks can make heroes, but it can also make enemies. For people who hold different beliefs from their family and friends, speaking out and fighting against oppression may mean losing relationships. Or, it could just mean some difficult conversations over dinner. Some people will be celebrated, and some will never have their stories told. These are decisions that can affect our whole lives, so every one of us should be allowed to define for ourselves the risks we are willing to take. This means equipping ourselves and others with the information we need to understand what we are risking.

We need to get better at motivating people to take risks and support and honor them when they do. Our strong relationships can empower us to risk, and so can our own determination to make a better world. We risk for ourselves, for our children, for the planet, and to grow our communities and be whole. We need to recognize where the front lines are, and celebrate those who take risks at the edges of their own comfort and ability. This might involve building ritual around risk-taking—with ceremony, special clothes, or the stories that bring our communities together.

One way or another, we will need to grapple with fear. The political or economic climate will never be perfect for transformation. At a certain point you have to take the leap, to be both ambitious and realistic, and reach for as much as you can. But it is less dangerous to leap when you’ve considered what you are up against. Taking risks usually means facing obstacles. At the end of the day, if your community or your group is committed to facing them together, taking risks can make you even stronger than you already are.

entries.title: Taking Back The Water System in Ramos Arizpe
entries.summary: Ramos Arizpe is a medium-sized city in the north of Mexico, about three hours’ drive from the Texas border...
entries.body:
Ramos Arizpe is a medium-sized city in the north of Mexico, about three hours’ drive from the Texas border. According to the 2020 census, its population was 122,243, with the vast majority living in the city’s urban area. Ramos Arizpe is located north of Saltillo, the capital of the state of Coahuila, and it houses more than half of the industries located in the metropolitan area of Saltillo.

From the beginning, the process leading to the privatization of the Ramos Arizpe water system was not transparent. In July 2012, Mayor Ramon Oceguera presented to the city council structural problems with the local water system. Because these problems caused operational and administrative failures, Oceguera said it had been determined that a public-private partnership would be established to work on the required structural changes. He did not specify who had determined this, though local press claimed that both the State Governor, and the State Secretary of Urbanism, Water and Land Planning, Oscar Pimentel—who was Saltillo’s mayor when that city’s water system was privatized in 2001—participated in formulating this plan. Although Mayor Oceguera promised that this process would respect the community, he did not inform or consult with citizens at any time.

The joint venture, called Aguas de Ramos Arizpe (AGRA), received control over the water system in October 2012. Its ownership was divided among the Ramos Arizpe municipality (owning 51 percent); Aguas de Saltillo (AGSAL), a subsidiary of Aguas de Barcelona, a multinational corporation based in Spain (owning 48 percent); and the Coahuila state government (owning 1 percent). The new company began operations on January 1, 2013. AGRA’s profit motive was evident right from the start. All consumption and service rates were doubled immediately to bring them in line with those in Saltillo. The minimum consumption rate was increased for users who did not have a meter (who were the majority). Water bills increased up to four times their original cost. Users were saddled with new fees for meter and household water intake replacements. Debts demanded by AGRA were exorbitant, up to tens of thousands of Mexican pesos. Users with more than two months’ debt were disconnected from services and charged a reconnection fee of approximately five times the previous minimum monthly rate.

During the 15 months of its administration, AGRA did not meet the city council’s explicit requests to guarantee the quality and supply of drinking water, ensure that tariffs were not significantly increased, and reduce leaks. The social cost of the utility privatization, meanwhile, was very high. A significant number of users filed complaints and legal processes (amparos) for violations of the human right to water.

When mayoral elections were held in July 2013, all candidates received a citizen petition asking them to remunicipalize the water system if they were elected, and all pledged to comply. Ricardo Aguirre won the election and was sworn in on January 1, 2014. The city council approved the remunicipalization of the system at its first session. On April 11, the new Ramos Arizpe Municipal Water Company (COMPARA) assumed control.

Efforts to remunicipalize the Ramos Arizpe water system did not come without challenges. The private partner, AGSAL, resisted surrendering its ownership share, as it was a very profitable business with huge financial compensation for company officials. AGSAL finally agreed to withdraw after being promised 24 million pesos (about 1.2 million US dollars) in exchange for shares that cost them 8 million pesos, only 15 months earlier.

Today, the remunicipalized water company is in a reasonably healthy financial position. COMPARA has drilled new wells and provided maintenance for existing ones. Community members are more satisfied; there have been no demonstrations against COMPARA by Ramos Arizpe inhabitants.

At the same time, due to scarce rainfall in recent years, supplying adequate water continues to be a problem. The main areas of improvement remaining for COMPARA concern the technical and administrative aspects of the company: physical leaks are still common; “potable” water quality is not very good; batch water distribution is common; and, the need to increase the participation of informed community members in the administrative council.

Despite these challenges, COMPARA remains an example in Mexico and throughout the world of what is possible when communities get organized and demand public ownership of their utilities.
entries.authorBio: Tobon de Garza is a member of the NGO Saltillo Water Users Association AUAS, who coached Ramos Arizpe citizens during their fight against Aguas de Saltillo. entries.title: Tandas
entries.summary: A tanda is an informal finance circle that is based on trust and community relationships. It is used by people all over the world and allows its participants access to cash that they can use to improve their lives.
entries.body:
Many communities around the world don’t trust financial institutions and governments. Many people, especially in the Global South, do not even have a savings bank account. Instead, communities have developed other ways to save money and take out loans. One method is through a community-based practice called *tanda* in Latin America, *susu* in West Africa and the Caribbean, *jam’eya* in much of the Arab World, *paluwagan* in the Philippines, and hundreds of other terms across different parts of the globe.

A tanda is when a group of friends, family, neighbors, or even colleagues pool their money together to help each other either save or borrow. For example, a group of six people might commit to paying $200 every week for six weeks, and then each receive a lump sum of $1,200 once during a six-week period. A tanda may also be organized if a community member is in a sudden need for cash due to a medical emergency, an upcoming event, or a purchase beyond what they could normally afford. Those in need will get access to a cash loan upfront and repay it later through their contributions. Others use it as a saving opportunity.

To organize a tanda, you first need to decide on who the participants are and how many. Then, as a group, you will decide on the amount that each person will pay and the frequency (which might be weekly, monthly, yearly, or otherwise).You will also decide the order in which people will get paid; it could be through a random draw or by order of urgency and need. Finally, you need to pick someone who will coordinate the tanda, which involves collecting and distributing payments.You can also add any additional rules that the group agrees on, such as that money will be pooled at weekly meetings or processes for exiting a tanda and swapping turns.

Traditional banking services often require credit history, monthly fees, lengthy forms, and identity screenings. These can be barriers to low-income communities, immigrants, or people who work in the informal economy. Tandas offer a flexible, transparent, and simple banking alternative to many community members who don’t have access to formal financial services.

When you participate in a tanda, you are also participating in a trust-building exercise. Oftentimes, people participate because they trust the organizer, and gradually they build trust with each other. Because of this, tandas offer a more comfortable space for a collective financial experience when compared to banks, given the participants work directly with their peers rather than with bankers, who have more power and authority and an incentive to exploit.

The beauty of this communal practice is that the space and trust created through a tanda encourages people to have vulnerable conversations about their finances and support each other in planning and budgeting. It helps break the taboo that many communities have around financial planning or discussing money. Additionally, technologies like video chat and mobile cash payments enable people to organize tandas across borders.

One criticism of tandas is that there are no mechanisms to prevent people taking advantage of each other. However, this criticism ignores the weight that relationships and societal expectations have on people’s behavior. Studies show that it is rare that tanda participants miss payments, likely because tandas are rooted in trust and relationships—this communal aspect serves as a form of accountability.

Many people find it easier to be disciplined with their savings if they are committed to a group or know that people are depending on their contribution. Also, some people will spend money if it’s laying around, so keeping it held in a communal fund can prevent needless spending. More importantly, the collective nature of the tanda offers an economy rooted in community, rather than in individualism, and in relationships rather than transactions.
entries.guidesBio: Baena is co-director of Siembra NC, a Latine political organization in North Carolina. She has worked with immigrant communities to develop power-building strategies sin, contra y desde el estado (outside, against and inside the state), of which tandas are an important building block.

entries.title: The Co-operative University of Kenya
entries.summary: The co-operative university of Kenya is a leading center for quality cooperative education, training, research, and consultancy...
entries.body:
The co-operative university of Kenya is a leading center for quality cooperative education, training, research, and consultancy. It was chartered as a public institution in 2016. Long before that, the college played a vital role in training and cultivating the co-operative movement in Kenya and other African countries. The first form of what eventually became the university started in 1952, during British colonial rule. Until 1964, it was known as the East African School of Co-operation, serving Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. As the three countries gained independence, each established their own cooperative colleges. The Co-operative College of Kenya was officially established in 1967. It was a semi-autonomous government agency under the Ministry of Co-operative Development and Marketing. In 2011, it became the Co-operative University College of Kenya, a constituent college of Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, before transitioning into an independent institution in 2016.

The cooperative movement in Kenya has a long history. In 1908, the first cooperative society in Kenya was founded by the colonial government. Colonial cooperatives were white-only, sidelining Africans from the mainstream economy. This remained largely unchanged during the struggle for independence.

When Kenya finally gained independence from British colonial rule in 1963, cooperatives became a central element in the post-colonial development plan, which saw the enactment of the first national cooperative policy in 1966. This led to the formation of the Co-operative College of Kenya to promote good management practices in cooperatives. It began in Nairobi with 40 students before the construction of the present campus in Karen, outside Nairobi proper. On June 18, 1970, the first president of the Republic of Kenya, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta, laid the foundation stone of the new college. President Kenyatta stressed in his remarks at the ceremony that “education and training are the surest road to overall efficiency in the business activities of the cooperative movement.”

With an increased need for cooperative education, the college continued to grow through the 1970s and ’80s. It expanded its role as a national institute for the training of staff for cooperative societies and unions, as well as for government officers who help to supervise cooperatives through the Ministry of Co-operative Development. Currently, the cooperative economy in Kenya accounts for about half of the country’s GDP, with significant numbers of cooperatives across every sector of the economy and half of Kenyans generating their livelihood through cooperatives. About 30 percent of cooperatives are agricultural; more than half are savings and credit cooperatives (SACCOs) that provide some of the only financial services in rural areas.

Compared to conventional business schools, studying at the Co-operative University of Kenya stands out; every student who joins the university for any degree program must study a unit or two in cooperative philosophy. The institution is also known to be the only college in Kenya with a savings and credit cooperative society that is fully owned and operated by students.

In 2005, the college launched its first degree program in collaboration with Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology. In 2012, the college established what would become its two foundational degree programs: a bachelor’s in cooperative business and a bachelor’s in commerce.

Between 2011 and 2016, the institution formed strategic linkages and networks of exchange with cooperative higher-education institutions around the world, including in Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Spain. The university college also entered into memoranda of understanding with Rwanda, South Africa, South Sudan, and Ethiopia, and it has continuously provided their cooperative sectors with technical support and staff training.

When the Co-operative University of Kenya was formally established in 2016 by Uhuru Kenyatta, it became the first university in the world entirely devoted to the cooperative movement. Today, it offers 14 degree programs, including a number at master’s level, and has over 150 faculty members. It serves about 7,000 students, both on campus and through a robust online-learning model. Currently, as the university grows, it houses three schools: the School of Co-operatives and Community Development, the School of Business and Economics, and the School of Computing and Mathematics. The university’s growth reflects how cooperative education can encompass all aspects of economic life.

entries.title: The Commons
entries.summary: When we take care of the earth, it takes care of us.
entries.body: We belong to the world. The world does not belong to us. We must understand our relationships with the land and water, the air and sky, medicine, knowledge, and all non-human life as ones of stewardship, not ownership. This means we must take care of our shared resources. The commons will only survive if we nourish it. We are led by Indigenous communities who have been fighting for many generations to defend and extend the commons, creating relationships rooted in cooperating with the earth, rather than exploiting it. Even though capitalism tells us that competition is the fundamental way of life, human history is also a history of cooperation. To survive we must relearn this lesson and tear down the walls that have been raised to hoard resources, so that we can share and contribute to the earth’s abundance.

entries.title: Travel Many Paths
entries.summary: There are lots of ways to get free.
entries.body:
There is no one path to a solidarity economy. Creating different economic practices requires creativity, a willingness to experiment, and the humility to fail and try again.

When a solution is working, it can be tempting to think that it is the only way, and to stop believing in or supporting anything else. But there are no easy answers in this work. Just because something is working in one community doesn’t mean that it will work elsewhere. Nor does it mean that it’s the only—or even the best—way to solve a certain problem.

When we elevate one path above others, we can become overly invested in the success of that path and less open to critical feedback. This is a losing strategy. Every solution deserves our loving critique and patience, especially the ones with the most promise. Any beautiful solution should welcome this kind of scrutiny. If not, it will eventually fail to live up to its expectations anyway.

We need to weave many different strategies together to solve our biggest problems. Trying to create one grand solution is more likely to fail. Building multiple solutions that reinforce one another increases the resilience of the whole. As conditions change, diversity creates more opportunities for adaptation.

Part of practicing resilience is learning to be comfortable with seeing others do things differently. This requires humility, respecting that other people may have answers that we don’t. Communitiy approaches to this work will be impacted by local cultures and histories. Some will be more willing to use direct action. Some will be more likely to work with governments or enter into strategic partnerships with large companies. Everyone will use different words. As long as the choices they’re making are not a major threat to our people and our places, many different approaches are worth considering.

Even within a single community, individuals and groups may take different paths to achieve shared goals. This can produce competitiveness, especially in our capitalist context. But we can also recognize that experimentation contributes to the knowledge and experience of the community, which gets passed on and makes it stronger. As long as a path doesn’t actively get in the way of other paths, or oppose our values, we should give it the chance to grow and flourish. Some paths will succeed. Many will fail. The best will make more room for other solutions to be possible. Our job is to learn from all of it and apply that learning to the new paths we travel together.

entries.title: vTaiwan
entries.summary: In the evening hours of March 18, 2014, a group of students occupied Taiwan’s parliament...
entries.body:
In the evening hours of March 18, 2014, a group of students occupied Taiwan’s parliament. Earlier that evening, behind closed doors, the Taiwanese government passed a controversial trade deal with China. A media watchdog group covering the news from the session shared the information, and it quickly spread online; soon the parliament was barricaded and surrounded by peaceful protesters. A local group of civic hackers called g0v (pronounced “gov-zero”) set up digital infrastructure to broadcast the proceedings from the occupied parliament to the nation. This was the beginning of the Sunflower Movement.

For 22 days, hundreds of thousands of people worked together to envision and demonstrate how an open, transparent decision-making process could function. They organized small group discussions and held public teachins in the streets, passing microphones to hear all voices and clustering sticky notes on poster boards to record divergent and convergent points. After half a million people on the street, plus many more online, had settled on a set of demands, students presented these to the government to illustrate a democratically derived decision.

The government took note. A few months later, government minister Jaclyn Tsai came to a g0v hackathon, and asked the civil society group to create “a process to allow the entire society to engage in rational discussion.” In two weeks, the vTaiwan platform launched. While not every radical’s perfect solution, it was an important step for the government to begin collaborating with civic hackers, and civil society at large, to run a digital rule-making process that involves diverse voices. A g0v participant, Audrey Tang, was appointed minister without portfolio by the Taiwanese government in 2016, taking on the unofficial English-language title of “Digital Minister.”

Rather than demonstrating for or against an issue, the critical intervention of those participating in the Sunflower Movement was to demonstrate how to facilitate collective sense-making—how to help large groups make sense of complex challenges democratically.

A generation of Taiwanese came of age in a democracy that was only as old as the internet. The island of 23 million people has been fighting for decades to protect its self-governance against incursions from mainland China. Taiwanese youth have also learned facilitation techniques from members of their parents’ generation who were veterans of the Chinese democracy movement. Internet connectivity is even more widely accessible than in the United States. But today, amid the rising global wave of autocracy and the consolidation of power by mainland China, Taiwan faces threats to its autonomy, just like many other Asian democracies. Pro-democracy protests were widespread before the pandemic, and democracy continues to be an active struggle in Taiwan, not just a legacy to be defended.

vTaiwan is not a singular application, and the platform does not only operate online. As an open community, vTaiwan runs a consultation process that brings together the relevant stakeholders around an issue. This process begins when an issue gets a certain threshold of votes on Join, a platform that lets anyone propose topics for deliberation. Issues can also be raised in person at weekly open sessions. Once an issue is identified, a facilitator agrees to steward the issue through the multi-step process.

Facilitators are trained volunteers. They gather facts from stakeholders, workshop the description of an issue, and share an initial set of varied position statements online. Tens of thousands of people can engage through a cardstyle interface that presents statements and offers the opportunity to respond with “agree,” “disagree,” “pass,” or “write my own.” vTaiwan uses a tool called Polis to generate visualizations that preserve minority and majority positions.

After this initial stage, a volunteer facilitator leads the stakeholder group through a series of open conversations to draft a proposition to legislators. Picture it like this: The facilitator stands in the center of a U-shaped seating arrangement. She wears a 360-degree live-streaming camera on her shoulder and holds a tablet that displays digital post-it notes from people across the country. Using dynamic facilitation, she organizes points by type and synthesizes points with high levels of consensus. This “facilitation as civic infrastructure” results in an effective deliberation that can swiftly settle deadlocked issues, such as how to sell alcohol online or regulate Uber. Since 2015, more than two dozen cases have been discussed through the vTaiwan process, and 80 percent of them have led to some decisive government action. This is a model that presents a direct alternative to partisan deadlock through a process of problem solving and listening.

By combining accessible technology with facilitation, vTaiwan lays out a blueprint for governance and democracy in the networked age. vTaiwan demonstrates a new means by which the public and government can work together openly to find solutions that satisfy the majority. It makes the dream of a responsive government and collective sense-making a reality, and it doesn’t require complex or expensive tools. Effective facilitation, transparency, and inclusive processes can synthesize thousands of diverse voices and take them from a sphere of heated debate to produce collective outcomes. The goal, according to Tang, is a society capable of “listening at scale.”
entries.authorBio: Barry is co-founder of Public Lab and TreeKIT, founding board member of the Computational Democracy Project and 596 Acres, advisor to Extinction Rebellion’s Future Democracy Hub, and a nobody with g0v. Sarahe is an organizational design consultant, facilitator, and strategist who has worked with Data & Society, Ford Foundation, Open Society Foundation, and Media Lab Prado. Barry and Sarahe, with other team members, co-organized the first English language vTaiwan Open Consultation and Participation Officers Training in NYC.

entries.title: Zero Waste
entries.summary: Communities around the world are finding alternatives to corporate waste management that demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of zero waste systems, wherein materials that are not needed are either repurposed, composted, or recycled.
entries.body:
Conventional waste management systems are damaging to the health of communities and the environment. The more waste that we send to landfills or incinerators, the more we pollute our air, water, and land, and the more cancer, asthma, and other adverse health consequences we create for those living nearby. Dump sites are often built in or around low-income residential neighborhoods, meaning that poor communities and people of color are much more likely to suffer the effects of dangerous environmental conditions created by waste processing. The need for zero waste is, therefore, an issue of social and environmental justice.

The scale of environmental injustice resulting from waste management practices is global. North Americans consume over 326 pounds of plastic per person per year, while for Southeast Asians the figure is about 53 pounds. Yet the negative health and environmental impacts of waste are not as visible in the Global North as they are in the South, because more money is invested in hiding waste through landfills, incinerators, and exporting. Though recycling is an important component of transitioning to zero waste systems, it doesn’t address the underlying problems of overconsumption and disposability. What’s not buried, burned, or recycled in the North is exported through the waste trade. Canada and the United States ship vast quantities of plastic waste to other countries, mainly in Asia, under the guise of recycling.

The Philippines, for instance, has had to contend with the consequences of waste from wealthier countries, as multinational companies based in the Global North have saturated the Philippine market with products in single-use plastics. Those companies and their home countries shirk the burden of managing their waste, and the hazards that the waste brings, particularly for the low-income communities that live near the dumping grounds. Some impacts include increased risks of flooding from clogged storm drains, threats to the livelihoods of people who rely on fishing, toxic emissions from burning plastic, dangers for wildlife that ingest plastic, and health hazards from small pieces of plastic entering human food systems. Meanwhile, the production of plastic requires fossil fuels that exacerbate climate change, the effects of which are felt disproportionately in the Global South.

In response, Fort Bonifacio, a village-sized district in Metro Manila, decentralized its waste management system and completed a material recovery facility in 2011 that composts food and stores recyclables for resale. This reduced waste by 95 percent and created new jobs locally. The new waste workers earn three times more than they would have as informal waste pickers by getting a fixed minimum income from the city, in addition to any revenue they receive from selling the recyclables and compost. Waste workers still face many hardships—such as social marginalization and the lack of a social safety net. But it makes a real difference when governments formalize these workers, pay them a living wage, and engage with them to help steer the governance of a zero waste system.

This effort is part of a global zero waste movement that seeks to extend the lifecycle of products and eliminate the injustices in prevailing waste disposal systems. Zero waste doesn’t mean that there won’t be anything to throw away; the goal is to reduce waste wherever possible by reducing the production and consumption of materials that turn into waste. It also means that discarded materials will either be reused, repurposed, repaired, composted, or recycled. Zero waste is about rethinking the usefulness of waste materials and organizing their circulation differently.

Also in the Philippines, the city of San Fernando in Pampanga has over 100 small-scale material recovery facilities. Before implementing a zero waste program, the city spent 70 million pesos (approximately $170,000) in waste hauling and tipping fees alone. Since the program began, waste has been collected from all residents and costs have dropped to just 12 million pesos per year, leaving more funding for education and health services. Cleaner canals have also reduced the mosquito population, resulting in a steep decline in dengue fever cases.

While zero waste practices do not depend on state regulation, legislation can influence industrial choices over products and packaging and can prompt action toward better waste management practices. Further, when initiatives are built and managed by communities, rather than imposed upon them by governments, power shifts into the hands of locals and away from waste-promoting companies.

No single person can challenge corporate waste systems alone, but when community groups come together, they can create shifts. Zero Waste Boston in the United States, for example, is a coalition of environmental groups that developed a worker-owned waste management cooperative, Cooperative Energy, Recycling, and Organics (CERO). CERO collects food waste from restaurants and other establishments and transports it to local farms outside of Boston for composting. In Baltimore, what started as a youth-led campaign to stop the installation of a new incinerator near their school is now a collaboration with the city to move toward zero waste.

Many companies have distorted the concept by claiming to be a zero waste organization while failing to enforce basic zero waste precepts like a prohibition of trash incineration. The success of zero waste efforts requires creative, grassroots solutions to manage waste and move power to the communities most affected by failing waste management systems. Amplifying local stories from all over the world is crucial in changing false narratives, preventing harmful waste management practices, and avoiding community health and environmental catastrophes. From policy to grassroots action, in the Global North and South, everyone’s efforts can move us toward a zero waste future.
